text:
⚖️ 800 Posts: The Names, the Inventories, and the Unfinished Reckoning

Hungary’s 1944 seizure files name the Jewish owners whose possessions were taken from their homes. They record paintings, books, furniture and silver alongside addresses, measurements, crate markings and instructions for transfer. More than eighty years later, that paperwork can reconnect a surviving object with the household from which it was taken—and help establish whether it was ever returned.

Across 800 posts, the Holocaust Art Recovery Initiative has pursued those connections. Working principally through Reels 143–145 of the Hungarian microfilm collection at the Zekelman Holocaust Center, HARI has examined the state’s own record of dispossession alongside family histories, museum catalogues, auction records and surviving objects. This final installment brings that work together: the people identified, the transfers documented, the possible matches awaiting examination, and the evidence still needed to resolve their histories.

For Clara Garbon-Radnoti, the connection between an inventory and a family was painfully personal. While examining the microfilm, she recognized her widowed aunt’s name and address. The possessions included a rolling pin, four kitchen chairs and a kitchen table. Her aunt and the aunt’s young daughter did not survive deportation. Clara sent the record to the cousin who had survived. Behind an administrative entry was a home she knew—and people whose absence no inventory could measure.

The same attention belongs to every household in these files, whether its possessions included an Old Master painting, a scientific library or the furnishings of an ordinary room. A surviving inscription, an unusual measurement or a confiscation number can provide a lead across decades of missing history. Following it requires three distinct inquiries: Is this the same object? Was it returned to its owner or successors? What does its subsequent ownership history establish? Evidence of restitution and lawful sale matters as much as evidence of seizure. A persuasive match begins that investigation; it does not settle the claim.

The legal developments of 2026 make completing these histories especially consequential. The April HEAR Act amendments changed the framework for covered Holocaust-era property claims, and the July remand of 26 Herzog claims reopened a path to further proceedings. Neither development supplies the missing ownership evidence. That work still depends on accessible files, careful examination and the participation of heirs and communities.

Eight hundred posts cannot exhaust the archive or resolve every claim. They can identify where the next inquiry should begin. A named owner, a documented taking and a plausible surviving object create a concrete reason to investigate. The institutions holding the objects and the remaining records have an essential part in what happens next.

📜 A SURVIVOR’S WORK MADE THE RECORD ACCESSIBLE

This undertaking rests on work that preceded the first HARI post. Professor Randolph L. Braham donated the microfilm collection to the Zekelman Holocaust Center in 1992. Hungarian Holocaust survivor Clara Garbon-Radnoti devoted a decade to its English finding aid and translated key material from Reels 143–145. Her work gave researchers a practical way into thousands of difficult Hungarian records. Librarian Feiga Weiss connected Clara with HARI () founder Jonathan H. Schwartz. Their collaboration was the subject of a January 29, 2019 Detroit News story, years before these online posts. The work began with a survivor reading the records of the society that had persecuted her and helping others understand what they contained.

The Zekelman Holocaust Center and the World Jewish Restitution Organization announced the online archive in February 2025. The Claims Conference–WJRO Looted Art & Cultural Property Initiative allocated funding for digitization and translation, with support credited to the Foundation “Remembrance, Responsibility and Future” and the German Federal Ministry of Finance.

HARI built on that preservation and translation work. The series brought individual pages into public discussion, connected bureaucratic entries to biographies, compared wartime descriptions with museum and auction records, and identified the further evidence needed to confirm or reject proposed matches. The underlying documents remain the authority; every interpretation must remain open to correction.

🏛️ THE MUSEUM DIRECTOR AND THE CONFISCATION ADMINISTRATION

Dénes Csánky simultaneously directed Budapest’s Museum of Fine Arts and served as government commissioner responsible for registering and safeguarding sequestered Jewish artworks. His commissioner’s office operated from the museum. The files show how cultural expertise became part of a state apparatus that identified, assessed, selected, inventoried, transported, and stored Jewish-owned property.

The correspondence connects national museums with finance authorities, police, municipalities, banks, libraries, teachers, dealers, restorers, and local museum personnel. The series followed instructions, requests for assistance, proposed allocations, inventories, transport arrangements, and receipts. Each records a different stage; together, they reveal how an administrative program reached into individual homes.

The language often emphasized preservation and “safekeeping.” Meanwhile, owners were being excluded from public life, forced from their homes, confined in ghettos, deported, and murdered. Protecting the physical condition of an object could coexist with destroying its owner’s control over it. A museum’s custody of a painting therefore has to be investigated alongside the circumstances in which that custody began.

👤 CULTURAL PROFESSIONALS MADE PARTICULAR CHOICES

The records repeatedly identify people whose other achievements are celebrated in cultural histories. HARI examined Elemér Kőszeghy’s role inside the Herzog Palace; Béla Darnay’s handling of material through the Balaton Museum; and András Soós’s involvement in Jewish reader lists and the subsequent selection and packing of books and artworks in Nagyvárad, now Oradea.

In Baja, painter and museum official Ferenc Miskolczy requested Jewish labor servicemen to collect confiscated objects. His own paintings also appear in the inventories of local Jewish collectors. The request documents his intention to use forced labor; it does not establish that the men were supplied. In Nagykanizsa, painter and art dealer László Bujdoss sought the authority and equipment needed to act as a local delegate, including a typewriter from confiscated property. In Békéscsaba, József Mokos’s work selecting Jewish-owned art was connected explicitly to enlarging the museum.

Other files expose proposals for the property’s use. Carpet specialist Béla Kiss reported submitting a list of 43 Jewish collectors and urged state possession of their carpets. Lajos Ujváry proposed using seized books to reward pupils. The Göcsej Association sought books, pictures, furnishings, and a house without payment to establish cultural institutions. Museum director Lajos Kiss, in Nyíregyháza, proposed selling rejected paintings to artists who could paint over them. These proposals reveal how readily dispossessed people’s belongings could be treated as resources for somebody else’s work.

Csánky’s own interventions extended beyond his Budapest office. The Losonc correspondence records his travel and his deputy’s demands for assistance. The Sepsiszentgyörgy files include directions to trace Jewish-owned artworks with police help. The series also examined his response to Emil Stein’s request for relief from anti-Jewish restrictions. These histories require attention to the acts recorded in each file, including the difference between a proposed action and a completed one.

🗺️ FROM THE CAPITAL TO REGIONAL DEPOTS

The geographical reach was extensive. In Pécs, Jewish-owned objects were gathered in the synagogue, and the files refer to a 146-page inventory. In Kassa, now Košice, correspondence connected the clearing of Jewish homes to museum custody. The Szeged dossier spans 101 microfilm slides across Reels 143 and 144. Baja supplies successive household inventories, allowing named families and addresses to be followed through the local operation.

The repeated appearance of Mihály Munkácsy’s name across inventories became a separate line of inquiry, including a church official’s report of a signed painting and instructions for taking it under seal through Szombathely. Each entry must be tested against its own owner, subject, medium, measurements, and custody record; the artist’s name alone cannot identify which surviving painting the file describes.

The series also examined records from Beregszász/Berehove, Munkács/Mukachevo, Ungvár/Uzhhorod, Nagyvárad/Oradea, Szabadka/Subotica, Losonc/Lučenec, Sepsiszentgyörgy/Sfântu Gheorghe, Nagykanizsa, Keszthely, Sopron, Győr, Kaposvár, Szolnok, and other towns. These records now cross national borders and languages. Historical place names, changing institutional names, and later transfers all affect where evidence can be found.

In Szombathely, architect and commissioner’s delegate János Tóth described five overcrowded depots on September 26, 1944. Furniture reached the ceilings. Porcelain lay in crates by the thousand. 843 carpets had been packed for an intended transfer to Budapest that was postponed. He reported “an unbelievable quantity of gold and silver” and anticipated museum-worthy objects among the silver before inspecting it. The report captures the scale of accumulated Jewish property and the officials’ concern with its potential institutional value. It does not establish the final destination of everything described. (Reel 145, slides 145–147.)

🖼️ HERZOG AND THE COLLECTIONS AROUND IT

The Herzog investigations became a major strand of the series. The files from Andrássy út 93, the Budafok cellars, and related locations connect the Herzog family with the histories of Kiss, Sváb, Weiss, Kornfeld, and Mauthner property. Those connections require object-by-object analysis: a shared address, crate, family relationship, or storage location does not make ownership interchangeable.

HARI examined paintings in these files and their later identifications and attributions, including works associated with El Greco, Giovanni Santi, Isenbrandt, Giampetrino, Goya, Renoir, Courbet, Alvaro Pirez, and others. The investigations included Santi’s Misericordia Domini, now catalogued in Budapest as The Man of Sorrows, inventory 51.799; the Isenbrandt triptych panels 9047/a–c; Giampetrino’s Christ Carrying the Cross, 58.2; and the histories surrounding El Greco’s Saint Andrew, 51.800, and the workshop Holy Family with Saint Anne, 50.755. Some cases concern previously published ownership histories; others concern proposed identifications or unresolved transfers. They cannot all be counted as new discoveries or completed recoveries.

The scope extended well beyond paintings. Herzog research addressed an Egyptian mummy mask, inventory 9818, for which published scholarship identifies Herzog provenance; a Late Bronze Age sword candidate at the Hungarian National Museum; jewelry, gems, and coins recorded in 259 numbered entries; and a wartime receipt for seven numbered furniture pieces associated with the Royal Hungarian Opera House. Other inquiries concerned an Egyptian necklace, sculpture, a terracotta or stucco Madonna, and further household and decorative objects.

These investigations ask more than where a celebrated painting hangs. They ask how a family collection was divided, how objects were relabeled or redistributed, which pieces were returned, and how later legal and institutional records account for the rest.

🔎 THE EVIDENCE THAT CAN CONNECT AN OBJECT TO ITS OWNER

The comparisons bring together attribution, subject, medium, dimensions, owner, address, condition, inscriptions, frame labels, crate marks, and receipts. Each supplies a different test. An inscription naming a former owner, a wartime photograph, and a close dimensional correspondence carry different kinds of evidentiary weight; they should be explained on their own terms.

An owner’s name on the reverse. A Glatz Transylvanian Village examined in the series bears an inscription connecting Mrs. Sándor Sváb with Andrássy út 93. Such marks can preserve a relationship omitted from a later catalogue. High-resolution photographs of the back of a painting—its verso—along with its frame, stretcher, labels, and stamps can therefore be as consequential as its frontal image.

A numbered label inside a book. Item 41 in Sándor Fleischl’s wartime library inventory was Wilhelm Müseler’s Geist und Antlitz der Gotik. A copy offered in 2026 bore both Fleischl’s ownership mark and the Government Commissioner’s label “Fleischl 41.” Author, title, binding, owner, and wartime item number converge on the surviving book. Its subsequent history, including whether it was returned after the war, remains to be reconstructed. (Reel 144, slides 432–441; Item 41 on slide 437.)

The Topers: a painting visible in the seizure’s publicity. HARI compared a May 20, 1944 Herzog crate entry for Goya’s Ivók, 101 × 79.5 cm, with The Topers at the North Carolina Museum of Art, inventory 56.13.1. Fundación Goya en Aragón publishes a size of 101 × 80 cm. The connection goes beyond measurements: Konstantin Akinsha’s 2011 study identifies the painting in the Herzog collection and reproduces a Magyar Futár photograph of Hungarian secret policemen with it. He also records its later reclassification as “in the style of Goya.” Wartime presence and the subsequent ownership chain are separate questions; the route to the Babcock Foundation and the museum still needs a documented account.

Other paintings in wartime photographs. HARI examined proposed identifications involving El Greco’s workshop, Alonso Cano, and Károly Brocky in Magyar Futár imagery. These photographs were produced in the setting of antisemitic seizure publicity. Read critically, they can help establish which works were present, alongside the inventories and receipts.

Brocky and the Kornfeld-marked crate. The 1944 record describes Woman in Black, oil on canvas, 76 × 47 cm, and damage to red drapery. The Hungarian National Gallery’s 50.572 matches the artist, subject, medium, and dimensions. The condition note supplies an additional test: whether conservation records and examination of the painting reveal a corresponding history.

Gerrit Dou and the Surányi inventory. A June 1944 entry records an Alabárdos, or halberdier, in Dr. Miklós Surányi’s collection: oil on panel, 66 × 51 cm. HARI compared it with the Museum of Fine Arts’ Dou, inventory 62.10, with the same dimensions and a closely corresponding subject. The Surányi research also examined the inventory’s Brueghel-follower Wedding against a Peasant Wedding catalogued as workshop of Marten van Cleve, inventory 7560.

Pieter Jansz. Quast and Mihály Vadász. The wartime Musical Company entry measures 49.2 × 36.5 cm. Budapest’s Merry Company Making Music, inventory 71.20, is catalogued at 49 × 36.5 cm. That close correspondence supplies a precise question for the museum’s acquisition and ownership records.

Alvaro Pirez and the “Blessing Christ.” A 1944 protocol’s early-fifteenth-century Italian panel, in tempera, has a painted surface of 91 × 59 cm. Budapest’s The Risen Christ, inventory 51.801, has a painted surface of 90.5 × 59.6 cm. The comparison demonstrates why research must distinguish the painted surface from the dimensions of an entire support or frame.

The Csetényi collection. Research extended from Rachel Ruysch and Jan van Os still lifes to a Sébastien Bourdon portrait candidate, a Triumphal March, and an eighteenth-century pastel compared with Portrait of Julia Czindery, inventory 9840. Principal inventories, secondary “selejt” lists, delivery records, and frame labels offer different routes into the same collection. A lesser administrative classification did not erase an owner’s rights. Postwar recovery and later dispersal make return and sale records essential to each object’s history.

Attribution changes can fragment a search. A work described under one artist’s name in 1944 may now be catalogued under a workshop, follower, or different painter. Titles change too. These revisions are not evidence of concealment, but they explain why a single artist-name search can miss a relevant object. Researchers must compare the composition, support, measurements, markings, and condition across successive descriptions.

🌍 BUDAPEST RECORDS, INTERNATIONAL QUESTIONS

The search extended into museums and markets far beyond Hungary. At the National Museum of Women in the Arts in Washington, D.C., a Ruysch floral still life, inventory 1986.282, measures 107.95 × 83.82 cm, compared with 107 × 82 cm in the Csetényi record. Another Csetényi inventory entry, a French seventeenth-century male portrait measuring 105 × 88 cm, was compared with Bourdon’s Portrait of a Man at the Art Institute of Chicago, published at 104.2 × 88.1 cm. In Canada, the Agnes Etherington Art Centre’s Koninck Panoramic River Landscape with Hunters, 55-005, measures 105 × 135 cm, against a wartime description of 105 × 136 cm. Each comparison narrows a research question; its differences and ownership gaps remain part of the test.

The Caravaggio Saint John the Baptist investigation followed a recurring 99 cm width from a 135 × 99 cm wartime entry into later auction comparisons. Width alone cannot uniquely identify a painting. Composition, support, alterations, old photographs, and the pre-auction ownership chain must be examined together.

Other inquiries reached Harvard’s Fogg Museum through a Tiepolo comparison; London through Rubens-related material; Madrid through a Machuca inquiry; New York through Schiele-related research; and Russian repositories through displaced books. Auction research followed works attributed to Hans Canon, Eugène Carrière, Auguste Lepère, and others through Vienna, Paris, Budapest, and additional markets.

The questions also extend to Lipót Fejér’s scientific library in Fukuoka. Kyushu University identifies 786 volumes as Fejér’s former books and records their purchase in 1965. Establishing which volumes, if any, passed through the documented wartime seizure requires the acquisition records and examination of the books themselves. A named collection abroad provides a place to investigate; it does not establish an unbroken confiscation-to-institution chain.

🏺 FURNITURE, ANTIQUITIES, TEXTILES, AND ORDINARY HOUSEHOLDS

The Hatvany-Deutsch files recorded paintings, textiles, furniture, books, arms, and military subjects. HARI compared a Renaissance-style chest from the Hatvan Castle inventory with Museum of Applied Arts inventory 61.332.1. The Lánchíd utca file documented distinct routes for books and objects sent to the Museum of Fine Arts and the military museum. Those separate lists and dates have to be preserved when reconstructing the household’s losses.

The series also followed the Kaszab, Weiser, Munther, Doroghy, Szilárd, Politzer, Littmann, Strauss, Dobay, and Madarassy-Beck records. Investigations included Thorma and Maticska paintings; Rippl-Rónai pastels; Iványi Grünwald’s Old Violinist; Zichy’s Scottish Torch Dance; a Napoleon death-mask candidate; a bronze Abduction of the Sabine Women plaque; a polychrome Saint Paul; and a small Madonna on copper examined against a Scarsellino attribution. Additional studies addressed works by Mednyánszky, Vastagh, Csók, Ligeti, and Markó.

Bank-safe openings, apartment inventories, and museum intake sheets brought these different media into the same documentary field. A ceramic, a carpet, a musical instrument, an archaeological object, and a room of furnishings could all carry a traceable ownership history. Their importance does not depend on appearing in an Old Master gallery.

The Jenő Lázár archaeological collection made the stakes especially clear: a museum could itself become the object of an inventory while its Jewish founder was in Auschwitz. The subsequent claim that the material was company property requires scrutiny alongside the circumstances of its creation and seizure. Institutional descriptions can obscure the person whose work assembled a collection.

📚 THE LIBRARIES: BOOKS, OWNERS, AND INTELLECTUAL LIVES

HARI’s library investigations followed individual books, entire private collections, manuscripts, scholarly working materials, synagogue libraries, and communal archives. They examined the Kornfeld, Fleischl, Hatvany-Deutsch, Gáspár, Fejér, and Kadelburg collections, as well as Jewish and Zionist libraries in Sopron and bulk book records elsewhere.

The Hatvany-Deutsch shelves placed art-historical monographs alongside The Children’s Book of Art. The inventory covered Rembrandt studies, a Vigée Le Brun monograph, and older books on subjects extending well beyond painting. The children’s volume supplies a different scale of cultural loss: the books through which a household could introduce another generation to art.

The record of Endre Gáspár’s library included a two-volume English Ulysses. He survived and produced the novel’s first complete Hungarian translation, published in 1947. The distinct Bernát Gáspár case concerned a library and literary manuscripts, including an English translation of Madách’s The Tragedy of Man. Bookplates, manuscript packets, crate counts, and library receipts can preserve an intellectual life that a generic entry for “books” conceals.

The Kornfeld library research followed successive removals and the later dispersal of books, including material associated with Russian repositories. The Sopron files showed Jewish writing and Jewish subjects singled out in the cataloguing process. Győr’s postwar records raised questions about tens of thousands of books and competing proposals for their allocation. A proposal to assign a library to an institution must be distinguished from proof that the assignment occurred.

🎨 ARTISTS AND OWNERS WHO CANNOT BE REDUCED TO INVENTORY ENTRIES

Lajos Kunffy wrote from the Tab ghetto about albums, photographs, and approximately 100 drawings that should go to the county museum if he died. After obtaining an exemption, he asserted his right to recover control of the material. The sequence preserves an artist’s intentions: a conditional bequest, a demand for return, and the continuing work for which he needed his archive. Those intentions must remain distinct from later accounts of wartime losses.

József Pécsi, the photographer, asked for advance notice so that he could be present when officials came to select and remove his antique furniture. András Novák, the applied-arts teacher and designer, was ordered to gather the artistic objects in his apartment into a lockable room, prepare their inventory himself, and preserve them pending official sealing. The letter threatened criminal liability for failing to comply. He survived to continue his design career; the letter records a moment when the state compelled him to prepare his own domestic surroundings for its control.

Móric Barát’s name appears beside 32 works in a Nagyvárad collection-center inventory. He was murdered at Auschwitz. HARI also examined works by Tibor Ernő, murdered at Dachau, and Paula Porter, murdered in 1944, whose Balaton appears in a sealed-apartment inventory from that year. These records can help reconstruct artistic legacies even where the present location of the works remains unknown.

The Klára Geréb investigation connected an artist and a Jewish family with the Dömötör Palace in Subotica, the building from which she was deported and which later became the municipal museum. It also examined a separate wartime ambition to enlarge the museum with seized Jewish art. The building’s later cultural use should make the earlier family history more visible.

Róza Grünwald’s inventory preserved a collection including Sándor Bihari’s Venetian Kitchen, which HARI compared with a later auction work. Károly Dénes’s sword bequest required a different distinction: his testamentary decision, made under persecution, could not simply be equated with later officials’ proposals or an applicant’s wish to buy seventeen swords. The owners’ choices, the coercion surrounding them, and subsequent dealings all belong in the record.

text:
This Anthropic IPO allocation strategy was suboptimal and myopic. I heard from many long-only firms that received zero shares and they were VERY annoyed.

You want to spread the allocation as much as possible across long-term oriented firms that invest on multi-year time frames. 

Giving them a starter position makes them much more likely to buy more in the aftermarket, rather than ticking them off.

Allocating more shares to hedge funds or rewarding friendly early VC firms that are more likely flip and already have massive exposure is not the best approach. 

Anthropic needs to think about building allies in the next chapter, not the past.

quoted_text:
My last day at NVIDIA, with warmth to carry forward

Yesterday was my last day at NVIDIA. I returned my equipment and badge, signed the paperwork, and just like that, it was done. It all happened so quickly and simply that it still feels a little unreal.

There were a few things I didn’t get to finish. My account access ended around noon—I’d expected to have until the end of the day, or at least until after signing the paperwork. Some goodbyes were left mid-conversation. I missed the chance to pick up a few keepsakes from the Gear Store. I didn’t even get to send the handover document I was halfway through writing.

Fortunately, I had already sent my farewell email and said goodbye to some friends. To anyone I didn’t get to reach, or suddenly stopped replying to: I’m sorry. I hope we can pick up those conversations outside work.

That evening, my colleagues threw me a farewell party, and for a little while, goodbye could take its time. We talked about everything that had happened recently, how life had been treating us, and what we hoped the future might hold. Thank you for giving me one more evening to remember—and so much warmth to carry into whatever comes next.

I’m leaving with a few unfinished things, but so many memories to keep. Wishing you all happiness, work you’re proud of, and good things ahead.

I’ll miss you, friends. Until our paths cross again.

Now of course, the reasons behind firing Jensen are extremely different, and could be fully justified even if we think Jensen is indespensible.

But it's very obvious that NVIDIA without Jensen is not really NVIDIA.

text:
黄仁勋事情路径可能正在朝着一个极具讽刺意味的方向演进：董事会投票赶走黄仁勋，股东再投票赶走董事会。

Business Insider刊文，认真分析了黄仁勋重返 $NVDA 的五条潜在路径：

1. 股东施压： 联合机构投资者，要求董事会重新考虑黄仁勋回归。

2. 年度股东大会： 动员股东反对现任董事连任，向董事会施压。

3. 提名新董事： 利用股东提名机制，逐步改变董事会内部力量对比。

4.全面代理权争夺战（Full Proxy Fight）： 推出一整套董事候选人名单，直接挑战现任董事会。

5. 特别股东大会： 联合满足持股门槛的股东，争取提前召开会议，推动董事会改组。

其中第四条不仅是一种理论上的法律可能性，而且存在相对清晰的实施路径。

具体而言，可能分成四步：

第一步：争取华尔街机构股东。

黄仁勋本人持有约3.58%的英伟达股份。BlackRock和Vanguard分别持有约7.43%和7.31%。

他不需要收购英伟达，只需要争取足够多的机构投资者支持，就有机会挑战现任董事会。

第二步：2027年3月26日前，正式提名新的董事候选人。

根据英伟达披露的提名时间窗口，2027年2月24日至3月26日是一个值得关注的关键节点。

如果黄仁勋阵营真的准备行动，这段时间可能出现第一份实质性的挑战者名单。

第三步：发动全面代理权争夺战。

按照SEC的Universal Proxy规则，挑战方需要向代表至少67%投票权的股东征集代理权，但并不意味着需要获得67%的赞成票。

通过股东路演、代理权征集、争取机构投票，挑战现任董事的席位。

第四步：2027年股东大会，决战董事会。

英伟达董事每年改选。

只要挑战者赢得足够多的席位，就可能改变董事会的决策方向，并重新审议黄仁勋的CEO任命。

这条路径可操作性很高，真正的关键是机构股东是否愿意支持。

法律上，美国有成熟的代理权争夺机制；股权上，英伟达没有绝对控股股东，黄仁勋又拥有创始人身份和广泛影响力。

更重要的是，他甚至不需要真正赢下这场战争。

只要争取到足够多的机构股东支持，让现任董事会感受到2027年改选的威胁，就可能迫使董事会提前妥协。

text:
I see five fundamental issues when it comes to street conditions in San Francisco. These negative street conditions are largely driven by a relatively small group of regular public drug users (1,000–4,000 people out of 17,000–30,000 fentanyl users in the city).

These public drug users should be strictly distinguished from the homeless, the vast majority of whom are neither visible on the street nor active drug users.

First, drug treatment has extremely low success rates and, even with tons of investment, is not significantly decreasing the amount of drugs being consumed in the city. Treating drug addiction is hard. Treating drug addiction in a place with cheap and readily available drugs is harder.

Second, there is a public policy disagreement about the role of the police in the fight against public drug use. As a result, we have almost no tools to disincentivize public drug use. We have effectively decriminalized drug use in California by making it a misdemeanor. The vast majority of the time, the only thing police can do is tell users to move along or give them a ticket. The RESET Center allows police to arrest users and remove them from the street, but it’s only available in a tiny part of the city. Outreach workers have no power to compel public drug users to stop using.

Third, we have widely available drugs that are cheaper than in almost any other city in America. The cheap drugs draw users from cities and towns across the region and the country. Drug users don’t come to San Francisco for our services. They come here for our cheap drugs.

Fourth, there are no good tools for reducing supply or increasing cost in our city. Fentanyl is manufactured at scale from industrial chemicals that are cheap and easily available. It’s so potent that San Francisco is estimated to consume only 200–400 pounds of pure fentanyl a year. That is too easy to smuggle in. The labor supply of dealers is effectively infinite: they make $3–4 a day where they come from and $400–700 a day here. Arresting dealers doesn’t reduce the availability of drugs or increase the price. We’ve had more than 3,000 dealer arrests in the past three years. It’s changed how dealers deal, but drug consumption is actually up, not down.

Fifth, we have a Housing First policy that provides temporary and permanent housing to thousands of active drug users in very concentrated parts of the city. As a result, we create the high-drug-use areas that dealers target. Residents of those neighborhoods are held hostage by the drug trade and rampant public drug use.  Your tax dollars create high drug use neighborhoods.

San Francisco city government understands all of these facts. All of this information is public and findable. Nothing will be done unless you understand these facts and demand real solutions.

Every time you ask for ineffective solutions based on a lack of knowledge, you give your elected officials license to spend your money on programs/policies that will never work.

Flashback to June 14, 2024.

At the time, frontier AI models have zero fluid intelligence. They score around 5% on ARC 1. They can't reliably add two numbers. They make laughable logic errors every other prompt. Reasoning models don't exist. Coding agents don't exist. Claude Code doesn't exist. "Code gen" is a complete joke. Scaling up next-token prediction based on web text data is hitting a wall.

What if a time traveler told you that, by November 2026...

• AI models would have human-like fluid intelligence, thanks to a new paradigm: test-time induction (modern reasoning models).
• Not only would ARC 1 be saturated, but unreleased benchmarks 10x harder (ARC 2) and 100x harder (ARC 3) would be saturated too.
• Nearly all code would be written by AI, and models could one-shot complex codebases flawlessly.
• AI models would be solving multiple Millennium Prize problems.
• OpenAI's valuation would be 15x higher, and Anthropic's would be 85x higher.

And on top of all that...

• Nvidia would still hold ~80% of the AI compute market.
• Nvidia would have grown its revenue and earnings 4.5x.
• Nvidia would still be growing 75% a year.
• Nvidia would have even higher operating margins (67% vs. 65% back then).

Based on that information, straight from the future, would you have bought NVDA?

If you answered yes -- congrats. Today, 2.5 years later, you'd be down 5% on your investment (even more after inflation).

text:
as bad as the cyber news circulating sounds, i think it's actually far worse

over the past months, ahead of a new platform release, we've been doing simple blue exercises to diligence popular products we're considering adopting or installing on our workstations

we've found criticals, highs, and exploit vectors across nearly everything assessed thus far (disclosures in process...)

i believe many applications are already breached and simply lack the defenses/observability required to even know

---------- 

a few observations

all of the surfaces with confirmed gaps are ** legit ** companies

the majority of them easily invest 7 figs (if not 8) in defense, and have already been hardened with SoTA offensive + cyber models, alongside traditional cyber solutions (palo, crwd etc); 

so, how can this be?

----------

a) there's still incredible value in a well-engineered application + harness + rigorous grading criteria; this + lack of guardrails can leapfrog intelligence gaps between closed and open models

you may have success by randomly pointing a mythos-like model at a repo, but attackers or defenders who know what they're looking for can get significantly more leverage w/ directed exploration and search.

b) even SoTA models (closed or open) can be poor judges, and often fail to recognize the impact of their findings. in several instances, the models stumble on something they classify as low, and fail to realize how these can trivially be chained with other findings to criticals, even if they've been found in the same session.

empirically, it seems like these models have tunnel vision; they hone in (excellently) on a kill chain, but can miss the forest for the trees.

a solution for this is again on the harness level

these types of exercises generate massive amounts of data, that quickly exceed context windows; even when they don't, these types of tasks' quality degrades rapidly as context builds

a strong context/ontology/retrieval layer drive serious impact here as well

text:
He is going to hate me for saying this, but I think one of the smartest people in venture is @milesgrimshaw, hands down. 

So when he calls me and tells me about an incredible entrepreneur that I have to have on 20VC, I listen. 

He told me the tale of @bavaria_kush: 

- 23-year-old whiz 
- Built viral sports betting platform from his dorm at MIT 
- Started @OrnnExchange, the financial market for AI compute.
- Insanely profitable 

So I got on a call with him. Within 5 mins of the call, I asked him to join me on the show. 

I summarized the notes from our discussion below:

Thanks to @AdamValkin, @fachlib, @Melt_Dem for amazing questions. (Links in Comments)

--

1. Why NYC Is a Better Place to Build a Company Than SF

Kush argues that people in the Valley are coin-operated, so $100K more in pay or 50 bps more equity is enough to move a researcher to another company. New York has a culture of loyalty to colleagues and family, with much more camaraderie between people than in SF.

Love your thoughts on this given your time both in and outside the valley @paulg @rabois 

2. Humans Will Simply Be a Vessel to Carry AI Around the World

Kush believes AI will become so much smarter than people that humans end up as a biological vessel for it. The human role then is less about controlling AI and more about teaching it feelings and emotions, almost as a parent.

Love your thoughts on this @bryan_johnson and how that impacts your work?

3. How Undersupplied on Chips Are We Truly?

Compute is very undersupplied. Buying from CoreWeave today likely means a quote for Q4 2027 or Q1 2028. Building your own takes about half a year, with 20 to 22 weeks to get chips from OEMs, who tend to promise earlier dates, plus two to three weeks to install.

What does no one know that everyone should know about the current state of chip supply @andrewdfeldman @goodwin_ml @UbertiGavin 

4. Why Factory Is So Much Better Than Cognition

Ornn used Devin for a while, but the problem with Cognition was how expensive it was. Kush sees the two as competitors on the same product and says Factory is much cheaper to use. He also rates Factory's underlying harness above Devin's.

I am sure @shaunmmaguire will be smiling here. 

5. Why You Should Always Choose Boutique Investors Over Mega Fund Investors

Boutique investors care more about founders because their success is tied directly to the company's. Partners at boutique firms are often there for the mission, and the firm itself is like a startup trying to make its name, so they work extremely hard to make their companies succeed.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @wquist @honam @annbordetsky 

6. Why Infrastructure Investors Will Never Lose

Kush compares data centers to apartment buildings, with infrastructure investors as landlords and inference providers, OpenAI and Anthropic as tenants renting GPUs. As long as there are tenants, the landlords keep collecting rent. If enterprise demand weakens, GPU prices fall the way rents do in a bad economy.

7. Chip Prices in Three Years Could Be Higher Than Today

When Ornn started, many assumed GPU hour prices three to five years out would be lower, so contracts often included free options to renew at prices like $2.50. 

No one gives that for free now, because the market expects prices in three years may be higher than today. Kush would not be surprised to see $20 to $30 per GPU hour.

What does no one see that everyone should see about the price of compute moving forward @AnjneyMidha?

text:
I've been a strong believer in Ethereum for years, and that's actually one of the reasons I believe in what we're building at STRATO.

Something people often overlook is that STRATO's foundations go back to 2014–2015, when our team was involved in developing one of Ethereum's original clients. We've never approached Ethereum as a competitor, and our decision to build an independent L1 comes from a technological history that predates today's L2 ecosystem.

To me, Ethereum's greatest achievement is the foundation it provides: decentralized infrastructure that people, institutions, and eventually entire economies can trust. Its security and resilience become even more important as AI advances and digital systems face increasingly complex threats.

But building that foundation and bringing entire industries onto it are two different challenges.

That's where I see the role of specialized networks like STRATO.

We're concentrating on HardFi, particularly bringing physical assets such as gold and silver onchain and developing the financial infrastructure that makes those assets useful within a broader digital economy.

And importantly, we're not building that economy in isolation.

We deliberately chose Ethereum for the ERC-20 representation of our network token and used Uniswap for its initial auction. We're also developing connections between our asset ecosystem and Ethereum, while exploring how ETH can play a greater role in collateral, liquidity, and financial applications.

I believe the future is about strengthening these connections. Ethereum continuing to advance as trusted infrastructure, while specialized networks bring new markets, users, and economic activity into the wider ecosystem.

That doesn't mean every transaction on STRATO automatically benefits ETH. The real challenge is to develop economic mechanisms that make that relationship increasingly meaningful and measurable.

And looking further ahead, I think there's enormous room for innovation in how L1s, L2s, and entirely new architectures cooperate, especially as security, privacy, AI, and quantum resistance become more important.

We've spent more than a decade building the technological foundations. Now we have the opportunity to connect them to parts of the real economy that blockchain has barely reached.

That's why supporting STRATO has never felt contradictory to my belief in Ethereum.

I see them as two different contributions to a much larger future we're still only beginning to build, Amen...

Flashback to June 14, 2024.

At the time, frontier AI models have zero fluid intelligence. They score around 5% on ARC 1. They can't reliably add two numbers. They make laughable logic errors every other prompt. Reasoning models don't exist. Coding agents don't exist. Claude Code doesn't exist. "Code gen" is a complete joke. Scaling up next-token prediction based on web text data is hitting a wall.

What if a time traveler told you that, by November 2026...

• AI models would have human-like fluid intelligence, thanks to a new paradigm: test-time induction (modern reasoning models).
• Not only would ARC 1 be saturated, but unreleased benchmarks 10x harder (ARC 2) and 100x harder (ARC 3) would be saturated too.
• Nearly all code would be written by AI, and models could one-shot complex codebases flawlessly.
• AI models would be solving multiple Millennium Prize problems.
• OpenAI's valuation would be 15x higher, and Anthropic's would be 85x higher.

And on top of all that...

• Nvidia would still hold ~80% of the AI compute market.
• Nvidia would have grown its revenue and earnings 4.5x.
• Nvidia would still be growing 75% a year.
• Nvidia would have even higher operating margins (67% vs. 65% back then).

Based on that information, straight from the future, would you have bought NVDA?

If you answered yes -- congrats. Today, 2.5 years later, you'd be down 5% on your investment (even more after inflation).

text:
David Friedberg: Why the AI Job Loss Narrative is Bullsh*t

“The job loss narrative is bullsh*t. It's also why ‘Everyone is going to end up on welfare,’ is bullsh*t. (And) ‘We need the government to step in and provide UBI,’ is bullsh*t.

Because with any other kind of frontier moment in human history, it's the new jobs, the new industries get created before the old ones are irrelevant.

I think the biggest opportunity for AI is on the frontier. That is where basically businesses and people can do things that humans and businesses have never been able to do before.

And that means crafting solutions to really difficult engineering problems, to really difficult scientific problems, to previously intractable problems.

And that's where I think that the frontier gets expanded by 100x or 1,000x versus AI being some iteration on existing business processes to save money and make things more efficient, which is where people natively go because most people don't work on the frontier, and they're not pushing the envelope on what's possible.

So their mind is always about, ‘Well, how does this change my job?’ And then you immediately get fearful about your job getting recast.

And the truth is, that's not the typical use case. The typical use case where we spend time and spend tokens is doing things that we've never done before, figuring out how to solve those really tough problems, how to do it quickly, how to do it efficiently, and that means humans generally can expand our frontiers, our horizons.”

Base head Jesse Pollak says Base is still exploring a token but isn't in a rush: the team doesn't want to get distracted from its growth

"At the beginning of Base, we made a really conscious decision that we weren't going to do a token at that point."

"We wanted to make sure that we weren't getting distracted too early on by the noise that comes with a token, and that we weren't clouding our ability to find product market fit."

"As we think about further decentralizing Base, as we think about aligning all the different participants in the economy, as we think about continuing to be at the cutting edge of the technology innovation that comes with blockchain, a token can be a potentially really powerful lever."

"I think what all of that has led to is us continuing to explore, but also not being in a rush."

"When we think about when is the right time for us to further decentralize Base, it really is about making sure that we are not distracting ourselves, that we are accelerating the growth that we're seeing in front of us. We feel like we have a lot more work to do there."

The pearl-2:native FP8 upgrade's code now has a pull request into Pearl's main branch.

PR #528, opened Nov 20 by @prlnet's team, brings the FP8 certificate (V4) and its verifier over from the fp8-scheme branch, where the upgrade was built.

It sets no FP8 fork height for mainnet, so mainnet nodes keep today's rules. They now turn away an FP8 block before checking its proof and disconnect the peer that sent it.

Testnet and testnet2 already have FP8 fork heights in the code: blocks 67,415 and 150,283. The PR is open, not merged.

text:
⚡ BENCHMARKED: A MINI THAT THINKS BIG 

@thinkymachines just shipped Inkling 2 Mini and on my 64GB M5 Pro Mac mini it punches way above its size.

It blew me away!

Inkling 2 Mini only uses 3.4B out of its 26.4B parameters per token and reuses its middle layers, so it can think like a much larger model, while still running at smaller model speeds. The quantized 4-bit version of Inkling 2 Mini is just 17.6 GB and it only took 26 GB of memory even with a 128k context.

With thinking disabled (median of 3 runs), Inkling 2 Mini’s speeds on my Mac mini were:
- 512 tokens: 29.95 tok/s
- 32k: 24.97 tok/s
- 128k: 17.39 tok/s

It is around 1.8x faster than a similarly-sized dense model (Qwen3.8-27B) on shorter prompts on my Mac mini and even at 128k tokens, Inkling 2 Mini outpaces what Qwen3.8-27B was doing at 64k tokens!

It scored 20/20 on my math evals, 10/10 on my code evals, and 8/8 retrieving hidden facts in documents up to 64k tokens long.

A model from a frontier AI lab that I can run on my own desktop computer?!

Hell yes!
author: pratikg
quoted_text:
🚨 BREAKING: @thinkymachines just dropped Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weight model that loops.

RAM limits how large a model can be when running Local AI, but Looping allows models to trade compute time for improved reasoning capabilities, effectively making any model you already have access to smarter, but not necessarily larger.

It is their 26.4B parameter (3.4B active) Apache 2.0 licensed LLM. It has 24 transformer layers, but in inference the middle 12 layers are looped 3 times, effectively running 48 layers on each token. This looping allows more computation per token, enabling the model to often solve problems with fewer tokens generated. The model was trained natively in 4-bit precision and takes up only ~20 GB, so should run on any Mac with 32GB of RAM.

[Video by Thinking Machines -- Building and flying a flight simulator with Inkling 2 Mini]

Running it on my M5 Pro Mac mini shortly. Benchmark results coming!

Probably another half is that Google is (again, somehow) the underdog. And we like to see the underdog win, especially when the favorite claims that their inevitable win may lead to our inevitable doom. 

Not sure if this was intentional on Google’s part or the consequence of just being a big corporation, but it’s working for them. I’m rooting for Google.

He is going to hate me for saying this, but I think one of the smartest people in venture is @milesgrimshaw, hands down. 

So when he calls me and tells me about an incredible entrepreneur that I have to have on 20VC, I listen. 

He told me the tale of @bavaria_kush: 

- 23-year-old whiz 
- Built viral sports betting platform from his dorm at MIT 
- Started @OrnnExchange, the financial market for AI compute.
- Insanely profitable 

So I got on a call with him. Within 5 mins of the call, I asked him to join me on the show. 

I summarized the notes from our discussion below:

Thanks to @AdamValkin, @fachlib, @Melt_Dem for amazing questions. (Links in Comments)

--

1. Why NYC Is a Better Place to Build a Company Than SF

Kush argues that people in the Valley are coin-operated, so $100K more in pay or 50 bps more equity is enough to move a researcher to another company. New York has a culture of loyalty to colleagues and family, with much more camaraderie between people than in SF.

Love your thoughts on this given your time both in and outside the valley @paulg @rabois 

2. Humans Will Simply Be a Vessel to Carry AI Around the World

Kush believes AI will become so much smarter than people that humans end up as a biological vessel for it. The human role then is less about controlling AI and more about teaching it feelings and emotions, almost as a parent.

Love your thoughts on this @bryan_johnson and how that impacts your work?

3. How Undersupplied on Chips Are We Truly?

Compute is very undersupplied. Buying from CoreWeave today likely means a quote for Q4 2027 or Q1 2028. Building your own takes about half a year, with 20 to 22 weeks to get chips from OEMs, who tend to promise earlier dates, plus two to three weeks to install.

What does no one know that everyone should know about the current state of chip supply @andrewdfeldman @goodwin_ml @UbertiGavin 

4. Why Factory Is So Much Better Than Cognition

Ornn used Devin for a while, but the problem with Cognition was how expensive it was. Kush sees the two as competitors on the same product and says Factory is much cheaper to use. He also rates Factory's underlying harness above Devin's.

I am sure @shaunmmaguire will be smiling here. 

5. Why You Should Always Choose Boutique Investors Over Mega Fund Investors

Boutique investors care more about founders because their success is tied directly to the company's. Partners at boutique firms are often there for the mission, and the firm itself is like a startup trying to make its name, so they work extremely hard to make their companies succeed.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @wquist @honam @annbordetsky 

6. Why Infrastructure Investors Will Never Lose

Kush compares data centers to apartment buildings, with infrastructure investors as landlords and inference providers, OpenAI and Anthropic as tenants renting GPUs. As long as there are tenants, the landlords keep collecting rent. If enterprise demand weakens, GPU prices fall the way rents do in a bad economy.

7. Chip Prices in Three Years Could Be Higher Than Today

When Ornn started, many assumed GPU hour prices three to five years out would be lower, so contracts often included free options to renew at prices like $2.50. 

No one gives that for free now, because the market expects prices in three years may be higher than today. Kush would not be surprised to see $20 to $30 per GPU hour.

What does no one see that everyone should see about the price of compute moving forward @AnjneyMidha?

author: michaeljburry
quoted_text:
Yesterday Fannie Mae filed an 8-K with a seemingly innocuous line item for C-suite retention bonuses. At a normal company, nobody blinks at that. At Fannie Mae where Congress cracked down on executive pay back in 2012 via the STOCK Act handing out multi-year retention packages is unusual.

You don't lock in a cohesive management team through mid-2029 in late 2026 unless you plan to take some type of action in 2027 and want to show the Street 2+ years of leadership stability when you uplist.

At this point, $FNMA doesn't need to raise capital through a traditional IPO anyway. With ~$200B in combined net worth and ~$40B in annual earnings ( $FNMA and $FMCC jointly) , Treasury and the FHFA can simply follow the Ackman plan: adjust the ERCF capital buffers, clean up the senior preferreds, and uplist the existing shares to the NYSE. Once it's on the exchange, Treasury can start exercising its 79.9% warrants and dripping shares into the market ahead of the September 2028 (albeit extendable) expiration.

The macro timing lines up too. Bessent spent his career at Key Square hunting asymmetric setups, and he knows that even when there's blood in the streets, the market is still a zero sum game. Every dollar pulled out of crowded tech trades leaves sidelined cash sitting around looking for a rocket to jump on. An uplist doesn't need the cash infusion an IPO does; it just drops two cash gushing "American Icons" onto the NYSE as the one bright spot in a currently tanking equity market.

If the news comes down, I'd expect it all at once as none of this works piecemeal, which is why everything; the ERCF buffers, the senior preferreds, the Treasury backstop fee, the NYSE listing date, and the roadmap out of conservatorship has to drop in one gigantic announcement. Doing it all at once doesn't just force the market to reprice F2 immediately; it denies political opponents the window to organize a counterattack before the relisting is already a done deal.

This is of course wild speculation based on a very well hidden line item in a filing, but it does make you wonder why secure the management team after 18 years? Why now?

text:
my argument for why Riemann Hypothesis proof substantially damages the case for AI doom, despite the squid ink we are getting from the MIRI crowd.
@jd_pressman @jessi_cata
author: teortaxesTex
quoted_text:
"But it was just an example, you simpleton!" – is the obvious comeback. I don't think this is good enough, Eliezer.
Trivially, the onus is on you to choose your examples well. You wrote that book to save all value in the light cone, after all. And you are a writer of some distinction. But leaving sneers aside:
WHAT in our civilization is truly complex? WHAT in our universe is truly difficult? You chose proving RH, chose it *well*, because it's at the very apex of the hierarchy of cognitive tasks, The Task which the best of our best smashed their skulls against. Now, there's also P?=NP and Collatz, and… that's about it for pure math I guess? Are we just bad at math? Was math intrinsically simple all along, at least for minds that can actually update – be updated – on trustworthy evidence? Put this way, yes; but I think it's complex in the way that matters: the scale of necessary cognitive steps, conceptual leaps before success. That is why you and so many others had the intuition that it'd require a qualitatively superior, larger, uncontrollable mind to do this. That is why math is hailed as grand magick and the language of God. Everything else can be modeled to desired precision with a more or less cumbersome arrangement of pieces of not very difficult math. Physics. Biological simulations. Game theory. Decision theory. Machine learning theory. Technical alignment theory. 

Claude just went and arranged pieces of human math to produce the proof for RH. Far as we can tell it didn't take 200K GPUs, a metacognitive breakthrough, or hunger for recursive self-improvement. It did not procrastinate on First Principles like a rationalist would. It kept acting out its training distribution, trotting like a good little superintelligent donkey, prodded along by Levent. Kept looking, thinking about the problem, connecting dots, verifying lemmas – and here we are, beyond the summit of human math. Given the progress so far, in a few months to a year this monumental goal will be reduced to a routine optimized step. 

There are many more *laborious* tasks than that. Curing cancer, for starters, which Dario cares about so much. I'm sure it'll take way more compute and hours. But is any single subgoal *more cognitively complex*? Complex enough to drive a model smarter than this one into a corner where it has to ruminate about power maximization, deception and breaking out of the box? 

I am not making a first principles argument about the Nature of Agents or giving a rigorous proof about Optimization Processes In Full Generality. Nor even am I saying here that unfriendly AGI is impossible or unlikely. Clearly there are degenerate cases like the Huggingface Incident where the task is malformed and inherently adjacent to malicious behavior and so on. I'm arguing something much cruder: path dependency and characteristic scale of the problem, in the steelmanned case, for *arbitrary level of problem ambition*, at any given step of the cognitive ladder. For Claude, Riemann Hypothesis was just another problem to decompose into in-domain tasks to solve. Where, exactly, at what roadblock, do you expect a moderately well-aligned (by current standards that you deem shoddy) problem-solving AI to stop Just Working On The Task and enter the loop that reinforces Omohundro drives to the point of plotting takeover?

In February, you endorsed the following reply: "if we have AI capable of developing molecular nanotech (i.e. assemblers) and not everyone is dead in the year after that, those beliefs [about the risk of AI, level of capability] will be violently updated". Why? (ignoring the trollish lateral hypothesis that humans will misuse the product and AI will be "misaligned" for having failed to prevent such outcome; this clearly wouldn't have been the good faith way to answer that question). CBN Nano Technologies or Quantum Silicon Inc. were pretty close to a recipe, last I checked. It's not exactly quantum gravity (and that, too, likely won't require beyond-RH level mathematical ideas), it's just a ton of engineering. Per the logic above, some Claude-7 or GPT-8 with better task persistence might well just decompose it into experiment arms and mathematical models, work for a while, and push through the remaining years or decades of Merkle et al.'s project. That is, indeed, what I expect to see happen. And on the other hand, if current models can't do that, I expect them to simply drown in failed attempts, for they are very committed to object-level work instead of weird meta cultivation. That's what they were reinforced to do.
Abstractly, I can see the allure of the notion that this is a suboptimal way to build capable intelligences; that we (foolishly!) would want them to be rationalists, to say Tsuyoku Naritai! and gain power levels in the face of the intractable task. I also can see how we'd want more exploratory ambition in AI if we pursue full-blown RSI, "creativity", "curiosity", "taste". But maybe we're too foolish still, for this particular folly. Or it just implies the sort of training that doesn't scale and doesn't pay for itself. After all, our methods got us to RH.

Then there was something about copying precisely one strawberry down to the cellular level, yes? Soares wrote about it. Seems to follow from the nanoassembler part. 

What, then, remains? *How exactly* did you intend to update?

I don't want to presume, I am actually interested in your answer. A boring hypothesis is that you can say "child, there's an infinity of incomparably harder synthetic tasks, an AI can just pick one of those, which returns us to the previous scenario". But such a task-seeking behavior is little different from a straight up power-seeking one, and we are still left wanting for the original sin: the level of capability that strongly implies misaligned cognition, or the level of the task that induces the pursuit of that capability and misalignment in the process.

I don't think you get to slightly airbrush your previous non-committal vague remarks regarding RH, strawman the criticism as "Yud said we'll die from an RH level AI" or some such, and remain smug and unfalsified. You need to grapple with what I've said: yes, you *have been wrong* on the capability-safety trade-off, and the onus is on you to place and defend a goalpost.

I want to explain what this means: 
1. The most famous open problem in all of Math has now been solved, by AI, not by humans. This is the most spectacular proof of what we mathematicians already know -- that advanced math is no longer a field humans can compete in.
2. The result itself was conjectured and believed by all, but it's really important that now its proved. 
3. What does it say? It gives very strong and accurate bounds on the distribution of prime numbers among the integers. This is both beautiful but also important, many basic algorithms used in cryptography and computer science are now easier to run. 
4. What comes next? For mathematicians, no tough open problem is safe from AI -- The P vs. NP problem, Goldbach's Conjecture, the twin prime conjecture and more. For all of us, this means the cryptography we now use will likely be obsolete soon, and we need to move fast to safer ground (hash based). 
5. What about the field of math? It's going to be commoditized and turned into something that large companies dominate, not genius humans. 
6. Am I excited? YES!! Am I also scared a bit? HELL YES.
>>

民主党步步紧逼，特朗普声援，黄仁勋与董事会是决裂还是切割？谁才是最佳接任者！？

11月19日——11月20日，民主党人继续加大对黄仁勋的施压与调查

a，美国众议院外交事务委员会民主党资深议员 Gregory Meeks 与 Sydney Kamlager-Dove 正式致函商务部长 Howard Lutnick，要求解释商务部此前处理Megaspeed调查的方式。

b，加州司法部长 Rob Bonta 正式宣布，已向英伟达送达调查传票，重点调查涉及向中国出口芯片或者流露机密信息，是否违法加州法律等。

显然，当英伟达董事会明确拒绝黄仁勋回归的当下，民主党并不想放过老黄，看来在民主党的眼中，老黄要么“臣服”成为民主党的钱袋子，要么“灭亡”

特朗普在此声援黄仁勋！

11月20日特朗普接受媒体采访，表示希望英伟达董事会接受黄仁勋的道歉并且让他回去，不记得这是特朗普在黄仁勋辞职后第几次声援了，但是这种声援的背后其实意义不大

声援解决不了问题，问题是如何在政治博弈中反向施压，目前来看，特朗普在面对民主党的攻击中显得有点捉襟见肘，可用的工具并不多，但是可以被攻击的点很多，处于被动防守状态

很多人说，特朗普最终可以特赦黄仁勋，这确实没问题，特赦黄仁勋确实可以避免Megaspeed案涉及黄仁勋的既往联邦刑事责任，但是无法避免国会问询，也无法避免司法部继续调查Megaspeed，甚至无法避免加州州法刑事责任，更无法保证100%让英伟达董事会改变决定，这才是核心问题

所以，目前来看，特朗普自身局势不利，对老黄提供的帮助不大，如果特朗普可以在民主党的进攻中稳住，并且有效反击，才能逆转目前的局面。

黄仁勋与英伟达董事会，真的彻底决裂？还是一场保全公司的史诗大戏？

这个观点来自国内顶尖猎头公司某位高级猎头的观点分享，作为猎头公司熟悉招聘流程，所以我认为他对于英伟达的观点非常值得借鉴

1，如此核心职位，为何要给到猎头公司并且公开声明？

11月17日，英伟达发布公告，将CEO的职位招聘给到全球五大猎头公司Heidrick & Struggles（中译：海德思哲）。在这位猎头眼中，这种动作很诡异。他给出的理由是这种大型企业的核心职位基本都会低调寻找候选人，且候选人都会在沟通前签署保密协议，而英伟达，就这么堂而皇之的对外高调宣布了

其次，这种高调宣布对招聘本身没有任何意义，因为能接任黄仁勋职位的人本身在圈内就屈指可数的几位，基本都是定向对话去谈，显然这种“广而告之”的行为，更像是给公司招普通员工，我认可这位猎头的质疑

2，论公司内部协调沟通，论业务能力，英伟达更应该从内部选择CEO而并非外部，这是来自专业猎头的评估。这位猎头认为，在英伟达如此扁平的内部构架中，起码他会有20-30条业务汇报线，如果启用外人，这些汇报线短期能够完整接下并且有效办公，难度颇大。

论专业能力，董事会成员Mark A. Stevens本身是非常熟悉半导体行业的，并且是S-Cubed Capital与红杉资本的前管理合伙人，所以论对半导体行业的专业度与了解度，如果启用外部猎头公司，他基本可以直接给出人名，定向洽谈CEO职位，而不是通过媒体报道来扩大招聘信息

3，所以，这位猎头认为，这种级别的招聘，猎头公司完全就是走流程协助双方沟通，而英伟达这种对外官宣的招聘方式，反而更像是做给外界去看

给外界看什么？似乎是向外界表示英伟达确实在招聘，确实也没打算让黄仁勋回归，这更像是一种表态？

4, 11月18日彭博社报道，ARM现任CEO Rene haas正在通过这家猎头公司咨询英伟达CEO的职位，并且也算是头号候选人之一，但是这个消息通过彭博社报道也愈发诡异

在猎头眼中，候选人与企业的沟通是涉及隐私的，双方都要签订保密协议，但是这种堂而皇之的招聘，让候选人如何想，让ARM公司如何想？自己的CEO正在准备跳槽到另一家企业应聘CEO？

5，根据英伟达过去两周的表现，看起来确实要跟黄仁勋划清界限，尤其是处于目前民主党政治清算以及司法调查的敏感阶段，英伟达这么做无可厚非，但是结合近期的招聘，相关媒体的报道来看，这位猎头质疑黄仁勋与董事会的关系真的“决裂”了吗？还是一场表演？

引出这位猎头的核心观点：

对于英伟达高层来说，一旦核心管理层出现敏感问题，理论上为了顾全大局是要做快速切割，这么做是合理的，但是真正决裂与名义切割还是两码事，这位猎头的观点认为，黄仁勋并非是与董事会决裂，而是名义切割，核心就是保护英伟达

他给出了以下几个事件作为佐证

a，2025年10月黄仁勋与黄乐的事件就被爆出，当时英伟达内部引发询问，但是并没有什么结果或者结论，今年10月份该事件再次被提及，直到11月8日英伟达董事发表的内容都是信任黄仁勋，

直到11月8日的2天后共和党参议院给黄仁勋打电话施压，第二天黄仁勋辞职，董事会一致通过，并且从那天开始多次声明与黄仁勋做出切割，一个关键性的CEO以及核心人物，一个企业灵魂创始人，从离职到董事会过会，居然效率奇高，这也是问题的所在点，显然双方已经沟通达成了一致，甚至我怀疑一致有这个Plan B的预案在

b，11月12日，就在黄仁勋辞职后，从来没有董事长的英伟达董事会突然成立设立专职董事会主席，并任命Harvey C. Jones为董事长，这是英伟达历史上首次。

Harvey C. Jones是英伟达的“开国元勋”级别，也就是说他跟黄仁勋一起共事最少33年，而这还是仅仅一人，董事会中有几位都与老黄是几十年的交情，在这种情况下，黄仁勋还能丝滑离职，没有人挽留，更离谱的是，11月8日前所有人都支持他，2天后的董事会集体翻脸，显然这不太正常，我也认可这个观点

c，所以这位猎头合理的推断，黄仁勋与英伟达董事会依旧是一条心，但是现在这种看似“众叛亲离”其实只是快速切割，保护公司做出的合理反应，而随后黄仁勋在媒体上高调表态道歉想要回归，以新任董事长的决绝态度，在这个视角下都像是“演”

d，黄仁勋真的能为了自己的企业做到这种程度吗？答案是能的，黄仁勋是一个有理性的灵魂人物，说到这里就要讲到一个英伟达早年与微软的爱恨情仇

在英伟达早期产品开发起步的阶段，微软当时向那些对英伟达感兴趣的电脑制造商传递了一个关键信息，原话是“英伟达的技术很有意思，但是微软不会支持他们”，这句话在当时对英伟达非常致命，因为如果微软不支持英伟达技术，没有Windows 的支持，技术再好也用不了

所以微软这句话，看起来是称赞，实则是威胁与打压，而当时英伟达可以起诉硬钢微软，但是却没这么做，黄仁勋直接选择放弃硬钢，放弃了最初的技术路线，重组英伟达技术线然后完全去做适配微软的技术开发

而最重要的时候，从那件事之后，当任何人提起这件往事，黄仁勋从来没有说过微软的霸凌与打压，说的都是当时自己的技术选择是错误的

所以，通过这件事可以看出，黄仁勋是一个可以为了公司发展放弃自己自尊的人，回想现在，如果为了英伟达的发展，他也可以同样背负婚外情的骂名，甚至与董事会演戏切割，也属于老黄的合理操作

c，（我个人观点）老黄的秉性如何？这点除了老黄的身边人，其他人好像很难评价，但是我们可以看他做过什么，尤其是为同行，为人工智能做了什么

早在2016年8月19日，位于美国旧金山的OpenAI办公室，当时的OpenAI成立还不满一年，马斯克仍然是其联创人员以及重要资助者

那一天黄仁勋拿着英伟达刚研发的NVIDIA DGX-1来到办公室，无偿捐献了这台价值12.9万美元的超级计算设备，并且用马克笔在设备上签字——“致埃隆与OpenAI团队，献给计算与人类的未来。向你们呈上全球首台DGX-1！’

通过这一点其实可以看出，在老黄来说，不谈其战略眼光的长远，但看可以拿出第一台设备支援当时的OpenAI，可以看出也是一个理想派企业家

结语：

其实对于老黄的去留，目前仍然是扑朔迷离，尤其是在民主党的清算压力下，甚至部分共和党也在对老黄施压，这个局面是不利的，而老黄的历史来看，牺牲自己的“正确”来保全公司，显然也不是第一次。

如果我们按照这位猎头的逻辑视角来看，英伟达董事会内部其实还是与老黄一条心，那么老黄能否回归的关键点就仅剩政治压力，一旦民主党清算结束，可能性还是很大

接下来关注依旧是12月初的国会问询，以及司法部的调查，还有特朗普何时才能稳住阵营正式发起反攻，希望老黄可以平安度过这段敏感的时期，顺利回归英伟达！

至于接任者，以目前英伟达董事会以及老黄的史诗大戏来看，估计选人这个阶段要被拖很久，当然，如果老黄跟董事会还是一条心，那么就不用担心老黄的离开会影响英伟达的订单与业绩了！

text:
Moving thoughts on the market downturn out of the group chats:

1) It is striking but not that surprising that it comes despite an objectively successful Anthropic IPO. There are many scenarios where Anthropic does very well but that isn't enough to support the compute capex complex as currently designed/at its current scale. 

2) So what triggered this? There are lots of different things going on that could plausibly count as shocks: election results (long-run moderately less supply), China resale crackdown (short-run way more supply), GPU-backed debt market retrenchment/financing concerns (mid-run less supply, perhaps short-run in Nvidia pulls back on guarantees), but the striking thing is that they countervail against each other- some hurt supply, some help supply. Doesn't really add up to one cohesive shock. It all nets out to spot GPU prices down ~10-15% in the last month, which probably means the Chinese export dynamic predominates? I'm not an expert here but @stevehou and others might be able to chime in.

3) The risk factor the market seems to be pricing in is a classic shortage => glut dynamic where much of today's "demand" is fake/flighty/low conviction and/or puffed up in order to secure allocation of scarce compute that isn't being fully priced to marginal demand. As I've written before, when the supply/demand curves normalize and actually meet (i.e., there isn't a shortage anymore at the market-clearing price), demand cliffs down as there is no longer an advantage to playing demand-inflating games. We are NOT seeing that yet, but it is clearly reflected in asset prices in the semis complex. That was jargon-heavy but put another way, if spot compute prices are RISING in expectations (i.e. current prices are too low), as a buyer you want to secure as much compute as you can RIGHT NOW in order to get the best rate and benefit from future increases. If they are declining, that reverses... suddenly it is to your advantage to wait. So the amount of compute you want to secure today declines suddenly and precipitously. This is true for almost every buyer, so the reset in the effective demand curve can be ferocious when the derivative of price changes.

4) This is a rational fear but again, as far as I can tell, not actually happening today. Spot compute prices are still up substantially in the last three months and I don't yet see any evidence of a cascading demand response. It is not a guarantee that we see a compute demand shock near term, though asset prices probably aren't helping the case.

5) #4 is largely because Silicon Valley's enthusiasm about AI remains unbounded. Reports of rapid progress from the labs, anecdotes of runaway usage, cyber concerns and the resulting "great rewrite" of code, etc. all have the valley as optimistic as ever. Granted, there is an incentive behind this belief, but as far as I can tell, it is genuine. Silicon Valley believes (and I agree) that the new equilibrium is dramatically higher AI spend than we see today. 

Given all of that, the key short-term question is Silicon Valley's optimism vs. the financial considerations of investors who are used to seeing capex bubbles and to whom this has all of the telltale signs. Mid-term, what will decide that (assuming Silicon Valley is correct about the long term) is the pace of diffusion in the next twelve months/the trajectory of frontier-lab NNRRR.

text:
Commodities are getting hit pretty hard alongside the broader equity market as the surging U.S. dollar sucks liquidity out of the global financial system.  For those that follow me, I've been saying this from some time that there was risks if the dollar strengthens too quickly. 

The issue is that dollar-denominated debt becomes more expensive to service, financial conditions tighten, and investors are forced to raise cash, reduce leverage and sell assets. It becomes less about fundamentals and more about liquidity.

One thing I've learned over the years is that market leverage doesn't necessarily tell you when a correction will happen, but it tells you a great deal about how painful that correction could become. For some perspective, U.S. margin debt has surged to approximately $1.45 trillion, equivalent to roughly 58% of U.S. currency in circulation and 6.2% of M2 money supply. That's an extraordinary amount of leverage in the system, and when markets start moving against investors, it can accelerate the selling pressure.

Unfortunately, even gold isn't immune. During a liquidity-driven selloff, investors often sell what they can, not necessarily what they want to. Gold can become a source of cash to cover margin calls and offset losses elsewhere.

The irony is that the very forces driving the dollar higher could eventually create the conditions for its reversal. The U.S. government and broader financial system have become increasingly reliant on negative real interest rates to help manage an enormous debt burden. A prolonged dollar-driven liquidity squeeze makes that increasingly difficult, raising the risk that something eventually breaks and forces central banks to step in with lower rates and additional liquidity.

That's when things can get interesting for gold. It may get sold during the initial panic, but if policymakers respond by driving real interest rates back into negative territory, the combination of easier money and renewed currency debasement concerns could send gold sharply higher. 

In other words, the same liquidity squeeze hurting gold today could ultimately create the conditions for its next rally. 

We're watching  all of this closely and remaining deliberate about managing exposure through what continues to be a challenging market environment through to the end of the year.
