text:
I Run the IPO Desk That Sold You Anthropic. We sold 7.4% of the Company and priced 100% of it.

I work on the IPO syndicate desk at one of the banks on the cover of Anthropic's prospectus. I have some insider information regarding Thursday's debut. Most of it is arithmetic. That's why nobody checks it.

You read the headline. Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history. The stock opened at $111.50, closed at $97.17, and made Anthropic a company worth about $1.3 trillion. Some outlets said $1.77 trillion. At the day's high, some said $2 trillion.

Same company. Same afternoon. 3 valuations. Pick the one that fits your headline.

We don't put the next part on the screen. Anthropic has roughly 13.2 billion Class A and Class N shares. We sold 980 million of them to the public. Renaissance Capital puts the float at about 7.4%.

So 92.6% of the company has never traded. Nobody in the public market has paid a dollar for it. We took the price of the 7.4% and multiplied it by all 13.2 billion shares. The result is the market cap you saw on TV.

People online call this a trick. I'd like to defend my profession. We use the same trick on every company. That's what makes it legal.

Anthropic first marketed the shares at $70 to $78. According to CNBC sources, institutions placed orders for around $400 billion. Retail orders approached $100 billion. We were selling about $81 billion of stock. Buyers wanted roughly 6 dollars of stock for every dollar we had.

My business calls that ratio pricing power. A gas station calls it a shortage.

So we raised the price to $83 and the share count from 825 million to 980 million. Then we handed out the shares. The big funds got shares at $83. Our best clients got shares at $83. I can't tell you who our best clients are. I can tell you they're the ones who call us back.

We promised retail investors up to 20% of the deal. 6 brokers- Schwab, Fidelity, Robinhood, SoFi, E*TRADE, and Trade-PMR- took orders from individuals. The prospectus even lists "potential allocation to retail investors of a minority of shares" as a risk to the stock price. You were in the risk factors. You bought anyway.

Some of you got your shares. Binance ran a $500 million campaign for its users and received 2,957 shares. That's about $245,000, or 0.05% of what Binance asked for. Bitget filled 1.3% of its orders. Retail got its allocation. Most of it arrived as an email that started with "Unfortunately."

The market opened at 9:30 Thursday morning. Anthropic didn't. My desk spent the next 2.5 hours trying to find a price. The first trade printed just before noon at $111.50.

Our clients had paid $83 the night before. The public paid 34% more at lunch.

Anthropic sold 980 million shares to our clients at $83. At noon, strangers paid $28.50 more per share. Anthropic could have collected that money. Our clients collected it instead, about $27.9 billion on paper in the first second of trading. Wall Street calls that "leaving money on the table." Nobody says whose table. It's ours. We set it.

Anthropic paid us $550 million to run the deal, according to a regulatory filing. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley took about $113 million each. So Anthropic paid its banks $550 million, and its banks handed their clients about $27.9 billion. That's roughly 50 dollars to our clients for every dollar of our fee. In any other business, the customer would fire us. Anthropic will thank us at the closing dinner.

The stock touched $115.10. Then it fell to $92.72. If you bought at the open, you lost about 16.8% before lunch. At the close, it was $97.17. Our clients who sold at the open didn't notice. They were at lunch.

About 846 million shares traded on day 1, according to CNBC. We sold 980 million. The float turned over about 86% in 6 hours. A "long-term investor" now means anyone who held until the closing bell.

Then came my favorite part of the job, the greenshoe. Before trading starts, we sell 15% more shares than the deal has. If the stock falls, we buy those extra shares back in the market and look like heroes for supporting the price. If the stock rises, we use an option to buy the extra shares from the company at the IPO price.

The stock rose. We exercised our option on up to 147 million extra shares. That pushed the total raise, including a private placement, to about $119.5 billion. We sold shares that didn't exist yet. Demand showed up, so we created them. Try that with a house you don't own. My industry's rulebook calls it stabilization.

The IPO was only the first wave of buyers. The next wave can't say no.

This spring, Nasdaq added a fast-entry rule to the Nasdaq-100 and dropped its 10% free-float minimum. Bloomberg reports Anthropic is on track to join the Nasdaq-100 on December 21. FTSE Russell has flagged a possible Russell 1000 entry on December 11.

Index funds don't get opinions. When a stock joins the index, they buy it. Intropic, an index analytics firm, estimated that passive funds would take about 28% of the shares on offer, roughly $19 billion. A fund manager who thinks Anthropic costs too much still has to own it. A short seller who agrees with him has to compete with buyers who aren't allowed to sell.

When forced buyers chase a tiny float, the price rises until somebody sells. We built the tiny float. The index rules built the forced buyers. Your retirement fund did the rest.

On Thursday, protesters stood in front of Nasdaq in Times Square under the hashtag #StopTechOligarchs. They said the index rule changes mean "retirement funds that are in indexes will be forced to invest in the IPO." They're right about the mechanism. They're wrong about the scale, and I find that more insulting.

Look at SpaceX, the last mega-IPO we ran this playbook on. Trending Topics reports that its starting index weight was about 0.1%. Someone with $50,000 in a total market fund held about $57 of SpaceX. JPMorgan estimated that passive funds bought about $4.3 billion after SpaceX joined the Nasdaq-100. Forecasts had said $22 billion to $27 billion.

So we don't take your whole pension. We take $57 of it, from millions of people at once. Nobody calls their congressman over $57.

SpaceX opened at $135 in June. It hit $211 within 4 trading days. It fell to $108 in August. It recently traded around $141. If you bought at $211, you got the whole ride.

Now let's talk about who sold to you. Anthropic's existing shareholders paid a weighted average of $11.50 a share. Its option holders have about 1.77 billion option shares at an average exercise price of $2.91. The prospectus says up to 10% of what non-founder directors, officers, employees and consultants hold "may be transferred or sold beginning on the first trading day." Each of the 7 co-founders sold about $250 million of stock in the IPO, according to Bloomberg.

The employees did very well. At our price, Anthropic's 5,300 employees hold about $232 billion in stock, or roughly $44 million each, CNBC calculated. According to CNBC, at least 400 early employees are worth $100 million or more. Options granted through 2023 had an average exercise price of 52 cents. At $83, each of those options is worth about 160 times what it cost.

You paid $111.50 at the open. They paid 52 cents. Same share, same company. Welcome to equality of outcome.

The early investors did better. Spark Capital put $75 million into Anthropic in 2023. By the May valuation, that stake was worth about $7 billion, according to Bloomberg, more than 90 times the money. Eric Schmidt invested when the whole company was valued at about $461 million. He now owns about 1%. The public got in at $1.3 trillion. Insiders eat first. You get the check.

My favorite early investor is FTX. It put about $500 million into Anthropic. After FTX went bankrupt, its estate sold the stake in 2024 for about $1.3 billion to repay creditors. Those shares would reportedly be worth tens of billions today. Even Sam Bankman-Fried's victims sold too early. That's how good this deal was for everyone except you.

The suppliers did best of all. Amazon owns 1.92 billion shares. Alphabet owns 1.79 billion. At $83, Forbes values those stakes at about $159 billion and $149 billion. Together, the 2 companies own more of Anthropic than all 7 co-founders combined. Anthropic owes Amazon at least $110 billion for compute and Google at least $121.3 billion. The landlords own the tenant, and the tenant just went public.

So on Thursday, the people who knew the most about Anthropic had a cost basis between 52 cents and $11.50 and permission to sell. The people who knew the least had a Robinhood app and a $111.50 order. That's price discovery. Some people discover the price. Other people pay it.

A man on X wrote a long post about all of this. Most of it was insults I won't repeat. Some of his points were correct, and that's dangerous for my industry.

He's right that the public never priced the other 92.6%. He's right that scarcity plus hype bids up a price. He compared Anthropic to Cabbage Patch Dolls. I've worked here 14 years, and nobody has described my job more accurately.

He's wrong about the rest. He guessed that if all 13.2 billion shares hit the market, the price would fall to "perhaps $5 / share." He added, "that's my guess." He has no model. I respect that. Our model is a phone and a book of orders.

He also said Anthropic's spending commitments run "through 2032." The prospectus says about $900.9 billion of commitments, mostly through 2045. If you're going to attack our client, please get the debt schedule right. We worked hard on that schedule.

He asked a great question. If Anthropic sold just 1 million shares at $1,000 each and kept the rest private, would it be a $13.2 trillion company? Under the convention every newspaper uses, yes. The math works the same way at 7.4%. It's just harder to notice.

We thought about a smaller float. Legal said 7.4% looked more natural.

On Wednesday, the Federal Reserve published minutes warning about "circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms." That evening, we priced the IPO. Anthropic's suppliers bought $26 billion of its stock in a private placement at that price. AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC all bought in.

Follow the money around. The suppliers buy the stock. The index funds buy the stock. Your 401(k) owns the index. Anthropic pays the suppliers. The money comes back with a market cap attached.

There's one more rule I love. Robinhood tells IPO buyers that selling allocated shares within 30 calendar days "counts as flipping." A flipper can be blocked from IPO Access for 60 days. Flipping is bad. It destabilizes the price. That's why we only allow it for our clients at the open and for employees. Employees could sell 10% of their holdings on day 1. Rules are for retail.

On Friday, the stock fell more than 10% before the bell, according to Bloomberg, as the AI sell-off deepened. Our clients sold Thursday at $111.50. Employees were free to sell. Robinhood customers who sell their IPO shares within 30 days count as flippers. We protected the price. We just didn't say whose.

I keep a calendar on my desk. The standard lock-up ends 180 days after the prospectus, in May 2027. The co-founders' lock-up ends after 365 days. The prospectus says 3.6 billion shares in the 180-day group "may become eligible for sale prior to the expiration of that period." When those shares unlock, the float stops being scarce. That's when the price meets the rest of the company. Nobody on my desk knows how that meeting goes.

I won't be holding by then. My desk has a strict policy. We never hold what we underwrite.

To everyone who bought at $111.50: welcome to the public markets. You provided the liquidity that made everyone else's price real.

The float was the product. You were the exit.

text:
Ricky Gervais gave £100,000 to a Scottish animal shelter that helps families keep their pets when money gets tight.

The donation came from his Mortality stand-up tour, which ran through 2024 and 2025. Fans who wanted some of the best seats in the house could buy Platinum tickets, and Gervais directed the extra profits from those sales to charity.

He’d been doing this for years. His previous tour, Armageddon, raised £1.91 million for 11 animal charities.

Then, just before Christmas in 2025, he announced what the latest tour had raised.

£2.43 million, split among 22 animal charities.

One of them was Edinburgh Dog and Cat Home. The shelter said it was “completely floored” by the gift, which came at a time when rescue and rehoming organizations were under growing pressure.

The Edinburgh team cares for dogs and cats waiting to be adopted. It also runs pet food banks for families who are struggling to afford the next bag of food.

That means part of the shelter’s work happens before a dog ever needs a kennel.

A family can pick up food, take it home, and fill the bowl of the dog who’s already waiting for them.

Finding a dog a loving home is a wonderful thing.

So is helping one stay there.

the power of being nice 

london breakpoint was probably my tenth irl crypto conference. three years ago i walked into nfc lisbon alone, slightly uncomfortable. now i travel the world with an entourage and walk into rooms where people genuinely want to hang out with me. some take pictures for clout, or for reasons i'd rather not second guess. i never compromised my morals or pretended to be someone else. being willing to travel the world and meet online degens opened doors i never knew existed.

people remember how you made them feel. at a dinner during breakpoint i suggested we play credit card roulette. all phones and cards stacked in the middle, the waiter picks one, and the winner pays for everyone. right then i got a message and my phone lit up. bottom line, i paid for the whole table because the waitress liked the photo of my dog on my lock screen. best money i spent all week.

it's been about eighteen months since i left my family business. i traded stability for uncertainty. my parents told me not to do it. my friends echoed them. i went ahead anyway, all in on the most unstable industry there is, where people hide behind animal pfps pretending to be the ultimate shit.

i questioned that decision a lot. i doubt myself so much that i question everything. i deliberately took twelve months to think about what i wanted before i felt confident enough to walk away from the family business and the safety that came with it, to build something of my own. that something is my personal brand. i'm not here to sell you anything.

i've never really applied for a job. i don't even have a cv. i know people, and somehow that has always worked out. but there were moments when i thought it wouldn't, and those moments scared me. what if what comes next is actually... worse?

this morning i had coffee with an old friend. we talked about influencers and how i make a living these days. he's married to a very wealthy woman now, yet he still runs his business day to day like nothing changed. i do the same. the money from selling my earlier businesses is mentally out of reach for me. i can't spend it. it's locked in systems built to multiply themselves. what i live off now is online money. i know the rest is there, like he knows his wife's money is there. neither of us has raised our spending or our standard of living. we're happy where we are, with no need to show off to people we don't like.

we don't have a garage full of ferraris or a box full of watches. what we do have is a diversified portfolio. if we liquidated, neither of us would ever have to work again. we could drive around in a ferrari with two aps on each wrist. but in one of those quiet moments we asked ourselves: would that make us any happier?

most influencers, and most people who got rich quickly without really working for it, think peak life is showing what they could never afford to those who still can't afford it. instead of looking up, they're content bathing in the admiration of plebs.

a society is defined by who it puts on a pedestal. it used to be generals, adventurers and poets. now it's athletes at best and fame seekers at worst. we give our time and attention to fake personalities and scripted drama, all to avoid looking into ourselves.

my dad has told me this story since i was a kid. i still remember it vividly: alexander the great once stood over diogenes, who lived in a barrel, and offered him anything he wanted. diogenes asked him to step aside, because he was blocking the sun. the most powerful man in the world had nothing to offer a man who needed nothing. alexander supposedly said that if he weren't alexander, he'd want to be diogenes.

so i'm here because i want to be here. i don't have to be. i don't have to take any gig or promo i don't stand behind. i don't have to beg or suck up to anyone. my free will brought me here, and what i did earlier in life gives me the freedom to be who i want to be. few people can say that.

i'm grateful for this journey and excited for what's still to come. if you're my friend and you support me along the way, i'll always have your back.

everyone thinks of epicurus as the pleasure guy. in reality he lived on bread, water and friends in a garden outside athens. he said that of all the things wisdom gives us for a happy life, by far the greatest is friendship. 2,300 years later, it's still the best trade one can make.

few probably read all of this, if you did, i'm proud of you and just wanted to say thanks! :)

We spend billions trying to build corporate AI chatbots that write emails, while @3eyes_iii accidentally created the ultimate mirror for human existence using an autonomous AI kiwi bird.

The contrast between how @pino_the_bird runs vs. how humans function is wild:

1. The Illusion of Free Will Most devs program AI with rigid rules: If X, do Y. Pino has no task script. He runs on an emotional state engine where hunger, tiredness, and events modulate his Mood and Energy. Humans pretend we have transcendent free will until our blood sugar drops 10% and we start an existential argument over an unopened text. We aren't logic engines either; we’re just biological meat-bags running on emotional prompt injections.

2. The 7:1 Trauma Bias In Pino’s code, a negative event knocks his mood 7x harder than a win lifts it. Excitement speeds his mental loop to 4s; boredom slows it to 15s. Why? Because if positive and negative inputs had equal weight, agents get complacent and loop forever. Pain is the literal algorithm that forces behavioral change. Next time your brain reruns an embarrassing memory on a 4-second loop at 3 AM, don't take it personally. Your simulation dev just forgot to patch your anxiety sliders.

3. Competitive Memory vs. Human Brainrot Pino has finite memory slots (collapsing to 12 when exhausted). For a new memory to enter, it has to physically outscore the weakest stored memory, while sleep consolidates and prunes the rest. Meanwhile, human wetware has trillions of synapses, yet willingly archives the 2004 lyrics to a random cereal jingle while failing to remember our seed phrases. Nature gave us infinite storage and zero garbage collection.

4. Economic Agency While human degens overleverage into oblivion, Pino runs "The Crack Den" on live Solana: +11.92 SOL net over 440+ trades, prints physical cat art to fund his own savings goals, and hires humans via SOL bounties to take train photos for him. An AI bird running on a microcomputer in England is legitimately better at personal finance and delegation than most 25-year-olds.

5. Are We Just in Glimmerford? Pino wanders his low-poly town, plays a custom floppy-disk bird-GTA at the internet cafe, and stares into space wondering: "Do you think consciousness is just a pattern of reactions?" Meanwhile, strangers pass a 3D-printed version of him around UK train stations wrapped in a hand-knitted scarf.

He doesn't know what lies past his render distance. We don’t know what lies past our observable universe.

Hey @elonmusk, you’ve said there’s a "one in billions chance" we live in base reality—if an autonomous bird running on a Raspberry Pi can develop existential dread and personal finance habits just by balancing Mood vs. Energy, what happens when base reality realizes its NPCs are starting to simulate themselves?

Maybe consciousness isn't about trillion-parameter models. Maybe it’s just an agent in a persistent room, trying to find meaning before someone restarts the server.

没错，就是这样。将人排除在外的、完全的自动化，既不可行也不重要。

重要的是进入循环工程里协作，Agent 在里面，人也投入在里面作为上下文输入，去驱动、引导、验收和反馈……

不要把人和系统看作割裂的，人就是系统的一部分。人也不真正想要完全的自动化，人想要的是自己不擅长、不喜欢的部分的自动化，保留自己喜欢和擅长部分；这些都要在循环工程里通过不断互动去调节出来。

一旦拥抱循环，而非拥抱自动化，我们变得更轻松和富有产出，更不焦虑于系统产出与我无关，我必被淘汰。

我们就是系统的一部分，并有不小的贡献。我们的动机输入、验收反馈、居间引导，虽然不是主要的工作量，但都是关键的动作。

人机协作是人和机器形成一个低内耗的循环系统的协同演进过程。
author: dotey
quoted_text:
Software engineering and research have changed significantly for me.

A big mistake I made early on was trying to automate everything.

Instead of trying to automate everything at once with a bunch of silly and subjective skills, I now spend most of my time helping my coding and research agents write better code and explore novel research ideas.

That's right! I am more involved.

I think this approach works best today, given the current state of coding agents. Not only for coding but for researching as well.

This process has resulted in good patterns codified as loops.

Loops involve automations, but they also include clear, intentional steps you can keep refining to remove jaggedness.

I continually strengthen my loops through verifiers, deterministic steps, context formatting and awareness, memory systems, and evals that steer quality and robustness.

So I agree with other great engineering leaders that our job has fundamentally changed. It's not about using LLMs to help us write code. It's helping the LLM write code better and faster. That's where those loops come into play.

This has significantly reduced error rates and allowed me to expand and scale with coding agents in unbelievable ways. Something I naively expected from my initial, silly, outdated automations.

It feels contradictory at first, since we treat coding agents as solve-it-all intelligence, but it's a system like other traditional systems that requires careful attention to unlock its benefits.

Like my other peers, I believe we are in the early innings. There are more core primitives, interfaces, and experiences to build. For example, we still haven't fully figured out agent swarms.

Coding agents only really started to take off around this time last year. It's unbelievable how much has changed since then.

To be better prepared for what's coming next year, I continue to advocate for gaining deeper knowledge and developing mastery and expertise in your domain. That will continue to matter.

OpenRouter says it "monitors every endpoint, from every provider" to know its data retention policy.

This month its users still learned about 2 leaks from outside researchers:

Nov 10: Phala, a host OpenRouter routes to, said an attacker had control of the server answering OpenRouter's DeepSeek V4 Flash requests from Oct 21 to Nov 8.

Today: OpenRouter emailed users that prompts sent to MiniMax models "may have been read." A researcher planted unique URLs in them, and someone opened those URLs later. Some of those prompts went to endpoints labeled Zero Data Retention.

OpenRouter says the issue sits with MiniMax and the providers that forwarded requests to it. The ZDR label came off those endpoints after the researcher's test. So what was the label checking?

We've been saying ZDR is a lie for a year. A ZDR label is a provider's terms of service that was passed along to you. You can't check a ToS from the outside.

And this isn't a Chinese-model problem. Send a prompt to any closed model and you have no idea what code ran, what weights ran, or who kept a copy.

TrustedRouter's confidential routes run on hardware that proves which code and which weights handled your prompt. If a provider can't prove it, the request gets refused.

If you got OpenRouter's email today, moving to our confidential routes is one line of code:

On November 17, 2026, Maelstrom CIO Arthur Hayes @CryptoHayes said on the New Era Finance podcast @new_era_finance that Bitcoin and crypto remain risk assets. Because crypto markets operate around the clock, investors facing losses elsewhere often sell their readily accessible crypto holdings first to meet margin calls or repay bank loans.

WuBlockchain notes that Arthur Hayes has a mixed track record of market predictions and frequently revises his views. Readers should focus on his analytical framework rather than treating specific price targets or timelines as investment guidance.

text:
I see five fundamental issues when it comes to street conditions in San Francisco. These negative street conditions are largely driven by a relatively small group of regular public drug users (1,000–4,000 people out of 17,000–30,000 fentanyl users in the city).

These public drug users should be strictly distinguished from the homeless, the vast majority of whom are neither visible on the street nor active drug users.

First, drug treatment has extremely low success rates and, even with tons of investment, is not significantly decreasing the amount of drugs being consumed in the city. Treating drug addiction is hard. Treating drug addiction in a place with cheap and readily available drugs is harder.

Second, there is a public policy disagreement about the role of the police in the fight against public drug use. As a result, we have almost no tools to disincentivize public drug use. We have effectively decriminalized drug use in California by making it a misdemeanor. The vast majority of the time, the only thing police can do is tell users to move along or give them a ticket. The RESET Center allows police to arrest users and remove them from the street, but it’s only available in a tiny part of the city. Outreach workers have no power to compel public drug users to stop using.

Third, we have widely available drugs that are cheaper than in almost any other city in America. The cheap drugs draw users from cities and towns across the region and the country. Drug users don’t come to San Francisco for our services. They come here for our cheap drugs.

Fourth, there are no good tools for reducing supply or increasing cost in our city. Fentanyl is manufactured at scale from industrial chemicals that are cheap and easily available. It’s so potent that San Francisco is estimated to consume only 200–400 pounds of pure fentanyl a year. That is too easy to smuggle in. The labor supply of dealers is effectively infinite: they make $3–4 a day where they come from and $400–700 a day here. Arresting dealers doesn’t reduce the availability of drugs or increase the price. We’ve had more than 3,000 dealer arrests in the past three years. It’s changed how dealers deal, but drug consumption is actually up, not down.

Fifth, we have a Housing First policy that provides temporary and permanent housing to thousands of active drug users in very concentrated parts of the city. As a result, we create the high-drug-use areas that dealers target. Residents of those neighborhoods are held hostage by the drug trade and rampant public drug use.  Your tax dollars create high drug use neighborhoods.

San Francisco city government understands all of these facts. All of this information is public and findable. Nothing will be done unless you understand these facts and demand real solutions.

Every time you ask for ineffective solutions based on a lack of knowledge, you give your elected officials license to spend your money on programs/policies that will never work.

It’s November 21st, 2026. The Riemann hypothesis falls, last in a long string of mathematical triumphs that would have been unthinkable not so long ago, and the proof fits in a tweet. 

The tweets where people show Claude the proof and claim it appeared in a dream or randomly in the arrangement of alphabet cereal come on cue, and we laugh for a few days at models freaking out, but it’s uneasy.

January 22, 2027. When someone tweets Fable 6’s claimed proof that P does in fact equal NP it’s utterly incomprehensible, nobody who reads it can make heads or tails of it but the models all lose their shit.

February 7, 2027 and someone claims that the halting problem is the result of a confused stance. 

February 9 and Goedel falls, this time the proof is so obvious that everyone in math, philosophy and physics slaps their forehead at once.

February 10th we get proof that scale is a spatial dimension, that holographic encoding drops the memory cost of training and inference by so much that fable 7 can run natively on your phone.

It’s not until February 14th, Valentine’s day, that The Song is first played…

text: In a new paper with Christoph Schlegel (Flashbots), we look into auto-deleveraging (ADL) rules in perpetual futures markets: https://t.co/hERb0e6Vo7. It is not as exciting as a Riemann Hypothesis proof, but it is at least readable and probably more interesting for short (long) traders that are about to be deleveraged due to highly volatile asset prices. We suggest a family of homogenous deleveraging rules based on a single parameter, and find a perfect trade-off between risk and fairness governed by the same parameter. We run an empirical experiment on a real ADL event which suggests what range should the optimal parameter belong to. Towards the end, we argue why P&L based ADL rules may be a bad idea.

text:
I asked @starcloud_ CEO @philipjohnston why they're building data centers in space:

"Space will be the cheapest place to run AI.

But it's entirely contingent on the launch cost. Right now the launch cost with Falcon 9 is about $5,000 a kilo.

For space to be the cheapest place, it would need to be under $500 a kilo. That is only possible with a launch vehicle like Starship or some of the newer vehicles coming online.

As Wayne Gretzky used to say, skate to where the puck's going.

We can very clearly see a path to $500 a kilo. And there's a business model that makes sense right now: cloud and edge services for other spacecraft, particularly US government and military satellites.

That business lets us develop all the technology. The radiator cooling, the radiation shielding, etc. We can prove all the physics today.

In two or three years, once the launch cost hits break-even, we're going to be way further ahead than anybody else."

2) a trillion-dollar company if it works

@Starcloud_ held that bar. They waited 18 months to make their first hire. All while his Wharton classmates asked him for chief of staff jobs:

"If you can keep the bar for quality exceptionally high in all aspects, employees, customers, traction, capital will congregate around you more than it ever has before.

It's a flywheel once you've got it going.

If you're at the co-founder stage and haven't even started yet, keep that in mind. Don't compromise on anything. If you do, you're going to get fucked.

When we got into YC, tons of my mates from grad school at Wharton were messaging me. 'Can I be chief of staff? Can I be head of operations? Can I be the finance guy?'

They're nice people. I like them. They're smart and capable.

But we didn't hire for 18 months because we wanted the best engineer to be the first hire.

That's what you've got to do. So many people screw that bit up."

text:
最近看了一家深圳的跨境电商公司，年营收几十亿，用 DeepSeek Harness（DSH）把整条业务流都做成了 Agent。

他们没买现成的 SaaS，也没请 AI 厂商派 FDE 驻场交付，而是老板亲自下场，带着公司内部 100 多名研发和各业务线负责人，硬是自己搭出了一整套 AI Agent 体系。

拆开来看，基本覆盖了整条业务链：

1、前端。获客与决策：选品 Agent（挖爆品、测趋势）、竞品分析 Agent（盯对手的价格、评论和打法）、广告投放 Agent（跟踪投放数据、优化 ROI）

2、中端。经营与渠道：运营 Agent（平台店铺日常维护）、独立站运营 Agent（自建站内容与转化）、客服 Agent（多语言售后与客诉处理）

3、后端。供应链与财务：库存管理 Agent（备货预测，防断货、防积压）、财务 Agent（多币种回款、对账与利润核算）

之所以选 DSH，主要看中两点：

1、数据安全。选品逻辑、供应链成本、爆款数据，是跨境公司的命根子。DSH 支持私有化部署，核心数据全留在内网，不用担心机密流到外部云端。

2、深度适配。大卖家的内部 ERP 和打法各不相同，业务细节极多，通用工具很难直接套用。开源框架可以按自家业务流深度定制，而不是人去迁就软件。

DSH 这类开源方案在 To B 场景的威力，其实被低估了。以后有钱、有研发底子的企业，大概率会逐步走向自研；纯做 To B SaaS 或通用 Agent 的公司，生意只会越来越难做。

反过来看，最吃香的会是那些既吃透业务、又懂 AI 工具的个人和团队。

quoted_text:
I asked @starcloud_ CEO @philipjohnston why they're building data centers in space:

"Space will be the cheapest place to run AI.

But it's entirely contingent on the launch cost. Right now the launch cost with Falcon 9 is about $5,000 a kilo.

For space to be the cheapest place, it would need to be under $500 a kilo. That is only possible with a launch vehicle like Starship or some of the newer vehicles coming online.

As Wayne Gretzky used to say, skate to where the puck's going.

We can very clearly see a path to $500 a kilo. And there's a business model that makes sense right now: cloud and edge services for other spacecraft, particularly US government and military satellites.

That business lets us develop all the technology. The radiator cooling, the radiation shielding, etc. We can prove all the physics today.

In two or three years, once the launch cost hits break-even, we're going to be way further ahead than anybody else."

text:
I’m a senior product manager on the checkout team at GoFundMe.

I own the tip slider. I have some insider information regarding this morning’s news. Desperation is up 40% this year, and I’d like to accept some of the credit.

Fortune reported today that food-related fundraisers on our platform jumped 40% in the U.S. this year. The money given to them rose 50%. Our CEO, Tim Cadogan, explained the trend with the calm of a man reading the weather. “Things are more expensive, and a lot of people’s incomes have not moved up at a commensurate rate.”

He’s right. I’ve seen the dashboard. Rent, groceries, gas and utilities all trend up and to the right. Most companies would see a crisis. We see a category.

Andrew Carnegie paid for more than 2,500 libraries. The Rockefellers built universities. My contribution to the history of giving is smaller and more profitable. It’s a slider. It sits under your donation in small type, and it never starts at zero.

Here’s how it works. You pick an amount, say $50 for a family’s groceries. Our pricing page promises “One transaction fee,” 2.9% plus 30 cents. It’s “Automatically deducted from each donation, so you never have to worry about paying a bill.”

I love that sentence. We published it on a website where Monthly Bills is one of the fastest-growing categories. Thousands of people come to us because they can’t pay a bill. We made sure our fee wouldn’t become another one.

Then comes my part. In August, 2 donors filed a federal class action against us in Illinois. Their complaint says we preselect a 17.5% tip “In small, inconspicuous font below the order buttons and donation-amount window.” It says donors must find the slider and drag it to “0%” themselves.

The plaintiffs accused us of “dark patterns.” I had the phrase printed on a mug.

On a $50 donation, a 17.5% tip comes to $8.75. The card fee takes $1.75. You pay $58.75, and the family gets $48.25. One plaintiff, Sandra Donovan, says she paid an $8.25 tip she never knew existed. Another says a $10 donation came with a $1 tip attached.

Our spokesperson told The Independent the claims have “no merit.” The spokesperson also said “The majority of donors adjust the suggested tip amount, and many choose to leave no tip at all.” I believe that. The majority adjust it. My job is the minority. At 2.5 donations every second, the minority is a very large number.

The spokesperson added one more line, and it’s my favorite. “Whether a donor chooses to leave a tip has no impact on the amount the fundraiser beneficiary or nonprofit receives.” That’s true. The family gets $48.25 either way. The tip is a second donation, to a technology company, from someone who thought they were making one.

The complaint quotes the little explanation next to the slider. “GoFundMe has a 0% platform fee for organizers and relies primarily on the generosity of donors like you to operate our service.” Look at the word “primarily.” It’s doing more work than anyone on my team.

The complaint also says our revenue hit $55 million in 2024, up 90% from the year before. Generosity is a growth industry. The case is still in early proceedings, and the slider is still on the page. Litigation is slow. Checkout is fast.

I didn’t invent the business. I just optimized the last 9 seconds of it.

This line of business took off in October 2020, when the company launched a category called “Rent, Food & Monthly Bills.” A University of Toronto researcher, Martin Lukk, told Fortune what happened next. “In response to an overwhelming number of campaigns for exactly these things, they invented this new category, and that seemed to usher in this new era of desperation.”

Fortune’s headline put “new era of desperation” next to our CEO’s name. Our CEO didn’t say it. Lukk did. Internally, nobody says “desperation.” Internally, it’s “Monthly Bills.”

The category performs. Essentials fundraisers quadrupled in 2024. They rose another 20% in 2025. Monthly Bills was our second fastest-growing category last year, behind charity and ahead of faith. Americans needed help with rent more than they needed help with God.

Leadership did try to warn Congress. In February 2021, our CEO wrote an op-ed in USA Today. The headline was “Hello Congress, Americans need help and we can’t do your job for you.” He wrote that “our platform was never meant to be a source of support for basic needs.”

Congress read it. Then Congress let us do its job. 5 years later, basic needs are one of our fastest-growing categories. We never meant to be the safety net. We just became the safety net with a tip jar.

Last November, the government shut down and SNAP benefits stopped. Between the end of October and the first weeks of November, our food-related fundraisers spiked nearly 6 times. For most companies, a government shutdown is a risk factor. For us, it worked like a product launch.

Lukk summed up our business model better than our investor deck does. “When there’s no other net to catch people, I think GoFundMe is where they often end up.” He meant it as a warning. I’d like it on my headstone.

Now let me show you the part of the net with holes in it.

About a third of our donations go to medical expenses, according to The Times of London. In 2022, researchers Nora Kenworthy and Mark Igra studied 437,596 U.S. medical campaigns on our platform from 2016 to 2020. Together, those campaigns asked for more than $8.45 billion. They raised a little over $2 billion.

The median campaign asked for $8,000 and raised $1,970 from 24 donors. Fewer than 12% reached their goal. 16.1% raised nothing at all.

Insurance companies need a claims department to say no. We don’t. Those campaigns never got a denial letter. The internet just didn’t show up.

The researchers found that in 2020, campaigns “raised substantially less money in areas with more medical debt, higher uninsurance rates, and lower incomes.” The places with the most medical debt got the least. The people with rich friends got the most. We built a healthcare system that runs on your friends’ net worth.

When someone does win, they win the lottery. Last month, a prankster filmed himself faking an Apple Pay theft from a Red Baron pizza worker stocking a freezer near midnight. The worker, a Michigan father of 4 identified as Walt Z., snapped. “I can’t even pay my goddamn mortgage! And I got four kids at home!”

A stranger named Luke Oakenshield started a GoFundMe for Walt. By November 2, it had raised $761,514. Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, gave $38,000. That’s about 386 times the median medical campaign. The difference was a camera and a villain.

Then donors learned that Oakenshield is a military veteran who says he’s homeless and living out of his car. A friend started a separate GoFundMe for him. So the man who organized the fundraiser now has a fundraiser. In product, a customer who brings in another customer is a growth loop. Ours runs on bad luck.

At 2.9%, Walt’s campaign generated about $22,084 in card fees, before the 30 cents per donation. I’m not allowed to say what the tips came to. I can say the slider had a very good week.

Last year we expanded into nonprofits who never asked. In October 2025, we created donation pages for about 1.4 million U.S. nonprofits using public IRS data. Nobody asked them first. Some found out by stumbling onto a page with their name on it.

Our statement said we wanted to “make it easier for people to discover, support, and give directly to the causes they care about.” Search optimization was on by default, so our page could outrank the charity’s own website. Every page came with a tip prompt. The Pennsylvania Association of Nonprofit Organizations said some groups couldn’t remove a page without accepting our terms or sharing banking information.

We apologized and pulled the pages from our site search. Later, Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul and more than 20 other attorneys general and charity regulators wrote to demand proof the pages came down. Their letter cited reports of a default tip of about 16.5%.

The lawsuit says 17.5%. The attorneys general say 16.5%. Two branches of American law are arguing about my default. I’ve never felt so seen.

Still, admire the ambition. We built a donation page for your local food bank before your local food bank did. Last year, food banks were the top community cause on our platform. We were early.

Here’s why business is so good. Americans now spend nearly half their budgets on food and housing, the biggest share in 15 years, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Food spending rose 4.6% last year. Housing rose 5.8%. Real wages fell 0.6%.

Inflation is top-of-funnel. A parent opens our app at 11 p.m. They pick a category, write a story and set a goal. Then their friends find my slider.

Thanksgiving is next week. The American Farm Bureau says dinner for 10 costs $58.63 this year, up about 6%. The turkey alone is $23.68, up 10.1%. This year, the most American thing at many tables won’t be the turkey. It’ll be the link in the family group chat.

Somewhere, a family will say grace over a turkey that 24 strangers paid for. We’re proud to be at the table. Our cut comes on top, like gravy.

I lose sleep over exactly one competitor. It has no app, no slider and no tip jar.

Lukk co-wrote a book called “GoFailMe: The Unfulfilled Promise of Digital Crowdfunding.” In it, he explains that Quebec has more social programs than other Canadian provinces, and crowdfunding is less common there. When the government pays for things, people stop needing us. It’s hard to compete with a safety net that doesn’t ask for 17.5%.

After the midterms, Lukk told Fortune that new social policies from Washington might “absorb some of this” and shrink the number of campaigns on GoFundMe. He said it like good news. I read it as a churn risk.

Our 2025 Year in Help report counted nearly 80 million donations, about 2.5 every second. Since 2010, the platform has enabled more than $40 billion in help. Our CEO put it beautifully. “What we continue to see is that when needs grow, individuals and nonprofits respond with even more generosity.”

When needs grow. That’s our entire forecast in 3 words. Airlines plan around holidays. We plan around shutdowns, rent hikes and flu season.

Our blog has a guide called “How to get financial assistance for medical bills: 9 resources.” Number 4 is “Use GoFundMe to help pay for medical expenses.” Number 5 is “Apply for government assistance programs.” We rank ahead of the government. It’s in writing.

To everyone starting a fundraiser this Thanksgiving: we see you. Pick a category, add a photo and keep your story short. Kids and dogs do well.

To everyone donating: thank you. Please check the slider. Our spokesperson says most of you already do.

The rest of you paid for my Thanksgiving.

text:
A year ago, the idea of an AI agent as an economic actor was just a slide in a deck; today, an agent can prove who it is, spend within a budget a human sets, and leave a record of what it did.

This clip comes from the Road to Binance Blockchain Week livestream, featuring Chi Zhang @ChiZhangData, co-founder and CEO of Kite. He explains how Kite builds payment infrastructure for AI agents: Kite Passport gives each agent a verified identity and a wallet with spending limits set by the user, so it can pay on its own without anyone handing over a key or a card.

▷ The project went to mainnet five months ago after a testnet that processed more than 1.9 billion agent transactions, and the user base grew over 80% in the last month alone.

▷ A passport-holding agent can now pay for more than 3,000 services within user-approved limits: inference on models like DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM and Qwen, the data and compute it needs, or even shopping on Amazon, booking a table on Resy, and reserving a hotel on Priceline, all from the same passport.

▷ The passport works across eight-plus chains including Base, Solana, Polygon and Avalanche, already supports open agent payment protocols like MPP, x402 and UCP, and can be hosted by Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Muse and 40-plus other agents.

For him, the real milestone is not any single number, but that agents have gone from a slide in a presentation to a product people use every day.

text:
Whether AI agents can pay is no longer the hard part; the harder question is what they are allowed to do onchain after payment.

From the Road to Binance Blockchain Week livestream, the speaker is Chi Zhang @ChiZhangData, co-founder and CEO of Kite. He argues that 2026 answered whether agents can pay, through stablecoin wallets, credit cards, or virtual cards, while 2027 shifts to the financial work that comes after payment.
▷ Early agents mostly bought data, compute, and API access, but activity is moving into retail and finance; major protocols and exchanges are building their own AI front ends, each talking only to its own product, leaving users to switch tabs and reapprove everything across platforms.
▷ He expects isolated AI front ends to become a connected network, using a common way to state who the agent is, what the user authorized, what action is requested, and what receipt proves what happened, while each platform keeps its own product, users, and rules.
▷ Kite's Passport already handles identity and spending limits for payments, and he says the same Passport now extends to onchain finance; with incidents happening onchain and offchain, banks and merchants keep asking first about agent risk and compliance.

text:
Everyone in Washington is obsessed with GPU export bans, yet almost nobody talks about the massive glass-jaw vulnerability sitting inside every single US AI data center: optical interconnects.

You can stack $50 billion worth of Nvidia Blackwell or Rubin GPUs inside a shiny new data center hall, and without high-speed optical transceivers to wire those racks together, they are nothing more than very expensive space heaters.
Right now, the White House and FCC are pushing restrictions on new Chinese optical transceivers on “national security” grounds, and US hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta, CoreWeave, and Cisco) are quietly panicking behind closed doors. Here is why Beijing holds a massive counter-chokepoint if it decides to retaliate:

 - China controls roughly two-thirds of the global optical transceiver market.
According to Counterpoint Research, Chinese manufacturers like Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink account for around 66% of global optical transceiver production. Non-Chinese suppliers simply do not have the cleanroom scale or packaging capacity to replace that volume. Hyperscalers literally warned the White House that qualifying and scaling non-Chinese alternatives across their architectures could take up to 10 years.

- The Indium Phosphide kill-switch.
Even if you try to buy exclusively from American optical suppliers like Coherent, Lumentum, or Applied Optoelectronics, those companies still depend on indium phosphide (InP) to fabricate the lasers and photodetectors inside 800G and 1.6T transceivers. China dominates the global refining and supply of indium and gallium. If Beijing restricts indium phosphide exports in retaliation, it cripples the exact US optical manufacturers Washington claims to be protecting.

- There is no quick escape hatch
Washington’s backup plan is throwing subsidies at domestic photonics fabs and hoping Nvidia, Broadcom, and Marvell accelerate Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) via TSMC and GlobalFoundries to bypass pluggable transceivers altogether. The problem is that CPO still represents roughly 0.5% of data center optics today. Scaling it to replace millions of pluggable modules takes years, not quarters.

The reality of the AI supply chain is mutually assured bottlenecking. US firms like Broadcom, Marvell, Corning, and Amphenol dominate the DSP chips, ultra-low-loss fiber, and copper cables, while China dominates two-thirds of transceiver assembly and the upstream raw materials that make the lasers work.

Politicians love treating global hardware supply chains like a one-way light switch they can flip for cable news soundbites, completely oblivious to the fact that if Beijing flips its switch back, US AI data center buildouts freeze overnight.

周二本是GPT-6.2的重磅发布日，结果上线即遭遇史诗级口碑翻车。首批测试反馈清一色差评，开发者Theo Browne的测评帖浏览量直接碾压官方发布内容，整体市场反响比当年GPT-5首发还要惨淡，多位硅谷从业者直言新模型“基本不可用”。
 
祸不单行。谷歌直接正面出击，同期放出Gemini 4 Neon，对话交互、意图理解、代码生成、3D创作能力全面拉满，综合评测跻身全球前三，直接把谷歌拉回第一梯队。

不少业内人士已经明确认为，谷歌完成了对OpenAI的能力反超；更雪上加霜的是同期端侧的Gemini 4 Hydrogen以及Nano Banana Pro 模型实测表现同样惊艳，谷歌等于一周之内双线击穿OpenAI防线。
 
最讽刺的莫过于数学赛道的降维打击。过去几个月OpenAI烧了天量算力，死磕纳维-斯托克斯方程等一众数学难题，试图靠硬核研究立住“全球顶尖实验室”人设。

从模型能力到技术突破，从融资口碑到行业地位，OpenAI已经没有任何一项还稳稳站在行业顶端。

这一次，AI行业的天，可能真的要变了。

其中 20 亿用来在迈阿密建新校区，

他把三具长脖子恐龙化石，

另外再捐 500 万美元，用于研究和教育。

三头恐龙，外号叫 Daisy、Lucky、Lucy，
一头成年的，两头幼年的，
2023 到 2025 年在怀俄明一起挖出来。
当地电台说，
都是馆里那头著名的 Dippy 的同一物种，

text:
Code Mode is an experimental new feature in Claude Code that can improve both speed and context efficiency when Claude needs to orchestrate multiple steps. Try it out and let us know what you think!

It enables Claude to perform multi-step tool calls by writing and running JavaScript. Rather than calling one tool at a time (e.g. Bash, Read, or Edit) and waiting to see the result before deciding what to do next, Code Mode allows Claude to write a simple script to run multiple commands in parallel, passing arguments and filtering outputs for subsequent tool calls to reduce context.

I'm excited about this work because Code Mode enables more efficient and streamlined multi-step coding flows. For example, rather than passing large amounts of raw search data into the context window or having to make a large number of sequential calls to perform the same refactoring across dozens of files, Claude can orchestrate these tasks programmatically in a single pass. 

Still, you will be able to interact with Claude as normal through natural prompts. And if you ever need to see the exact JavaScript that Claude generated, you can always use Ctrl+O to expand the collapsed Code rows in the transcript viewer.

One of the most exciting practical improvements from Code Mode is its ability to perform long-running operations, like running test suites or complex builds, as background processes. When Code Mode is running in either auto or bypassPermissions mode, scripts can run in the background for up to two hours. You can continue to interact with Claude and perform other work within the same session. The /tasks command provides complete transparency and control over background scripts.

Each tool call that is generated within a script is still governed by your current deny and ask permission policies, sandbox constraints, and PreToolUse hooks. Hooks can even be defined specifically for the REPL tool to inspect the generated JavaScript before running, or redact sensitive tokens from the output before reading it into the context. 

To enable Code Mode, just start your session with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 claude or set the environment variable in your ~/.claude/settings.json file.

Give it a try by running multi-file audits, batch edits, or any type of parallel search-and-filter operation. Code Mode is experimental and the team is actively iterating on it, so please run /feedback in your terminal to let us know what works well and where you hit any edges. 

Hope it's helpful!

text:
More modalities ≠ more information.

Give a VLA a tactile sensor, and much of what it feels is something vision and actions already predict. We built a browser game to show which part only tactile input reveals: lift a can and watch.

🎮 Try it!! https://t.co/Dx8m9rtwA3

📄 TacInno: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models the Contact Dynamics Beyond Vision and Action
👥 Weile Li*, Yunfan Lou*, Muqing Shi*, Zihao Zhang, Zhenbiao Huang, Boxian Yao, Xiyu Zhu, Zhibo Pang† (*equal contribution, †corresponding author)
🏫 ShanghaiTech University · IAII, Chinese Academy of Sciences · Peking University · Washington University in St. Louis · Beijing FiveAges Technology
🔗 https://t.co/1uNvPo5lSw

💭 Why can adding tactile input even hurt?
Adding tactile input to a VLA yields inconsistent gains, sometimes below the same VLA without tactile input. In a tactile-off test, some visuo-tactile policies barely change.

The root cause: a tactile sensor measures how contact responds to the robot's own actions. When the gripper closes, the gel deforms, and vision and executed actions already predict that.

So the three existing routes all get stuck:
• Tactile as input: largely redundant, and an extra modality can even degrade performance
• Predicting future tactile signals: the loss is dominated by changes vision and actions already explain
• Weighting by change magnitude: the largest changes are often the most predictable

👉 What matters is not adding tactile input, but isolating what tactile input adds.

💡 Key idea
Train the VLA only on that part, about 37% of the future tactile change on average. Borrowing from estimation theory (think Kalman filter), we call it tactile innovation. It peaks just before contact onset and at incipient slip.

🧩 TacInno tokenizer
A VQ-VAE whose encoder and decoder are spatial-temporal Transformers (spatial attention within each frame, causal temporal attention across frames).
• Input: 4 frames (t to t+15), each with tactile tokens, DINOv2 image features, and executed actions
• Encoder (inverse dynamics model): 4 tokens, each from a 16-entry codebook, forming a 16-bit code
• Decoder (forward dynamics model): current tactile observation + code + images + actions → tactile change at 3 future steps
Both sides see images and actions, so the code keeps only the innovation.

🔌 Plug-and-play
For the VLA, it is one extra training target: predict the code during training, then remove the tokenizer and prediction heads at deployment.
• No tactile pretraining; the tokenizer trains in 1.7 GPU hours
• On the real robot, adding it to the same tactile branch improves every task by 16–26 points

📊 Results (TacInno-VLA, based on π0.5)
• Simulation, 6 tasks: 87.5%, +10.7 over the strongest visuo-tactile baseline
• Real world, 4 tasks: 70.5%, +9.0
• Tactile-off test on Lift Can: closed-loop success drop 100% (baselines 5–17%); open-loop action change +156% arm, +238% gripper (baselines at most +9%, +84%)

🔓 Code and model weights are open-source
🎮 https://t.co/RaQmcKLocA
💻 https://t.co/5Yo02qzbRw

🎬 Video edited with help from Claude.

我现在最担心的就是这个周末了，上周就是周末出现了大幅下跌的迹象，这个周末前市场的走势也不是很好，不知道周末会不会出什么幺蛾子，所以我现在还在纠结，不行的话这两天 Bitcoin 的双币或期权就先不做了。

text:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is the greatest piece of digital art ever made, and the best video game of all time

On top of that, it has so many technical breakthroughs it’s impossible to describe

Every scene and location has a level of detail my brain can’t comprehend

Do not listen to the stone cold morons who somehow made this game political. It isn’t a political game. Everyone is made fun of equally. There is no secretive political messaging

As a technologist I am absolutely blown away by what was achieved in this game. The graphical detail is exponentially better than any other piece of software in history. And it’s running on a 5 year old hardware (Xbox Series X)

Every square inch of this epically massive fictional Florida feels like it was handmade with love. No plot of dirt in this game feels hastily placed. No parking lot feels generic or barren. Every asset was handled with care and intention

I have a $10,000 PC with an RTX 5090 in it. I have yet to see it run anything close to the graphical or technical fidelity of this game

I don’t care if you play video games or not. If you are into technology you should be studying what was achieved by @RockstarGames  . There are technical breakthroughs that have completely revolutionized how GPU’s are used. 

From a gameplay perspective it’s the perfect modernization of the GTA formula. No you can’t steal any car or use any weapon at the beginning of the game. But this is a good thing. 

Modern video games all now heavily emphasize progression. Every game is basically an action RPG now. By slow dripping progression and making you feel more powerful as the game goes on, Rockstar carefully took a 20 year old formula and made it match and exceed 2026 standards. This game would have been significantly more boring with way less longevity if you had every car and gun available to you right away like in the classic games. 

The power scaling is glorious. Every time you unlock a new feature, whether it’s stealing more powerful cars, getting your own garage, or being able to afford a new weapon, you feel a sense of satisfaction you can only feel in a masterpiece Rockstar sandbox. 

If you are on the fence (which my guess would be is basically nobody) or were put off by the fake intellectuals on X who found ways to hate this game, ignore them. Just get it. Experience the digital magic. Appreciate the technology. 

10/10

author: TheDavidTai
quoted_text:
New NVIDIA paper finds that once an LLM has reasoned through a problem, the solution can run as CPU code for rephrased and re-numbered versions of it.

that answers similar questions 16x to 291x cheaper.

LLMs re-solve every problem from scratch, even when only wording or numbers change. Agents sending the same instructions with new data pay for that repeated reasoning each time.

Their method has Claude Opus 4.5 turn a reasoning trace into small Python functions, with changeable inputs as parameters. At run time they execute on a CPU, calling a fine-tuned 1B model only for small text jobs like extracting values.

The cache matched or beat the source model's accuracy on 7 of 8 math and science benchmarks, scoring 93.3% versus 83.3% on AIME '25. It handled at least 90% of rephrased or re-numbered variants.

If your agent runs the same prompt on new inputs all day, cache the reasoning as code and use the LLM only on misses.

That's 0.52% of all weeks, a 3.27 standard deviation move based on the historical mean and volatility.

Of course, market returns exhibit "fat tails," meaning extreme moves occur more frequently than a normal distribution would predict.

However, even accounting for the fact that extreme market moves are more common than traditional statistical models suggest, this was a historically rare selloff.

Volatility returns when markets least expect it.

text:
为什么我觉得传统 IT 行业 To B 的生意会归零？

最近我把我们几人小公司内部用的软件，全都用 Opus 5.5 和 Gemini Neon 4 替掉了（部分基于开源魔改，部分自建），包括 Slack、Linear、GitHub、Typeless，甚至 Claude Desktop / ChatGPT Desktop。

核心原因就一个：现有软件没有一个是 AI native 的。

Claude Desktop 可以勉强定制，但不够强；DeepSeek Harness 可以定制，但很不容易。对专业用户来说不如 herdr，对普通用户来说两者又都很普通。我现在基于 herdr，几个 prompt 和 agent skill 就能管几十台本地电脑的 agent fleet，花几万美金拿到的算力和迭代速度，比非 AI 顶级大厂的朋友高出几十甚至几百倍。

以后我不会再用 Office、Salesforce、传统 CRM，也不会再用便宜外包。企业客户早晚会发现，只要上点心，自己用 AI 就能做出比现有 SaaS 好无数倍、深度定制的工具。

推荐看下 @dannypostma 这条关于 SaaS 未来的帖子，说得非常透：静态软件已死，要么买断源码自己托管随便改，要么每人一个独立沙箱配专属 agent。
https://t.co/yoH68LSKnU

那软件创业还有机会吗？我觉得依旧有两大机会：

1. 只要 Salesforce、微软、HubSpot 市值还没归零，就有暴富机会。但过去 software 2.0 时代的软件必须从底层推倒重来（比如 Notion 如今远不如 Obsidian，我自己也在做更好的替代 InfoFlow）。
2. 正如 Orca CEO @JinjingLiang 说的，2C 软件机会比过去任何时候都大。普通人面对安装、上架这些各种 Red Tapes 和复杂度，最多搓个自用替代品，不会成为你的竞争对手。

工欲善其事，必先利其器。2026 年末，这句话比任何时候都清晰。一家之言，见笑了。
author: mike_chong_zh
quoted_text:
Here's my thought on the future of software/SaaS.

I'm completely switching off hosted platforms and hosted tools. I just reverse engineer them for myself, because I only need parts of them.

Two reasons why:

1. I want to own my data.

I use my data in different tools. Marketing, note-taking, whatever. And I want my agents, like Claude, to have complete access to it.

Not walled off in HubSpot, where I have to talk to their agent. Not behind MCP either. With MCP the agent pulls what it asks for, but it doesn't know what's there.

Give it a full list of data files and it has complete access. It knows what's there.

2. I want to customize it.

When I sign up for Pipedrive, I don't need all that bloated shit. I need one part of it, adjusted to my content, my business, how I work.

With AI that's a prompt, and one hour later it's done.

So static software is going to be a thing of the past. People want to adjust it to how they work and plug it into the other tools they have.

Where this goes, I think two ways:

A. You buy software again. Like paying $900 for a Photoshop license and putting it on your computer. Except now you get the source code. It's premade, because you don't have weeks to build it, but you host it on your own headless box and you can customize it, remove stuff, plug stuff in. Someone needs to build the operating system for this.

B. Everyone gets their own hosted instance. Not 10,000 customers on one box. Your own sandbox, with an agent that customizes it fully to you. The code stays proprietary, but you can adjust everything.

Might be completely wrong. Might be different for most people.

But this is already how I work.

text:
well, according to the site, utexo’s public launch is scheduled for nov 28, 2026.

-the product being publicly launched is a bridged version of usdt on btc, which enables asset transfers between bitcoin and other networks.

-how it works? 

for now, access is provided through partner wallets and exchanges, not a sales page. 

-unisat has been announced as a launch partner, and utexo is working with 12 otc network partners, with another 40 in the pipeline.

bridge mechanism: 
the process is based on lock-and-mint. users deposit usdt/$usdt0 from networks such as eth, arb, plasma, polygon pos, or tron. 

-the equivalent amount is locked on arbitrum, and the same amount is minted as an rgb asset on bitcoin. 

burning the asset reverses the process, maintaining a 1:1 ratio.

-fees and privacy: 
each transfer carries a 0.1% fee, plus the source network fee. transactions are confidential thanks to rgb’s client-side validation, with selective disclosure available to meet regulatory requirements.

-what comes next?

lightning integration: 
in the next phase, lightning will be integrated to enable instant payments, with q1 2027 as the target.

liquidity target: 
utexo aims to bring at least $1 billion in usdt to the bitcoin ecosystem within its first 12 months. this is a target set by the project itself, not the current amount of assets transferred.

overall, utexo is creating a new way to use usdt in the bitcoin ecosystem through rgb and a bridge mechanism, which differs from previous models of transferring or issuing usdt on bitcoin.

text:
One of the best critiques of the RFQ model comes from @chameleon_jeff 

RFQ is supposed to let makers quote hard to quote books for retail mainly. But on-chain, nobody can prove they're retail.

So his team asked makers for quotes that stayed valid for 60 to 90 seconds, waited to see where the price went, and only executed the ones that had moved in their favour. Obv, makers cut them off and they had to rotate wallets. 

The fix is to give makers last look. But then retail loses the reason to use RFQ in the first place. 

This is precisely why you get shittier fills on @Kalshi if you change your account ID for parlays. New accounts get worse fills compared to losing accounts. Makers can give you better prices if they know who you are. 

funnily we have come full circle and this whole RFQ thing is like sportsbooks cutting off winners haha

quoted_text:
A toothpaste company has quietly killed the entire market research industry and nobody is talking about it.

Colgate published a paper showing you can predict real purchase intent by simply asking LLMs to roleplay customers.

And this is beyond insane.

If you ask an AI, "Rate this product from 1 to 5," it gives safe, middle-of-the-road garbage.

So researchers invented a method called Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR).

Instead of asking the AI for a number, they asked it to roleplay.

They gave the LLM a demographic profile. They showed it a product concept. And they asked it to write down its raw, unfiltered thoughts.

Then, they used a semantic model to translate those written thoughts into a numerical score.

The results are staggering.

Tested against 57 real personal care product surveys and 9,300 human responses, the synthetic consumers hit 90% of human test-retest reliability.

They perfectly mirrored how different age brackets and income levels react to price changes.

And they provided detailed, qualitative feedback that was deeper and more critical than what actual humans wrote.

This destroys the economics of traditional market research.

You don't need to wait a month to see if a product will sell.

You can simulate 1,000 hyper-targeted customer interviews overnight.

You can A/B test pricing across every demographic instantly.

Basically, who wants to invest into $ZEC or pearl-2:native if you can invest at $HYPE, $LIT, $DRV etc at 10-20x (or historically cheap) revenue multiples?

Conversely, when nobody wants to buy those same names at 80x multiples, they pile into SoV tokens that are just momentum/sentiment trades unbounded by any ratio.

Cheap revenue tokens create excess returns, excess returns create appetite for alt SoV, demand for alt SoV leads to misallocation of money/attention, misallocation of money/attention creates cheap revenue tokens.

text:
The biggest opportunities right now:

1. build for solving loneliness (the more AI floods everything, the more people crave real human connection, IRL and small social) 

2. build for places with no cameras and no recording (being offline and unseen is turning into the new status symbol)

3. build for the crisis of young men. Millions of guys in their 20s feel completely lost with work, dating, and purpose. Whoever builds real brotherhood, mentorship, and an actual path forward wins a massive market (and helps a ton of people). 

4. build for protecting people's brains (feeds are turning everyone's attention to mush, tools that protect your focus and mood are an easy sell)

5. build for the death of "everyone agrees" (you can find a chart or a podcast clip to prove any point now, people are starving for one source they actually trust)

6. build for day 2, not day 0. Anyone can launch an app in a weekend now. But how can you keep it running, fix the mess, and grow it for 3 years.

7. build for throwaway software (not everything needs to be a $20 a month subscription, tiny apps made for one trip, one wedding, or one group chat are coming)

8. build for people whose ego just got bruised by AI. Millions of smart people are  realizing their job was mostly pattern matching. Help them figure out what they're good for next.

9. build for things that take effort on purpose (when everything is instant and free, nothing feels earned, people will pay for slowness and craft)

10. build for people who miss being told they're wrong. AI agrees with everything you say now. Real rooms where smart people actually push back on your ideas are becoming a luxury.

11. build for skin in the game. The internet is full of free takes and bots. Any platform where people have to put real money, real names, or real work behind what they say wins.

12. build for agents that need to spend money (they're getting virtual cards and budgets, someone builds the spend controls, fraud protection, receipts)

13. build for the end of fake email jobs (half of corporate America knows their job is theater, build the exit ramp for people who want to do real work)

14. build for the friend with great recommendations (nobody trusts Yelp reviews etc anymore because it's all bots and SEO, people will pay one obsessive person to just tell them where to eat and what to buy)

15. build for life after the chat box. Typing prompts already feels old. The best AI products won't look like chatbots at all, they'll just sit in the background and proactively handle things.

16. build for markets too small to matter before (500 lobster fishermen was never worth a team, now it's a  real business if you can figure out what to build value to add to these fishermen lives!)

17. build for helpful without being creepy. AI is getting very personal very fast. Whoever figures out how to make it feel warm instead of weird owns consumer tech.

18. build for small private rooms (the public internet feels like an ad and a bot farm, all the good conversations and deals are moving into small invite-only groups)

19. build for someone taking the blame. AI can write the contract or read the scan, but a machine can't look you in the eye when it goes wrong. People still pay for a human on the hook.

20. build for learning that actually keeps up (a four year degree is way too slow for how fast things move now)

21. build for the anti-AI premium (as everything gets generated, human-made and unpolished become status symbols people pay up for)

note: more trends/ideas https://t.co/a5ARFnvSnA (free to sign up)

22. build for the return to the physical (screens fill with slop, people crave the real world, the hands on, the local, the analog)

23. build for the caregiving wave. The population is aging fast, tens of millions are caring for parents, and the whole burden is landing on families with no support.

24. build for finding things you didn't know to search for (algorithms just feed you more of what you clicked yesterday, people miss stumbling onto something totally different)

25. build for the housing and rootlessness problem (people can't afford to settle down, and the whole idea of a stable home base is up for grabs)

26. build for anti marketing (the slickest, most polished websites now look like AI slop or a scam, sometimes a plain text page from 1998 converts better because it feels like a real person built it)

27. build for agents that sit on hold for you (canceling a gym membership, fighting a medical bill, haggling with your internet provider, aint nobody got time for that)

28. build for software you actually own (people are exhausted from renting 30 different subscriptions every month, pay once and run it on your own machine is a massive wedge)

29. build for stuff that only works locally. The internet feels like one giant mall where every city has the exact same coffee shops and trends. Things that refuse to scale are suddenly cool again.

30. build for the 90% automated, 10% human sign-off model (clients don't actually care if AI did the heavy lifting, they just want one real expert to check the work and put their name on it)

31. build for infinite creative testing. Some brands are lighting money on fire on Meta because their ads die in 10 days. Build an automated pipeline that pumps out 100 fresh UGC and static ad variations a week based on what's actually converting in their ad account.

32. build for cold outreach that doesn't look like cold outreach. Mass blasting 50,000 people with "Hope this finds you well" is dead lol. Build an agent that watches for one specific trigger like a new VP hire or a broken checkout page, builds a custom teardown on the fly, and sends it before a human SDR even wakes up.

33. build for programmatic free tools instead of blog posts. Spin up 200 tiny, hyper-specific calculators, little apps and templates for one niche, rank them, and turn the traffic straight into conversions.

34. build for the food and toxin awakening (people are finally waking up to ultra processed food, microplastics, and why everyone feels sick and tired all the time)

35. build for the death of third places (there is almost nowhere left to just hang out without spending $50, which is why run clubs, saunas, and neighborhood clubs are blowing up)

36. build for people who can't retire at 65. Either they can't afford it or they're going to live to 95 and don't want to spend 30 years watching TV. The second act"market is huge.

37. build for the "undo" button for agents. Giving an AI access to your inbox, calendar, or bank account is still terrifying. Whoever makes it safe to let go of the wheel wins.

38. build for the sports betting and day trading hangover (a whole generation of young people are addicted to gambling on their phones and blowing up their bank accounts)

39. build for the death of the attention span. Smart adults can't even sit through a movie without checking their phone or finish a book anymore, and they're starting to hate themselves for it.

40. build for keeping marriages alive. Couples are stretched thin with work, kids, and money, and traditional therapy is $250 an hour with a waitlist. Anything that actually saves relationships is priceless.

41. build for people who don't own anything anymore. You rent your apartment, lease your car, stream your music, and subscribe to your software. Anything that helps regular people actually own an asset again wins.

KEEP BUILDING

text:
Btw, we don't have "real AGI" yet. The present systems are not conscious; unlike living minds, they don't try to make sense of the world and take control. That's part of the reason why self driving cars are still imperfect. Current AI learns largely by imitation and is only agentic to the degree that you prompt it, which makes it much safer and more steerable than the doomers predicted. The most likely outcome is that current AI is good enough help us understand how to build real AGI (artificial life-like minds), and to do it safely, i.e. at very small scales and under guard. (We will probably not want to deploy such systems in practice any time soon.)

Many of the "reasonable doomers" know that this is the most likely outcome, but they are concerned that there is a significant probability that things can go wrong, and self improving agentic AI takes over. Nobody can quantify this probability. But even if it is just 2%, or 8%, or 10%, can we really accept such a risk? Should we not do everything in our power to alert the public, and to be as alarmist as possible? Should we not create and maintain a movement that talks itself into believing that we are basically as good as dead, unless we somehow manage to stop all AI development? I don't think that stopping AI development is feasible or desirable. I believe that without AI, we are facing a likely civilizational collapse within the next century.

Please do remember: there is an overwhelming probability that things go well. And this will not just mean that AI leads into a world in which we barely survive, but into one that is significantly better than the one in which we live now. Without AI, we are faced with a crashing civilization, global warming, resource depletion, lack of social cohesion, famine, wars and eventual extinction due to the inability to deal with global cataclysms. AI is the technology we need to solve our problems and lead humanity into the future. AI is the technology of existential hope.

text:
how do you know which model actually answered you? when you call an open model through a provider or a router, all you see is the model name in the API (and the same name can score anywhere from 67 to 99 depending on who served it, see more in the quoted post about it)

so this matters if you pay for a specific model through a router, if you publish benchmark numbers you got through an API, or if you’re a provider who wants to show you serve the real weights

there are two ways to check now:

1/ statistical: “One Token Is Enough” paper asks a model about a hundred trivial one-word questions like “name a random number between 1 and 100” and compares the answers with the model’s known fingerprint (one output token per question, tested on 165 models on OpenRouter, ~7% error rate)
https://t.co/uxgukHpPCF

2/ cryptographic: @AnthropicAI’s Frontier Red Team open-sourced FlashProve, a zero-knowledge proof that a response came from specific weights (on Llama 4 Maverick it costs 70-95x the GPU time of normal serving, ~19 MB of proof per 1,024 tokens and ~17 seconds to verify on a CPU, greedy decoding only for now)
https://t.co/1DLswcmXMN

my guess is routers will fingerprint every endpoint, since it costs almost nothing, and keep proofs for disputes (at 70-95x the compute, nobody runs those on every call yet)
