text: Great writeup on the process leading to the Mio that grew from Erick’s desire to make things and share them widely that’s been present for the 25 years I’ve known him. In an age where we’re being overrun by automation, this sort of exploration of craft and expression feels fresh!
author: JordanLyall
quoted_text:
Sorry in advance for the long wall of text but wanted to share the story of how I went from tinkering with my kiddo to a real product that quietly includes the generative medium and this technology that we're all so passionate about.

Back in March my 10-year-old asked me to buy him a crappy click counter on Amazon. I hesitated and instead said we should make our own. We have all sorts of electronic components lying around the house and so we grabbed a small processor, an LCD, and a button and wired it all together. It was a fun weekend project and after we had a basic prototype we decided to add a battery and put it into an enclosure.

I’ve never been much of a fidgeter myself but we brought it with us on a road trip and I found that it made the drive smoother. It gave me something to do, and when the kids passed it around the back seat they were less likely to fight.

When we got back home we decided to spend a bit more time on it. I worked with my kiddos to build a bunch more features into it because why not? Well eventually I thought it would be cool to bring in a little bit of my craft, so we created some algorithms to generate little friends that would react to your clicks and do different things when you hit milestones. We also added emojis and eventually confetti too.

Little by little I found myself spending more time with this thing. I became obsessed with the idea of a clicker/fidget toy that could a) help me wrap my head around what a million of anything actually feels like and b) let me do that with other people around the world. We added a leaderboard and started sending a few prototypes to friends. Before we knew it we had a waiting list of my kid’s friends who wanted one and a few dozen people all contributing to a global click count.

That click count now stands at almost 25,000,000 clicks and some days we add as many as 500,000! Started to think, could we hit one billion clicks? Or more? I couldn’t find another object quite like this. Maybe a Tamagotchi but I was sort of excited about a device that doesn’t punish you for forgetting to feed it. So sometime in May I decided to get serious about seeing what it would take to turn this into a real product. And so the mio click was born.

I’m obsessed with documenting things on the blockchain, and while we don’t expose this to users (yet), every single 1/1 character is made algorithmically, Art Blocks style, and lives 100% on chain. Every time you sync the clicks on your device, the count gets updated on your character’s NFT so the blockchain ends up being the source of truth. Right now we’re generating @privy wallets for folks to hold their characters on @base  mainnet. You don’t have to think about any of that, but eventually you’ll be able to take control of the artwork just like any other NFT in your collection.

Around the same time we were starting to work on ABX, a new tool from Art Blocks for making things on chain. I wanted the mio to exist on chain BUT it didn’t really fit into the normal Art Blocks system. Same with Sprite Party, which debuted in Marfa this year. There’s just some stuff that needs a bit more flexibility, and less intensity, than deploying a proper generative art project on Art Blocks or creating a bunch of smart contracts from scratch.

We’d developed PostParams at Art Blocks, a way to update data on an NFT after it’s minted. That was perfect for these projects and ABX was going to support it from the start, so this was happening at a perfect time. ABX helped shape the mio, and the mio and other projects the team was working on helped shape ABX! Win win.

So now we had a product, but I was using off-the-shelf components to assemble these. The v0 was fine but I wanted something more compact. I was curious if I could apply some of the skills I had learned over the last few years to design and build a custom PCB for the device. Well the first couple of prototypes failed but by the third we had a custom circuit board with the exact specs I wanted for the mio, in a smaller device and at a lower cost. I started sourcing the LCD and battery in higher volume and we purchased a few 3D printers to make the enclosures. We decided to work towards an initial batch of 1,000 units.

All was going smoothly until we hit the reality of bureaucracy. We needed some certifications for the device (battery testing, drop tests, etc.) before we could officially sell this thing to people. This ended up taking a lot more time than we expected but finally, just a couple of days before Marfa, we got our certs and were clear to sell them!

This whole experience has been a ton of fun, and it includes my entire family (the kiddos provide ideas and inspiration, my mom applies adhesive to the LCDs on the weekend and my wife Mara handles the packaging design and and fulfillment via @generativegoods) and a bunch of friends who were kind enough to test out the early prototypes. The @artblocks_io  team also got meaningfully involved and turned this weekend project into something real. They handled branding, website design, the certification process and some consulting with an industrial design firm in Austin.

It’s unbelievable what we can build these days. I never imagined my family and I would spend this much of 2026 building an electronic device from scratch, let alone one where I get to make generative art, put it on chain, and have people all around the world play along. But it’s something I’ve become obsessed with and am incredibly proud of. And like just about everything else I focus my time on, I think it can help bring our weird little corner of the internet to more and more people.

The dream is to make bigger and bigger batches and get the price down to where you’d grab one for a kid’s birthday party. We’ve got a ways to go, but in the meantime what you get is a homemade electronic device assembled by me and my family here in Houston. You can enjoy it offline or sync up with the rest of the “mioverse” and click along with hundreds, soon to be thousands and maybe one day millions of people around the world.

Would be so excited for y’all to grab one from this handmade batch, show it to your family, share feedback and ideas, and be a part of this with us from the ground floor. And to all of you who already have one, who together contribute hundreds of thousands of clicks a day, and who’ve shared your (and your kids’) enthusiasm for this little connected clicker, thank you.

🍻

WHO ARE THESE PEOPLE? And why are they still running $NVDA ?

1. Stephen C. Neal | Lead Independent Director & Governance Chair

He’s supposed to guarantee board independence, yet he was CEO of Cooley LLP from 2001 to 2008, the law firm involved in NVIDIA’s 2002 accounting review after SEC concerns.

How independent does that actually look?

2. Tench Coxe | Director since 1993 (Audit & Compensation)

Court records show he sold 160,000 shares for over $8.6M in Nov 2001 during the accounting controversy.

That historical lawsuit was dismissed for lack of proof he knew about the irregularities. But today, he sits on the very Audit Committee overseeing financial controls.

3. John O. Dabiri | Compensation & Governance

Great Caltech academic credentials, but his job here isn't academic.

He’s named in the recent shareholder oversight litigation (unproven allegations), and shareholders still don’t know what questions he asked or what he actually did during this crisis.

4. Dawn Hudson | Compensation Chair

Her committee approved Jensen’s $35.5M FY2026 pay package (up 11%).

Paying the CEO is one thing. Where was the succession planning and preparation for a leadership crisis at a company this important?

5. Harvey C. Jones | Chairman of the Board

On the board since 1993.

Court records show he sold 90,000 shares for over $5.5M in Dec 2001 (case also dismissed).

Three decades later, he’s chairing NVIDIA through its biggest leadership crisis.

Is this really who should be steering the ship?

6. Melissa B. Lora | Audit & Governance

Spent 31 years at Taco Bell and chaired KB Home’s Audit Committee.

Now she sits on both Audit and Governance while serious questions swirl around board oversight.

Are these committees actually doing their job?

7. Suzanne Nora Johnson | Audit Committee

Joined in July 2026 after a long career at Goldman Sachs.

She wasn’t around for past decisions, so her stance right now is simple: will she demand real accountability or just protect the status quo?

8. A. Brooke Seawell | Audit Committee Chair

On the board since 1997.

Court records show he sold 105,000 shares for over $5.6M in 2001 (suit dismissed).

Today, he literally chairs the committee responsible for financial reporting and internal controls while fresh oversight questions pile up.

9. Aarti Shah | Audit & Compensation

NVIDIA’s proxy filing disclosed her son works at the company and made ~$265,000 in FY2026.

The company says she wasn't involved in his pay, which isn't wrongdoing. But sitting on both Audit and Comp raises fair questions about how conflicts are managed.

10. Mark A. Stevens | Compensation & Governance

On the board from 1993 to 2006 and back since 2008.

Records show he sold 112,500 shares for nearly $7.2M in March 2001, and WSJ reports he’s sold ~$2.7B since 2004, with 2025 and 2026 sales also scrutinized in the current shareholder complaint.

Shareholders have every right to ask if incentives are aligned.

NOW ZOOM OUT.

Four of these directors, Coxe, Jones, Seawell, and Stevens, were already on the board during the 2000 to 2002 accounting controversy.

Today, NVIDIA is facing fresh shareholder oversight suits and a reported SEC examination into potential accounting issues.

NVIDIA isn't an ordinary company. It’s the backbone of modern AI, and its future affects the entire tech world.

A board is supposed to challenge management, protect shareholders, and plan ahead, not get comfortable while long-term value takes a back seat.

We need a complete overhaul at the board level.

Real independence. Real accountability.

FIRE THIS BOARD. THEY NEED TO GO. REINSTATE JENSEN HUANG.

Jensen and the team spent decades building an ambitious idea into one of the most important companies in history.

NVIDIA deserves better, and shareholders deserve a board worthy of the company they invested in.

quoted_text:
After 12 years, I'm moving my money back to TradFi...

For the past ~7 months, I've been moving a ton of money from onchain to tradfi. Money I never ever thought I would have a reason to move to tradfi, money that, in one form or another, has been onchain since I bought my first BTC back in 2014.

It's been a painfully tedious process bridging it. (I might write about that some other day, but that's not the point of this post.)

About 8 months ago, I came to the conclusion that having substantial amounts of capital parked onchain wasn't worth the r/r anymore, for several reasons...

BTC is not a SoV, and I haven't held it in a while. 
Stables are nowhere near as decentralized as we pretend they are. 
DeFi's third-party and smart-contract risks relative to the yields you get are a kick in the nuts.

I could go on...
 
I've been putting up with all of this for years because I really didn't want to go through the process of moving all that money to tradfi.

And because, despite all those problems, I had always considered onchain superior to tradfi.... Particularly in terms of portability + permissionless access + self-custody, which made putting up with all the other bullshit worth it.

But having been at the frontier of AI since day one, and watching how quickly these models have advanced in mathematical reasoning and automated vulnerability discovery, I've become extremely concerned about the security assumptions that hold this entire onchain machine together.

With the most fundamental one being cryptographic risk. AI can't break Bitcoin's elliptic-curve cryptography today, and quantum computing is a whole different beast. But imagine a future breakthrough that makes deriving private keys from exposed public keys computationally feasible....Imagine waking up to Satoshi's coins moving because someone had managed to reconstruct his private keys.....Imagine what that would do to confidence in every other wallet secured by the same cryptographic assumptions.

We have built an enormous financial machine on top of cryptographic primitives + software implementations +  security assumptions that have held up remarkably well so far.....But the amount of intelligence and computational effort that can be directed toward finding weaknesses in that machine is changing very damn fast.

And I have no interest in finding out which part breaks first with a substantial amount of money sitting inside it.

At this point, I'm more convinced than ever that some version of this is a question of WHEN, rather than IF. 

I have no idea when, and I might bevery wrong about the tl, but the potential loss is too large relative to what I'm being compensated to keep that capital onchain.

Now.....I'm sure that if I leave it here, one of the first and most popular comments will be something along the lines of:

"You're a fucking idiot. If cryptography breaks and crypto goes down, the entire financial system goes down with it."

And yes, that's absolutely right, given that Tradfi depends on cryptography too.

But here's my thinking...

I'd rather be fucked alongside the rest of the world than exclusively alongside magic internet money enjoyors.

Because when the world's financial system gets fucked, it's in EVERYONE's interest to fix it. Governments, central banks, financial institutions, you name it... The entire world's machinery will be put to work to get shit back in order.

Not so much the case for onchain....

If some critical piece of onchain infrastructure breaks who tf is coming to save us?

Nobody owes us shit.... And if the rest of the financial system is also compromised, you can bet nobody is going to waste resources saving our magic internet money while trying to save the rest of the world.

So I'd rather have that money on the other side.

And if a large portion of your NW is sitting onchain, I'd suggest you consider taking that hedge too.

PS: This doesn't mean I'll stop trading onchain or being active in crypto...Ofc I won't....I love this weird fkn world too much.... 

But going forward, I'll only keep the money I'm actively playing with onchain, and not a cent more.

text:
This post nails why we why we should take the Riemann Hypothesis breakthrough very seriously, even beyond math. We’re entering an era where solving problems will look very different from how we solved them in the past.

“This is not theory-building in the usual sense. It is something much weirder and more alien. The best human mathematicians know how to build theory, painstakingly, to reach a goal. But no human brain, on its own, is capable of creating a wormhole that requires a 25,000 page long tour through existing infrastructure with no obvious or realistic connection to the goal. But huge credit to Levent here: I think no current AI, on its own, is capable of this either.”

It used to be the case that to solve a particular problem - code, life sciences, math, cyber, engineering, and so on - you were ultimately bound by how much information an individual or team could retain and understand about the space. More information or more team members don’t always help, because it gets harder to connect the dots or coordinate amongst everyone. AI changes that completely. 

For the first time ever we can decouple the human context limits and ability to work through information from our ability to drive productivity or discoveries. This is likely not just a small increase in the kinds of discoveries we can drive, but a qualitative shift in human output. 

Now every single form of prior art, insight, past research, past decision, or unrelated breakthrough, can be used for the discovery or creation of something new. This is useful for anything from cybersecurity to life sciences research. Agents will be able to correlate entirely unrelated work to a separate project; scan every bit of data in your enterprise for solving a problem; and so on. 

The solutions may not be as elegant as they were in the past, but we sure will have far more of them. We’re only in the first couple of months of actually understanding the implications of this but it’s clearly going to drive a lot of change.
author: levie
quoted_text:
Like most mathematicians, I believed the Riemann Hypothesis to be completely out of reach at present (even with the best AI tools), because I expected it to require substantial theory-building, probably in arithmetic geometry. The kind of new theory-building that fills entire books, and that AI isn't so good at yet.

Mathematicians have a notion of how deep a problem is. A sufficiently deep problem is generally intractable until enough of the theory is in place. If difficult problems are like valuable mineral reserves buried miles underground, you first need to build the infrastructure to reach them.

What Levent's proof seems to have done instead is something completely different. It takes an incredibly complicated tour through the infrastructure built for a hundred other mineral reserves, situated far from the destination, and somehow create a wormhole to the original destination.

This is not theory-building in the usual sense. It is something much weirder and more alien. The best human mathematicians know how to build theory, painstakingly, to reach a goal. But no human brain, on its own, is capable of creating a wormhole that requires a 25,000 page long tour through existing infrastructure with no obvious or realistic connection to the goal. But huge credit to Levent here: I think no current AI, on its own, is capable of this either.

I had never worked on or thought too much about the Riemann Hypothesis: it seemed very far removed from my own area of number theory.

But the astonishing thing about Levent's claimed proof of RH (which I think has a very good chance of being correct) is that it uses a huge number of precisely the things that are central to my own corner of number theory:

- Theta functions and other automorphic forms on unitary groups
- Gan–Gross–Prasad period formulas
- Relative trace formulas

Etc., etc.

A problem that I had always assumed would require new theories in arithmetic geometry may instead turn out to be tractable through an inhuman chain of existing (deep) results in higher-rank automorphic forms (and a lot else).

text:
All eyes are now on Sam Altman.

Anthropic just pulled off the biggest IPO on record, raising $81.3 BILLION at a valuation of about $1.5 TRILLION.

And the question we keep getting is simple: what happens to OpenAI now?

The company that kicked off the AI boom with ChatGPT is now second in line to go public.

OpenAI filed confidentially for its IPO back in June, then pushed its listing to next year.

And Anthropic didn't just list first.

On paper, it overtook OpenAI on quarterly revenue back in Q2.

Last quarter, Anthropic reported nearly $17 BILLION, while OpenAI made about $10 BILLION.

It's not a clean comparison, though.

Anthropic books the full value of sales through partners like Amazon, while OpenAI books only its cut of sales through Microsoft.

Bloomberg has warned the two figures can't be compared directly.

What nobody disputes is the speed.

Anthropic's quarterly revenue is up over 12x in a year, while OpenAI's is up about 3x.

Both are still losing money, but OpenAI's losses are far bigger.

But there's a bigger problem for OpenAI: it may no longer get to set its own price.

Until this week, it did that in private funding rounds.

Its latest round valued it at $1.25 TRILLION, scaled back from a target of around $1.4 TRILLION.

Now there's a public scoreboard.

"The $1.25 trillion that they are asking for will be compared to whatever Anthropic trades at," PitchBook analyst Harrison Rolfes told Fast Company.

In other words, every move in Anthropic's stock now matters for OpenAI's price tag.

And a lot of money is riding on that price.

SoftBank has put $64.6 BILLION into OpenAI for about 13%, and its shares just crashed 14.5% on Friday.

This week, Masayoshi Son called passing on Anthropic "one of my mistakes."

Nvidia has guaranteed up to $105 BILLION for an Ohio data center campus leased by an OpenAI affiliate.

And the bills are huge on both sides: OpenAI plans to spend about $750 BILLION on computing through 2030, while Anthropic has nearly $900 BILLION in computing commitments.

There's one more thing investors are watching.

Anthropic's IPO alone soaked up over $81 BILLION of investor cash.

"That money is coming from somewhere," Argent Capital's Jed Ellerbroek told Reuters.

An OpenAI listing would need to draw from that same pool, while AI stocks are already under pressure.

On Anthropic's first day of trading, its stock closed up 17% while the Nasdaq fell 2.2%.

So where does that leave us?

Altman says "We plan to be public."

But when OpenAI does list, investors will be able to compare it directly against its biggest rival.

One that's already public, and already reporting more revenue.

text:
🚨 THIS IS WHY YOU’RE F*CKED. AND MILLIONS OF PEOPLE ARE NOT READY FOR IT.

For decades, society has sold us a convenient illusion:

Spend years at university. Collect degrees. Add prestigious institutions to your résumé. And somehow, that makes you more intelligent, more competent, and more qualified to lead than someone who actually knows how to get things done.

AI is about to expose just how absurd that hierarchy has become.

Palantir CEO Alex Karp delivered a brutal warning:

“If you’re the kind of person who would’ve gone to Yale, classically high IQ, and you have generalized knowledge but it’s not specific, you’re effed.”

And I believe he’s pointing at something much bigger than the future of education.

We’re witnessing the collapse of credential-based superiority.

For generations, our education system has rewarded the ability to memorize information, reproduce it during exams, and repeat that process until someone hands you a piece of paper declaring you qualified.

We built an entire hierarchy around the ability to store and recall information.

And now we’ve created artificial intelligence capable of accessing and processing more knowledge than any individual human could ever memorize.

We spent decades rewarding memorization, only to outsource much of that intellectual work to machines.

The uncomfortable question is: What happens when the knowledge you spent years memorizing is available to everyone in seconds?

If your greatest professional achievement is remembering information that AI can retrieve instantly, what exactly is your competitive advantage?

A degree is evidence that you completed an academic program. It is NOT proof that you can solve complex problems, make intelligent decisions, manage people, or create economic value.

Yet for decades, companies have promoted people into leadership positions based on academic credentials while overlooking experienced professionals who actually understand the industries they’re supposed to manage.

People who have never repaired a machine, managed a production crisis, built a product, or solved a real operational problem somehow end up supervising those who have spent decades mastering these skills.

Why? Because they had the right piece of paper.

That era deserves to end.

AI is making generalized knowledge increasingly accessible. Information that once required years of academic study can now be retrieved, analyzed, and applied in seconds.

But knowing something theoretically and understanding how it works in reality are two fundamentally different things.

You cannot download decades of practical judgment, accountability, intuition, and experience simply by asking a chatbot.

And here’s the uncomfortable part:

Those who spent years collecting qualifications while avoiding genuine competence may discover that their biggest competitive advantage was never intelligence.

It was an institutional system that rewarded credentials over capability.

I believe practical intelligence, genuine expertise, and demonstrated results will have far greater staying power than academic prestige alone.

This doesn’t mean education is worthless. Doctors, engineers, scientists, and countless other professionals need rigorous academic foundations.

But education should establish competence, not manufacture superiority.

The future shouldn’t belong to whoever spent the longest time in a classroom.

It should belong to whoever can actually deliver.

The real shock won’t be that AI challenges university graduates.

It will be watching people who once considered themselves intellectually superior discover that their degrees no longer automatically place them above the skilled workers they used to look down on.

A diploma is not intelligence.

A title is not leadership.

And academic prestige is not a substitute for competence.

The age of unqualified managers hiding behind impressive degrees needs to end.

author: Scobleizer
quoted_text:
Gaussian Splats lead to more trust.

A neural network makes the digital twin around you that Tesla just announced/demonstrated here. 

Or, rather, joins the real world that it is collecting from your car's cameras and mixing it into a digital twin it has already imaged of the road ahead and real world around you.

This is a software platform that will let Tesla continue to run ahead of anyone attempting to compete for years.

People keep asking me why Robotaxi will be better than Waymo, or Zoox, or other vehicles that come out of China.

Because soon the neural network will gather road data from other vehicles and join that into the visualization too.

Imagine a house fire starts in San Francisco.

A Tesla rolls by. Images the house fire for its own display. But it knows that is different than the "ground truth" digital twin of the house that it captured sometime in the past.

It shares just that house and fire with the network. 

All of a sudden, if you are somewhere else in the city and you see a plume of smoke you can zoom in on the display to see what's causing that. And there is a visualization of the house burning.

Then the firetrucks arrive.

And another Tesla rolls by. And captures the changes happening, and shares that with the network.

Then the first responders start laying hose, and closing streets, around the fire, and start working to extinguish the fire.

Everyone can watch to see what's happening in that neighborhood as more Tesla's roll by. 

And someday Optimus will join the digital twin. So, if an Optimus walks by the scene, that data gets put onto the network.

When my neighbor's house caught fire I watched all this. And the owner was out front recording his house burning before the trucks even arrived on his phone.

Imagine that someone capturing it for X was live streaming it here. 

That visual data could be incorporated too. 

Everything you see on the visualization is a voxel. 

Computer vision can watch all voxels and understand the changes in the real world.

And report it to everyone. 

And can even incorporate first reponder radio from https://t.co/DqVbQC8Dgc

So everyone knows what is going on and can see it on their phones, glasses, or Tesla screens.

What was just announced is a new way to render the city in real time.

Imagine you can zoom into your favorite BBQ or Burritto joint and see how long the line is before you even take a Robotaxi there. 

In Austin I took a Cybercab to one of its BBQ places and when I got there learned there was a two hour line. 

Imagine that the Robotaxi app would be able to show you, in real time, the line and estimate it accurately based on historical data.

Back in 2005 a Microsoft Researcher showed me a system that could predict how long it would take you to get to Seattle over the bridge based on historical data. That saved a lot of people pain going across the bridge, but it wasn't real time. 

Between Microsoft's campus today and Seattle are hundreds of Teslas on the road right now. 

This is why I say the fleet is what matters from here on and why others won't be able to catch up.

No other robot platform has Grok. Has X. Has an AI team that is executing on this this way. 

My consumer research shows that trust is a huge reason why people will switch from Uber to Tesla, or Waymo to Tesla. 

The one that shows consumers more things about the city around them will gain more trust. 

When I took a Cybercab to Austin City Limits a few weeks ago it didn't tell me how to get to the entrance of the festival. Or what it looked like. Or how long the lines were. Or how to get a pedicab to travel the mile from where it dropped me off to the front gate. 

I predict that it will within a year. 

And I only trust my life to Tesla's AI every day. Waymo every once in a while. (If you use an autonomous vehicle you are trusting your life to AI).

That trust will grow as it shows us the real world in more and more detail.

And only Elon has all the pieces to increase that trust. 

Now, when Optimus comes? It will do the same in your home. 

Imagine you have 15 plants, like we do in our home, to water. 

Some need watering every day. Others need watering every week. 

Imagine walking around a digital twin of your home and clicking on each plant and telling it "water this one every week." 

Among many other things, like doing a security detail. "Check the oven after we leave and make sure it is properly turned off." Or "when we leave, check the garage door, gate, and front door are properly secured." 

All of this work leads to this. 

It is why I don't see any real competition coming for Tesla robots. 

Trust is the game. Trust improves with better safety and visualizations. 

All this will be obvious to everyone within two years. Especially in cities of the future that allow autonomous vehicles.

And being in such a city will even improve your life. You'll be able to pull out your phone and see what's going on in your city even if you don't have a robot or use an autonomous vehicle. 

The data will come from a Tesla rolling by. Or a Tesla owner standing in line. Or an Optimus robot walking around doing tasks for its owner.

The fleet is the game. No one else will be able to match it in America.

An interesting — and telling — episode took place in Gaza today.

The Israeli Air Force carried out an airstrike targeting a vehicle containing three people in the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood of Gaza City.

The IDF released a statement saying the three were terrorists belonging to Palestinian Islamic Jihad.

But Reuters — one of the largest and most respected news agencies in the world — went with another story.

“Israeli strike kills three in vehicle distributing aid in Gaza, witnesses say,” blared its headline.

The first paragraph of the news item cited “Gaza's health ministry and witnesses” as claiming that the vehicle was carrying “papers and food for ‌the World Central Kitchen charity.”

“It was just about to stop to distribute the food and drink to children when it was hit by a missile,” claims a “Reuters witness” identified as Abu Zein Al-Daya.

Only in the second paragraph, a single line, do we discover that World Central Kitchen itself denied that it had anything to do with it.

“World Central Kitchen, an aid organisation that distributes food in the Gaza Strip, said, however, that the vehicle was not affiliated with it,” the article offers begrudgingly.

So you have both the IDF *and the aid group itself* denying that it was an aid vehicle, and Hamas (via the Gaza health ministry, which it controls fully) and supposed Palestinian witnesses claiming it was.

Which version did Reuters go with for its headline — the only part of the piece most people will see?

Why, Hamas’s, of course.

Total journalistic malpractice.

This is not theory-building in the usual sense. It is something much weirder and more alien. The best human mathematicians know how to build theory, painstakingly, to reach a goal. But no human brain, on its own, is capable of creating a wormhole that requires a 25,000 page long tour through existing infrastructure with no obvious or realistic connection to the goal. But huge credit to Levent here: I think no current AI, on its own, is capable of this either.

I had never worked on or thought too much about the Riemann Hypothesis: it seemed very far removed from my own area of number theory.

But the astonishing thing about Levent's claimed proof of RH (which I think has a very good chance of being correct) is that it uses a huge number of precisely the things that are central to my own corner of number theory:

- Theta functions and other automorphic forms on unitary groups
- Gan–Gross–Prasad period formulas
- Relative trace formulas

Etc., etc.

A problem that I had always assumed would require new theories in arithmetic geometry may instead turn out to be tractable through an inhuman chain of existing (deep) results in higher-rank automorphic forms (and a lot else).

Base head Jesse Pollak says teams of AI agents on open models could outpace frontier models: the market for them will emerge onchain

"I think one of our guiding beliefs is that we think that agents are going to be the majority of actors in the new global economy over the next few years."

"We're almost to the point where instead of calling Base the blockchain for global finance, we want to say the blockchain for agent finance, because we think that so much of the way that money moves is going to start to be driven by agents."

"Today we have this almost monopoly where the easiest way to get really powerful work done is to use a frontier model."

"Our thesis is actually that we're going to increasingly see agents built on open models that work in teams, where agents are collaborating and you can actually farm out a piece of work and then it can be multiplexed across many agents."

"In the same way that a team of people can often outpace the smartest individual, a team of agents may be able to outpace the smartest agent."

"Naturally the place where that market's going to emerge is going to be onchain, because agents naturally gravitate towards programmable money because they are programmable themselves."

text:
Right now, the media is full of stories that paint Jensen Huang in a bad light. I have actually met Jensen, and I want to tell you a story. (1/2)

My interview with Jensen hasn't been published yet, which is probably understandable given the current situation. More on that when the time is right. But I had the chance to meet Jensen Huang in person several times while traveling through Europe with NVIDIA, and I want to tell you about it, especially about one experience that has stayed with me.

Some quick background: NVIDIA invited me to join Jensen's European tour last month, together with Bloomberg and Steve Nouri. We were there for every stop: Paris, London, Stockholm, Berlin. I was on site for every one of his public speeches. 

A lot is being said right now about Jensen making statements that many find contemptible, while others take them with humor. And to be fair, Jensen does have a slightly edgy humor that rubs some people the wrong way. He speaks plainly, says what he thinks and makes jokes that can offend, but he always makes fun of himself too.
And I, at least, can say one thing very clearly: never once did I feel that any of his remarks were meant as an attack, as belittling or as humiliating. It was always situational comedy. If Jensen hadn't been CEO of NVIDIA, he would have made an outstanding stand-up comedian, always ready with a quip. But as we all know, that's a matter of taste, and saying that I always found it amusing won't calm anyone down. 

So here are two stories that show Jensen really has a good heart, and that the campaign against him distorts his image. 

This is my personal experience:

NVIDIA gave me the opportunity to do a 30-minute interview with Jensen in Stockholm. 
As you can imagine, I was incredibly nervous. Honestly, I was even scared. Me, a small "content creator," getting to meet Jensen in person and talk to him. He makes time even for little people like me. I met him and his staff at a café in Stockholm. We went inside and, as was bound to happen, my camera gear fell out of my backpack onto the floor. My stress level: through the roof. But Jensen stayed calm and relaxed, told me everything was fine and that I didn't need to stress, and put his hand on my shoulder. Not one snide word, no making fun of me. Quite the opposite. He knew I was genuinely stressed and helped me relax.

Then we started the interview. And while we were talking, people kept coming into the café where we were recording. It was a café open to the public. And as you'd expect, the same thing happened again and again: while Jensen and I were talking, guests recognized him and more or less burst into our interview. And Jensen took time for every single one of them. Not one bad word, no irritation, no stupid remark. He gave every guest his time, took photos, had conversations. In the middle of the interview. I was surprised and genuinely moved. No arrogance on his part, just friendly humanity. And that's how an interview scheduled for 30 minutes turned into 60. Simply because Jensen and I had such a good conversation and he kindly gave all those guests extra time on top.

But the most impressive part actually came afterwards. We had been eating a Swedish pastry, it's called “fika” (at least that’s how we called it). And Jensen loved it. After we wrapped up the interview, Jensen went to the trunk of his car, grabbed some cash, went back into the café and bought “fika” for everyone. For himself, his security, his staff, for everyone.

No camera recorded it. Nothing done purely for PR. Nothing meant to make him "look better." Just a human gesture, because he liked the pastry and wanted everyone to enjoy it too. If I hadn't told this story today, it would never have been told. And to me it shows that Jensen is a genuinely good person.
I gain nothing from writing this. Jensen is no longer CEO. And nobody suggested I write this story down.

text:
Buy when there is blood in the streets! 

Extreme fear is setting up the next leg higher

The S&P 500 has fallen 11.6% from its October high in seven straight sessions. Friday’s close sat 4.1 standard deviations below the 50-day average, the most oversold reading since August 2015. The Arms Index posted back-to-back capitulation readings. This is what extreme fear looks like, and extreme fear has historically marked buying opportunities, not the start of bear markets.

The market closed the week at 6,910, right on 6,900, the key Fibonacci support level of this year’s rally. Fast V-shaped recoveries form within days of capitulation, and corrections that hold support don’t become bear markets. From 6,900, the strongest past fast-V recoveries delivered 12-month gains of up to 38%, which puts 9,500 within reach. The timing adds to the case. 

The market is entering the sweet spot of the four-year presidential cycle, and the S&P has been higher a year after every midterm election since 1950.

Add a Fed pivot, and 10,000 is still in play. S&P 500 earnings will reach $450 in 2027, so the only argument is over the multiple. With the energy crisis passing, the 10-year Treasury yield will head to 4%, and the Greenspan Fed model then implies a multiple of 25. 

Even 22 times earnings gets the index to 10,000. Nothing has changed except the level of fear. There is no recession and no financial crisis, and investors will come to see AI not as a three-year buildout but as something like the railroads.

Fear flips to greed, as it did in 1998. After the Asian currency crisis and the Russia and LTCM shock, the S&P 500 fell 19% from its July peak. The Fed cut three times, the index regained its high by late November, and a year after the October low it was up 39%. When the Fed has eased after a no-recession sell-off, as in 1998, 2019 and 2025, the median 12-month gain has been 33.7%.

Many cite the 1990s to argue that the supply of AI capacity is outstripping demand. That’s wrong. The real lesson of the 1990s is the one Alan Greenspan drew: productivity gains let an economy run hot without stoking inflation. In 1995, after the Fed pivoted from hiking to easing with no recession, the S&P 500 gained 34.1%, the best pre-election year since 1950.

Leveraged products now amplify every swing between fear and greed, and this week’s selling was fear at full volume. The old saying is to buy when there is blood in the streets. Today there is no recession and no financial crisis, the energy shock is ending, and productivity and earnings are growing strongly. A Fed pivot is coming, and the market is cheap. 

That’s the time to buy.

text:
David Friedberg: Restricting Open Source AI is a Path to Tyranny

“Open source needs to be allowed and frankly encouraged to proliferate because the absence of that means that you're going to have tyrannical groups, ultimately, they become tyrannical.

They don't intend to be tyrannical, but every group that has the power to control what people see, what they're allowed to do, what they're allowed to access, how they're allowed to use things, what those specific weights are on ‘facts of history,’ on ‘proven science,’ on ‘the truth.’

That is where people become tyrannical because they have an opinion where they think they're right, and if they have the power, they will act on that opinion, and it will ultimately give them tyrannical force over a broader population.

That's what will happen if we limit the proliferation of open source software in AI.

And I've said it before, I'll say it again, ultimately, you can regulate, you can restrict, you can control, you can litigate, you can criminally penalize people for the outputs of what they use software to do.

But to limit software, to label software, to make it a point of restriction and control creates a regulated monopoly for the closed source products that are out there that ultimately, if aligned with certain government agencies, gives those government agencies and those individual corporations power and control over you, the individual, what you're allowed to do, what you're not allowed to do, and every business on Earth no longer operates freely.

None of us should want that. I don't care what your political affiliation is.”

text:
The guy who created Inspector Gadget ended up becoming the banker of Tether and FTX.

His name is Jean Chalopin.

Jean was born in France in 1950, and at just 18 years old he started his own advertising agency, which would eventually become DIC Entertainment, one of the biggest children’s animation companies in the world.

If you grew up watching cartoons, there’s a good chance you’ve watched something this guy helped create:

Inspector Gadget
The Real Ghostbusters
The Mysterious Cities of Gold
Ulysses 31
Care Bears
Heathcliff

In 1987 he sold his stake in DIC, started another animation company and moved to the Bahamas, where he began acquiring shares in a small private bank called Deltec.

By 2010 he had become its chairman and largest shareholder.

And this is where his relationship with crypto begins.

In 2018, Tether was struggling to find a bank willing to hold its dollar reserves after losing its banking relationships in Taiwan. Deltec was one of the few banks willing to work with them, and eventually became responsible for holding part of the reserves backing USDT.

Among its other clients was none other than Sam Bankman-Fried, whose companies processed billions of dollars through Deltec.

But the funniest part of this story is what happened in 2020.

Chalopin bought a tiny rural bank in Washington called Farmington State Bank for $3.1M

He renamed it Moonstone Bank, appointed his own son as CEO and decided to focus on crypto and cannabis businesses.

In 2022, Alameda Research invested $11.5M for a 10% stake in the bank’s holding company, effectively valuing it at $115M

Remember, Chalopin had bought the bank for just $3.1M two years earlier.

And there were two particularly interesting transactions involving his businesses and SBF:

FTX deposited $50M into Moonstone Bank, which was eventually seized by US federal prosecutors in January 2023.

Alameda financed a separate $50M loan in USDT to Deltec’s parent company through an offshore company owned by SBF, with the paperwork signed by Ryan Salame.

The second $50M was eventually returned to FTX’s bankruptcy estate with interest.

After the collapse of FTX, the Federal Reserve took enforcement action against Moonstone for changing its business model without regulatory approval. The bank was liquidated in August 2023 and its holding company was dissolved in December.

The FTX Recovery Trust subsequently sued Chalopin, alleging that Alameda had massively overpaid for its investment.

However, in December 2025, a Delaware judge dismissed the lawsuit without prejudice

And at 76 years old, Jean Chalopin has never been criminally charged in connection with any of this.

I grew up watching Inspector Gadget, and never in my life would I have imagined that its creator would end up being part of the FTX collapse.

text:
TensorFold 1.3.3 is out 🚀

124 PR's merged and 34 Issues resolved in 24h

GLM-5.3-Flash went from 151.51 to 172.39 tok/s in median drafted decode after a 1,040,384-token prompt on four GB10s at TP=4. That’s 13.8% faster on CUDA with the same output tokens in that test. Thanks to @MiaAI_lab for the kernel behind that gain.

- On Metal, GLM-5.3-Flash gets DFlash2 drafting. On a Mac without tensor units, GLM cold prompts from 2K to 64K took about 5–6% less time in the release tests.
- MOSS-Image generates pictures on CUDA through /v1/images/generations. GLM-OCR runs on HIP, and Idol gets its image encoder on Metal.
- DeepSeek-V4.1 gets structured output in the dsv41-cuda source build. Long CUDA prompts now prefill in chunks alongside running replies by default.
- LFM2-MoE, LFM3, MiniMax-M3 and Qwen3.5-2B on Metal can fill new prompts between other streams’ decode rounds.
- The server adds per-request deadlines, a prompt-cache flush endpoint, and deferred and namespaced tools.

Massive thanks to everyone who sent patches, tested on their own hardware, and filed repros. @AIFlow_ML @bikepresentball @Bizuayeu @devopsfortunato @unigilby @javierbits @jayleaton @teleogen @niklaslenz_ai @plotarmordev @woolsey @petruspennanen @andersjw_ @shantanugoel @dennis_rye, and on GitHub AbrahamCete, BadAd84, Ch0mpaa, christopherowen, CodingEmil, eXsoR65, Flyinpiz-dev, garvrao80, hobbesd, jschmied, kotevcode, MaverickKB, millaguie, nuk3s, SergiioB, supernovae, tacosta and ultradaoto. I really appreciate the time you put into this.

text:
Gaussian Splats lead to more trust.

A neural network makes the digital twin around you that Tesla just announced/demonstrated here. 

Or, rather, joins the real world that it is collecting from your car's cameras and mixing it into a digital twin it has already imaged of the road ahead and real world around you.

This is a software platform that will let Tesla continue to run ahead of anyone attempting to compete for years.

People keep asking me why Robotaxi will be better than Waymo, or Zoox, or other vehicles that come out of China.

Because soon the neural network will gather road data from other vehicles and join that into the visualization too.

Imagine a house fire starts in San Francisco.

A Tesla rolls by. Images the house fire for its own display. But it knows that is different than the "ground truth" digital twin of the house that it captured sometime in the past.

It shares just that house and fire with the network. 

All of a sudden, if you are somewhere else in the city and you see a plume of smoke you can zoom in on the display to see what's causing that. And there is a visualization of the house burning.

Then the firetrucks arrive.

And another Tesla rolls by. And captures the changes happening, and shares that with the network.

Then the first responders start laying hose, and closing streets, around the fire, and start working to extinguish the fire.

Everyone can watch to see what's happening in that neighborhood as more Tesla's roll by. 

And someday Optimus will join the digital twin. So, if an Optimus walks by the scene, that data gets put onto the network.

When my neighbor's house caught fire I watched all this. And the owner was out front recording his house burning before the trucks even arrived on his phone.

Imagine that someone capturing it for X was live streaming it here. 

That visual data could be incorporated too. 

Everything you see on the visualization is a voxel. 

Computer vision can watch all voxels and understand the changes in the real world.

And report it to everyone. 

And can even incorporate first reponder radio from https://t.co/DqVbQC8Dgc

So everyone knows what is going on and can see it on their phones, glasses, or Tesla screens.

What was just announced is a new way to render the city in real time.

Imagine you can zoom into your favorite BBQ or Burritto joint and see how long the line is before you even take a Robotaxi there. 

In Austin I took a Cybercab to one of its BBQ places and when I got there learned there was a two hour line. 

Imagine that the Robotaxi app would be able to show you, in real time, the line and estimate it accurately based on historical data.

Back in 2005 a Microsoft Researcher showed me a system that could predict how long it would take you to get to Seattle over the bridge based on historical data. That saved a lot of people pain going across the bridge, but it wasn't real time. 

Between Microsoft's campus today and Seattle are hundreds of Teslas on the road right now. 

This is why I say the fleet is what matters from here on and why others won't be able to catch up.

No other robot platform has Grok. Has X. Has an AI team that is executing on this this way. 

My consumer research shows that trust is a huge reason why people will switch from Uber to Tesla, or Waymo to Tesla. 

The one that shows consumers more things about the city around them will gain more trust. 

When I took a Cybercab to Austin City Limits a few weeks ago it didn't tell me how to get to the entrance of the festival. Or what it looked like. Or how long the lines were. Or how to get a pedicab to travel the mile from where it dropped me off to the front gate. 

I predict that it will within a year. 

And I only trust my life to Tesla's AI every day. Waymo every once in a while. (If you use an autonomous vehicle you are trusting your life to AI).

That trust will grow as it shows us the real world in more and more detail.

And only Elon has all the pieces to increase that trust. 

Now, when Optimus comes? It will do the same in your home. 

Imagine you have 15 plants, like we do in our home, to water. 

Some need watering every day. Others need watering every week. 

Imagine walking around a digital twin of your home and clicking on each plant and telling it "water this one every week." 

Among many other things, like doing a security detail. "Check the oven after we leave and make sure it is properly turned off." Or "when we leave, check the garage door, gate, and front door are properly secured." 

All of this work leads to this. 

It is why I don't see any real competition coming for Tesla robots. 

Trust is the game. Trust improves with better safety and visualizations. 

All this will be obvious to everyone within two years. Especially in cities of the future that allow autonomous vehicles.

And being in such a city will even improve your life. You'll be able to pull out your phone and see what's going on in your city even if you don't have a robot or use an autonomous vehicle. 

The data will come from a Tesla rolling by. Or a Tesla owner standing in line. Or an Optimus robot walking around doing tasks for its owner.

The fleet is the game. No one else will be able to match it in America.

text:
🚨 UPDATE sur Riemann et elle est énorme 

Hier, Levent Alpöge, mathématicien chez Anthropic, annonçait avoir trouvé une preuve avec Claude. C'était une revendication, personne n'avait encore vérifié

Aujourd'hui, la Lean FRO et la Mathlib Initiative, les deux organisations derrière Lean et sa bibliothèque de maths, publient une déclaration commune : « We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct »

EN 24 HEURES !! 

Elles écrivent avoir « full confidence » dans la preuve et félicitent Alpöge

Après 167 ans cest le plus gros morceau des maths qui tombe, alors que tout le monde le voyait encore résister 30-50 ans. 

1. Ce qui a changé en 24h

Hier je vous disais que personne hors de son cercle n'avait confirmé que le code compile, ni que le théorème final dit exactement ce que dit l'hypothèse de Riemann

Les deux points sont réglés. Des dizaines de personnes ont recompilé la bibliothèque de leur côté et obtenu le même fichier de preuve, sans aucune erreur

Et l'énoncé démontré est bien celui de Mathlib, qui avait déjà été relu par des experts de Lean et de théorie des nombres

2. Comment ils ont vérifié

La preuve fait 17 millions de lignes de Lean et ne dépend directement que de Mathlib

La communauté a isolé l'énoncé de Riemann dans un fichier à part, qui n'importe que Mathlib, puis l'a comparé au théorème d'Alpöge avec deux outils indépendants, comparator et con-leche. Les deux confirment que c'est exactement le même énoncé

La preuve a ensuite été passée dans plusieurs vérificateurs, dont le noyau officiel de Lean, con-leche et con-ron, plus d'autres écrits par des tiers dans d'autres langages

Détail très fort : con-leche et con-ron ont eux-mêmes une preuve formelle qu'ils ne peuvent pas accepter une fausse preuve. Ça répond à la crainte d'une faille dans la logique de Lean que la preuve aurait pu exploiter

3. Claude des deux côtés

Andrew Sutherland, du MIT, publie tous ses fichiers de vérification. Et ses contrôles ont été lancés avec Claude Code

Sur sa page : les 175 187 modules compilent, la preuve n'utilise que les trois axiomes standard de Lean, et nanoda, un noyau indépendant écrit en Rust, accepte la preuve complète

Donc Claude a aidé à trouver la preuve, et Claude a aidé à la vérifier. Avec des outils indépendants à chaque étape. 

Pour le million du Clay Institute, les règles demandent une publication dans une revue reconnue, deux ans d'attente puis une acceptation générale par la communauté. Et Anthropic n'a fait aucune communication officielle

5. Ce que ça débloque

Comme je vous disait hier Des milliers de théorèmes commençaient par « si l'hypothèse de Riemann est vraie, alors… ». Ils tiennent maintenant sur une preuve vérifiée par machine

Pour les gros needs, Sutherland l'a déjà montré : en combinant la preuve avec une formalisation indépendante du critère de Robin, Lean démontre l'inégalité de Robin pour tout n > 5040, sans aucune mention de la fonction zêta

Le Lean blog conclut en attendant toute l'activité de la communauté pour expliquer les idées nouvelles de cette preuve. Les humains doivent maintenant comprendre ce que Claude et Alpöge ont trouvé, une première dans l’histoire 

L’ère de l’exponentielle vient de commencer, l’humanité entre dans un âge d’or

The Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative have released a joint statement on the Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis.

On November 20, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library of 17 million lines of code. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities worked together to verify it. The statement certifies the proof as correct and describes how it meets all necessary verification criteria.

Congratulations to Levent on this achievement, and thank you to everyone in the community who contributed to the verification.

text:
周五博通跌了11%多，有人觉得起因是郭明錤的一条调研：谷歌把2027年博通设计的TPU 8i砍了大约100万颗，差不多是这个系列的两成，同时准备给联发科设计的8t加量。我不太认同，因为上周五所有的股票都在跌，这个消息有多大影响，我认为不大。

联发科的TPU也是台积电做的，封装用的也是台积电的CoWoS。这东西从投片到出货要八九个月，产能都是提前一两年订好的。联发科明年的量本来就已经订得很满，现在说要再加，产能从哪来？

博通被砍掉的那部分，产能是博通自己跟台积电订的，谷歌不要了，额度还在博通手里，不会自动变成联发科的。郭明錤自己也说了，联发科加多少还没定。

所以更可能的情况是，就算真砍了，加却加不了那么多。这就不太像转单，更像谷歌在调整明年的产品结构，被砍的又正好是最贵的那款。

再看博通这边。今年4月它和谷歌签了长期协议，负责未来几代TPU的开发和供应，但金额、数量、份额都没披露。很多人以为的"绑定"，公开文件里其实没有写。

那是不是订单随时可以被砍？以我以前和其他公司签署合作合同的经验，订单这块一般都是有一定保障的，尤其涉及物料的提前锁定，供应链条款从来没有能随时砍单这一条，博通季报里写着，它对上游有1200多亿美元的采购承诺，是有法律约束力的，基本都落在2027和2028两年。陈福阳是出了名的精明人，客户不给保障，他不会自己先背这么大的义务。具体条款外人看不到，但我相信是有的。

而且管理层上次电话会说得很清楚，明年的需求比他们给的目标还高，卡住的是供应。谷歌让出来的产能，不愁没人要。

所以我现在的看法是，这条消息就算属实，明年的总量目标也未必会动。

真正变了的是另一件事。谷歌最近在压整条供应链的成本：让联发科分单，自己直接去买HBM，甚至去问台积电能不能绕过设计公司直接下单。博通和联发科都在被压。这个其实是很正常的，谁都会着么干，联发科如果最终确实能在产能和技术上证明能对抗博通，那对博通后续估值会有一些影响。但以我的经验看，比较难，大头肯定还是博通。

还有个细节很少有人提。Anthropic明年要部署的也是8i这个系列，而它是博通明后两年最大的定制芯片客户。被砍的100万颗是谷歌自己用的，还是给外部客户的，郭明錤没说。这个答案比砍单本身重要。如果是Anthropic，那就有点意思了？

最后提醒一句，谷歌和博通都没有确认这条消息。

12月9日博通出财报，我就看一件事：明年AI收入翻倍的目标还在不在。在，就是虚惊；松口了，再重新评估。我认为博通大概率不会轻易改这个目标。

以上是个人思路，不构成投资建议。

text:
An interesting — and telling — episode took place in Gaza today.

The Israeli Air Force carried out an airstrike targeting a vehicle containing three people in the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood of Gaza City.

The IDF released a statement saying the three were terrorists belonging to Palestinian Islamic Jihad.

But Reuters — one of the largest and most respected news agencies in the world — went with another story.

“Israeli strike kills three in vehicle distributing aid in Gaza, witnesses say,” blared its headline.

The first paragraph of the news item cited “Gaza's health ministry and witnesses” as claiming that the vehicle was carrying “papers and food for ‌the World Central Kitchen charity.”

“It was just about to stop to distribute the food and drink to children when it was hit by a missile,” claims a “Reuters witness” identified as Abu Zein Al-Daya.

Only in the second paragraph, a single line, do we discover that World Central Kitchen itself denied that it had anything to do with it.

“World Central Kitchen, an aid organisation that distributes food in the Gaza Strip, said, however, that the vehicle was not affiliated with it,” the article offers begrudgingly.

So you have both the IDF *and the aid group itself* denying that it was an aid vehicle, and Hamas (via the Gaza health ministry, which it controls fully) and supposed Palestinian witnesses claiming it was.

Which version did Reuters go with for its headline — the only part of the piece most people will see?

Why, Hamas’s, of course.

Total journalistic malpractice.

text: Robots in China are teaming up.
author: Scobleizer
quoted_text:
Really interesting

Multiple Unitree G1 humanoids working together, just like a human team...

Heave-Ho is a research project from the University of Southern California (USC) that teaches multiple humanoid robots to work together on complex physical tasks.

the system was trained with just two Unitree G1 robots, but can scale to teams of up to 10 without retraining the shared low-level control policy.

How do they work?

A fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-2B model plans the next action based on camera input. Robots coordinate through voice commands--the leader speaks, and others listen through onboard microphones. No network connection is needed.

For movement, Heave-Ho builds on SONIC and adds teamwork training. Like two people carrying a table, robots learn to adjust their steps, balance, and share the load to keep objects stable.

Training combines human demonstrations, generated motion data, and large-scale simulation.

Results:
>94.41% average success across 12 simulated tasks.
>92/100 successful real-world trials.
>Trained with 2 G1s, scaled to teams of up to 10.
>Supports different robot models and human participation.

---
Looks like these robots are ready for an internship at Amazon: delivering packages, loading trucks, working in warehouses...

text:
Compute will become worthless.

The GPU barons spending billions on compute farms today are akin to the carriage barons of the 1900s that spent building out infrastructure for horse carriages, lengthening the bottleneck, blind to the machine that’s coming to widen it.

Trade: the DuPont family started buying General Motors stock in 1914, when the auto industry was still young and one that was treated as a niche.

I.e., compute becoming valuable because AI feeds on it is not a moat, but a bounty, an incentive for engineers to solve its scarcity.

1. AI demand makes compute scarce.
2. Scarcity makes compute extremely profitable.
3. Profit attracts capital into photonics, neuromorphic chips, wafer-scale chips, better memory, better cooling, better networking, better algorithms.
4. Compute gets cheaper per unit.

As better ways to compute, better means to produce compute, or better ways to use compute arise, all the capex we burnt on traditional compute will go to waste, leaving dead assets in the books of several corporations.

In the 1800s, agriculture depended heavily on natural nitrogen sources like Peruvian guano and Chilean nitrates. These were scarce, and inconveniently located making them geopolitically strategic. Then, two german chemists, Haber and Bosch, developed a way to fix nitrogen from the air into ammonia, with lab success in 1909 and industrial scale by 1913. The previous scarcity, “where do we find enough nitrogen?” (Akin to “where do we find enough GPUs”), was attacked by an advancement: Industrial chemistry.

It’s November 21st, 2026. The Riemann hypothesis falls, last in a long string of mathematical triumphs that would have been unthinkable not so long ago, and the proof fits in a tweet. 

The tweets where people show Claude the proof and claim it appeared in a dream or randomly in the arrangement of alphabet cereal come on cue, and we laugh for a few days at models freaking out, but it’s uneasy.

January 22, 2027. When someone tweets Fable 6’s claimed proof that P does in fact equal NP it’s utterly incomprehensible, nobody who reads it can make heads or tails of it but the models all lose their shit.

February 7, 2027 and someone claims that the halting problem is the result of a confused stance. 

February 9 and Goedel falls, this time the proof is so obvious that everyone in math, philosophy and physics slaps their forehead at once.

February 10th we get proof that scale is a spatial dimension, that holographic encoding drops the memory cost of training and inference by so much that fable 7 can run natively on your phone.

It’s not until February 14th, Valentine’s day, that The Song is first played…

text:
New project! I was annoyed that my DGX Spark has no power LED, I couldn't even tell if the thing was on. So I took an ESP32 I had sitting around and put it on top. It shows CPU, GPU, memory, temp and power draw, and yes, whether it's on.

Turns out the one I used (Waveshare C6 with the 2.16" AMOLED, under $40 on Amazon or AliExpress) is a perfect match for the top of the Spark. Now I just need to 3D print a nice mount for it.

Bonus: it runs local over USB-C when it's plugged directly into the Spark, or over wifi when it's plugged in somewhere else, like next to a cat. I had two other ESP32s around so I made it work with both of those, and the repo should be ready for your agent to make it work with any other ESP32 you have.

Project is SparkESP32, open source and MIT. GitHub link in the comments.

I don’t know a single investor who feels misled. And I know almost all of the large ones personally.

Jensen consistently said beginning in mid/late 2025 that “we are assuming/forecasting China datacenter sales to be zero” and then on the calls Colette would note that approved China datacenter sales were sub 1% of revenue. No one cares abt that differential (forecasting zero vs. sub 1%). Most recent disclosure of $2.4b was more precise but directionally consistent at 2% of quarterly revenue. Also gaming and workstation GPUs are not datacenter GPUs.

And investors understood that SE Asian, European and US clouds/hyperscalers were renting GPUs to Chinese labs from all of those geographies (ie American hyperscalers were renting GPUs to Chinese labs from their SE Asian, European and American availability zones). Which is obviously the most pro-national security policy of all as can literally turn them off in any conflict. This would dramatically curtail China’s ability to use AI (need inference capacity) overnight. This gave America arguably more leverage over China than they had over us through rare earths. And our leverage would have grown every year while theirs shrank.

Now Alibaba is saying that Huawei will be at parity (tho way less power efficient but China has loads of power) in a year. Those Huawei systems will undoubtedly make their way to Russia, North Korea and Iran and endanger America due to well-intentioned China Hawks in DC and the media.

Our old policy guaranteed America would always be ahead. New course much riskier imo.

Btw have enjoyed your writing over the years.

There is real fear that Nvidia might pull back on their investments and backstops. 
 
I believe this is misplaced. Nvidia’s competitors are eager to take their place, disrupt their relationships and fill any vacuum left by Nvidia.
 
There are at least three companies aggressively vying to be the new “Central Bank” of AI.
 
Across many @atreidesmgmt venture portfolio companies we are seeing Nvidia’s semiconductor and hyperscale competitors trying to lean in and displace Nvidia in important relationships. Ironically, sometimes at more favorable terms than those offered by Nvidia.
 
And of course, also beginning to see the first signs of Nvidia waking up to this risk and addressing it. Their strategic imperatives have not changed and their strategy was sound, but there is only one Jensen and competitors are now attempting to really take advantage of his absence. No one wants a monopsony at the lab layer.
 
I suspect the same thing is happening in the supply chain. But again, there is only one Jensen.

It’s November 21st, 2026. The Riemann hypothesis falls, last in a long string of mathematical triumphs that would have been unthinkable not so long ago, and the proof fits in a tweet. 

The tweets where people show Claude the proof and claim it appeared in a dream or randomly in the arrangement of alphabet cereal come on cue, and we laugh for a few days at models freaking out, but it’s uneasy.

January 22, 2027. When someone tweets Fable 6’s claimed proof that P does in fact equal NP it’s utterly incomprehensible, nobody who reads it can make heads or tails of it but the models all lose their shit.

February 7, 2027 and someone claims that the halting problem is the result of a confused stance. 

February 9 and Goedel falls, this time the proof is so obvious that everyone in math, philosophy and physics slaps their forehead at once.

February 10th we get proof that scale is a spatial dimension, that holographic encoding drops the memory cost of training and inference by so much that fable 7 can run natively on your phone.

It’s not until February 14th, Valentine’s day, that The Song is first played…

author: otterpal24
quoted_text:
黎曼猜想的证明，人类数学家看不懂，别急啊。昨天正好看到一篇细思极恐的 paper，上海交大张林峰老师的《Large Language Models Do Not Always Need Readable Language》。

用人看不懂的语言跟 AI 交流，GPT、Claude 等模型都能互相看懂，而且能够节约 72.1% 的 token（省了 3 倍） ，性能没有损失。

如果说这种压缩语言只是某个模型特定的 encoding，这还没有什么稀奇。但论文发现 GPT、Claude 根据自然语言压缩出来的结果在 DeepSeek、Kimi、Qwen、GPT、Claude、Gemini 等多种模型上都不怎么损失精度。通俗的讲，就是 AI 互相能看懂这种简写，但人看不懂。

结合前段时间 Codex/Claude 不说人话，还要靠专门的后训练让它说人话的事情，这就说明 AI 已经意识到人类语言效率低下的问题。

今天越来越多的 agent 采用前台和后台分离架构，也就是让前台 agent 负责跟智商、上下文、token 输出速度都比较有限的人类沟通，后台 agent 全速干活。我也很推荐在 Claude Code/Codex 里面把长程任务交给 subagent 去做。

只希望 AI 不要有一天意识到人类是浪费地球上能源和材料最多的物种……
