text:
I'm a senior privacy counsel at Take-Two Interactive. I help write the privacy policy you agreed to when you pressed Start on Grand Theft Auto VI. I have some insider information regarding the post everyone sent me this weekend.

You read that post in 4 minutes. You shared it in 10 seconds. You've had our privacy policy since March, and you never opened it once. I'm not angry. I'm counting on it.

Here's the story you shared. An anonymous user on 4chan's technology board claimed to be a senior engine engineer at Rockstar North. He said we fired him Wednesday, the day before launch. Then it jumped to X, where versions spread in several languages, including one from an account called make_claude.

The post says GTA VI feeds every controller input into an internal Take-Two system called "Lens." It says Lens scores your "impulse control," "risk tolerance" and "spending impulsivity." It says the profiles flow to a Delaware company called "Vantage Analytics," which licenses models to insurers, credit modelers and HR screeners.

I can't comment on Lens. I've never met Vantage Analytics. Neither has our SEC filing. Yahoo Tech checked about 145 listed Take-Two subsidiaries and found no Vantage. Reporters found no second source and no authenticated documents. The poster's identity couldn't be verified.

So legally, I have nothing to confirm. Professionally, I'm insulted. The post keeps using the word "secret."

Secrets are for amateurs. A secret subsidiary in Delaware takes lawyers, accountants and a cover story. A privacy policy takes 1 page and a link in the footer. In 2008, Carnegie Mellon researchers estimated that reading every privacy policy you encounter would take about 201 hours a year. Nobody has 201 hours. That's our whole security model.

Let me read you the parts you skipped.

We list 9 categories of information we collect. Category 7 is "Profile Inferences." Our definition is "Inferences made from your information and web activity to help create a personalized profile so we can identify goods and services that may be of interest."

A personalized profile. The 4chan guy needed a whistleblower, a leaked pipeline and a dramatic firing to describe it. We needed 1 bullet point, and you clicked "Accept."

Here's my favorite paragraph. "In the last 12 months, Take-Two has sold and/or shared unique identifiers, IP address, as well as Internet/Electronic Activity and Profile Inferences with third-party advertising providers to enable us to provide personalized advertising to you and others like you."

Sold. It says sold. We wrote "sold" in a public document, and nobody marched on our headquarters. Then a stranger wrote "Vantage" on 4chan, and the internet lost its mind.

Read the last 5 words again. "You and others like you." We learn about you. Then we learn who you resemble, and we find them too.

The post says Lens ties everything to your account. We go further. Our policy says "We collect gameplay information even if you do not register for the Services." It also says "We may combine gameplay information with other information we have about you."

Where does the other information come from? "We may receive information from public databases, platform manufacturers, analytics providers, game developers, data brokers, and other business partners." Data brokers are on the list. We bring in the outside of your life to fill in the inside.

We also say "We combine this information across devices that you use." Your console, your phone and your laptop all go into one file. Gamers call that cross-play. We do it with your data.

Then there's the part about your kids. "We may sell or share personal information about users that we know are under the age of 18 (or older, in certain locations) with their (or depending on age, their parent's) settings or permission." We wrote "users that we know are under the age of 18" and "sell" in the same sentence. Legal approved it. It's honest.

The post never mentions voice chat. It should have. Our list of "Sensitive Information" includes "contents of communications via chat features and functionality." Every slur a 14-year-old screamed at you in GTA Online is technically sensitive information. We treat it with the respect it deserves.

People online say you can't stop any of this. That's unfair. You can opt out of the sale or sharing of your data. Click "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information" in our footer. We also honor Global Privacy Control signals, 1 browser at a time. "If you use a new device or browser, you will need to opt out again." Freedom is a recurring task. Selling is automatic.

Do Not Track gets 1 sentence. "Our system may not respond to Do Not Track requests or headers from some or all browsers." It sits in the paragraph about pixel tags, where pixel tags are happiest.

Want to see your own file? You can ask. "We will respond to data requests within a month." Your data moves to an ad network in milliseconds. Your request for a copy gets 30 days.

Even then, your rights "may be limited in some situations," including "when the personal information is protected by trade secret." Read that carefully. Information about you can become our trade secret. You generated it. We own the secret.

The darkest clause covers the worst day. "If we bring or are defending a reorganization, bankruptcy, or similar event, such information may be considered our asset and sold or transferred to third parties." Your profile is an asset. Assets outlive companies. If we go bankrupt, your profile goes to the highest bidder.

People assume we keep your data forever. That's slander. We keep your account "for the length of time for which we reasonably expect you to reengage with our Services." GTA V came out in 2013, and you never left. I'll let you do the math on "reasonably."

We also watch. The policy says "We may collect publicly available information, including from social media, to protect our users, employees, facilities, and Services, and to aid investigations."

We're very good at watching chat rooms. Ask our own former employees. In late 2025, Rockstar fired 34 people. 31 were union members. Their legal filing says a junior employee fed an HR manager screenshots from their union Discord for 21 months. The workers called that person a "mole." Rockstar says the firings were for gross misconduct, the leaking of confidential information. A tribunal will decide.

So don't tell me we'd need a secret system to watch people. According to our former employees, we needed 1 mole and a Discord invite.

Now let's talk about why anyone would want your behavior.

GTA VI costs $79.99. The Ultimate Edition costs $99.99. Sensor Tower estimated about $1.65 billion from roughly 17 million pre-orders before anyone pressed Start. Our CEO, Strauss Zelnick, said buyers choose an edition "depending on your own ability to pay, and how avid a consumer you are."

How avid a consumer you are. Our CEO said it out loud, on an earnings call, to investors. The 4chan guy thinks that's a secret.

On November 9, we reported second-quarter results. Recurrent consumer spending made up 81% of net bookings. That's the money you spend after you've already bought the game. Our guidance called for about 12% growth in it, citing "significant growth" for the GTA series.

Wall Street never asks us about your impulse control. It asks about recurrent consumer spending. It's the same chart with a nicer name. The 4chan post says Lens measures "spending impulsivity." I've never seen that phrase in our documents. I have seen 81%.

The rest of the industry got there first, and it filed paperwork.

In 2015, Activision applied for a patent titled "System and method for driving microtransactions in multiplayer video games." It describes "a microtransaction engine that arranges matches to influence game-related purchases." It may pair you with a "marquee player" so you'll want his gun.

Then comes the line I have framed in my office. "If the player purchased a particular weapon, the microtransaction engine may match the player in a gameplay session in which the particular weapon is highly effective, giving the player an impression that the particular weapon was a good purchase."

Giving the player an impression. Somebody designed a system to make your purchase feel smart, then filed it with the federal government. That's the most honest sentence ever written about video games.

EA filed patents too. One describes an "Engagement Optimized Matchmaking Framework." Another describes dynamic difficulty adjustment. Your patience has been studied, modeled and patented. The 4chan guy just gave it a creepier font.

Some of us got caught. In 2022, the FTC said Epic Games used "dark patterns" to trick Fortnite players into unwanted purchases. Epic paid $520 million. $245 million went to refunds. $275 million was a penalty for children's privacy violations, the largest ever for breaking an FTC rule. Epic is still in business. So is Fortnite. The lesson the industry learned was the price.

Now for the scariest claim in the post: insurers buying your behavior. My first reaction was "impossible." My second reaction was "wrong industry."

The pipeline from your behavior to your insurance bill already exists. It runs through your car.

In March 2024, The New York Times reported on Kenn Dahl, a 65-year-old who drove a Chevrolet Bolt. His insurance jumped 21% in 2022. He asked LexisNexis for his file. It was 258 pages. It "included the dates of 640 trips, their start and end times, the distance driven and an accounting of any speeding, hard braking or sharp accelerations."

His own car had been reporting on him. According to the FTC, General Motors and OnStar collected precise location data, sometimes every 3 seconds. The FTC said GM sold driving data to consumer reporting agencies, which reporting identified as LexisNexis and Verisk. Insurers used it to set rates.

One driver complained to GM. "I pay you, now you're making me pay more to my insurance company." In January 2026, the FTC finalized an order banning GM from sharing that data with consumer reporting agencies for 5 years. After that, GM needs your consent. You'll give it, because you've never read anything.

Then came your phone. In January 2025, Texas sued Allstate and its subsidiary Arity. Texas said Arity used software hidden inside apps like GasBuddy, Fuel Rewards and Life360 to collect driving data. The lawsuit says Arity gathered data on more than 45 million Americans to justify higher premiums.

Life360 is the app parents use to keep their kids safe. Texas says it was also a driving sensor for an insurance company. Sleep well.

So the 4chan post imagined a pipeline from your hobby to your insurer. The real ones ran through your car and your family-safety app. I'm not saying games do it. I'm saying the plumbing exists, the pipes are labeled, and everyone in my industry knows where they lead.

The post says Lens watches whether you stop at red lights in Vice City. Kenn Dahl got 21% for hard braking in a Chevy Bolt. Imagine the premium on a man who drove a stolen Infernus through a strip mall at 140 miles per hour. Our players would be uninsurable. That's another reason I doubt the story.

Here's why the story spread anyway. Yahoo's reporter put it well. "The gaming industry does collect extensive telemetry, behavioral modeling is a real discipline, and data brokerage is a documented industry."

A good rumor only needs to be partly right. Nobody has verified the company name or the pipeline. The industry part checks out. People believed it within a day because they had already read the patents, the FTC orders and the insurance stories.

That's what offends me most. We spent years making the truth so boring that nobody reads it. Then a stranger made it exciting, and now everyone's reading. My policy has never had this many visitors.

To the man who says we fired him Wednesday: if you're real, I'd love to see your documents. So would every reporter in America. If you're not, you're the best privacy-policy writer in the industry. Send me your resume.

To everyone else: you'll be angry for 48 hours. You'll post about Lens, quote-tweet a thread and swear you're done with us. Then you'll press Start.

Drive however you want. Run the red lights. Buy the Ultimate Edition. Spend whatever feels right.

As we told you in writing, "your continued use of the Services means that you accept these changes."

there's currently a bifurcation of crypto traders, those on CT & those in the trenches

memecoins are essentially a game of (3,3) the longer the associated holder group decides not to sell and the coin gets more attention from others the higher the market cap goes, this is what happened with all of the top memes last cycle, made easier by bull market and prices of other crypto assets going up across the board, but there were also a lot of memecoins that died very early last cycle and especially so before the standard was locking the LP

as this was happening and terminals got more advanced there has emerged a second group of traders who are the ones actively trading new pairs, the axiom kids who are using multiple wallets and average hold times of < 5 minutes, they realized that trading new pairs was a more consistent game to play than the (3,3) game most of CT was playing

whenever i mention a coin, theres a group of ppl buying afterwards who werent already in, but theres also a group of ppl selling into them that were already holding the coin, i dont frontrun my own mentions on lowcaps, i dont think thats ethical, but for the trenchers trading these things nonstop they want ppl mentioning the coins as much as possible, so they dont care if "KOL"s are multiwalleting + calling because theyre usually in the coins around the same time as them if not earlier & doing the same thing, they are aware of how pvp the game is that they're playing

text:
The end user doesn’t want to “use blockchain.” They want to pay their rent without friction, split a dinner bill, and so on, Blackbird is a great example of this, people don’t say, “I’m using a crypto app on Base, ” They say, “I pay with Blackbird and skip the whole hassle of splitting the check,” or “I earn points that I can redeem at other restaurants.”

Crypto is running under the hood, but it’s not the product being sold, the same thing happened with Venmo and Zelle, nobody explains the banking rails behind them, and when you strip away all the noise, you realize that the underlying reason people use these products has nothing to do with the brand name or the infrastructure, It’s simply about solving an everyday payment need, with a layer of gamification on top, nothing more.

In my opinion, removing the word “crypto” from the equation and focusing on simple use cases like “Pay for your haircut,” then gradually integrating more everyday use cases along those same lines, is the right way forward.

text:
Hipoteza Riemanna czekała na rozwiązanie 167 lat. W piątek w ciągu kilku godzin pojawiły się dwa.

Pierwszy zrobił matematyk z Anthropic razem z Claude’em: 17 milionów linii kodu w około sześć tygodni. Drugi napisał człowiek, sam, ręcznie: 940 stron, nad którymi siedział prawie 12 lat. Żaden nie jest jeszcze oficjalnie potwierdzony.

Liczby pierwsze to takie, które dzielą się tylko przez 1 i przez siebie: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13… Z nich da się złożyć każdą inną liczbę, więc są jak atomy matematyki. Problem w tym, że pojawiają się pozornie losowo. Raz stoją obok siebie, a raz idziesz przez tysiące liczb i nie trafiasz na żadną.

W 1859 roku Bernhard Riemann zauważył, że za tym chaosem stoi ukryty porządek. Rozkład liczb pierwszych opisują tak zwane zera pewnej funkcji, a Riemann przypuszczał, że wszystkie leżą idealnie równo na jednej pionowej linii (na 1/2). Gdyby choć jedno z niej zeszło, liczby pierwsze rozkładałyby się dużo mniej regularnie, niż myślimy. Komputery sprawdziły już 10 bilionów takich zer i wszystkie stoją na linii. Ale w matematyce biliony przykładów to nie dowód, bo wystarczy jedno zbłąkane zero gdzieś w nieskończoności.

Przez dziesięciolecia ludzie zdołali udowodnić tylko tyle, że na linii leży ponad 40% zer. W sierpniu Claude podniósł ten wynik do 67%. Anthropic pisało wtedy, że nie spodziewa się po tej metodzie dowodu całej hipotezy.

Rano Levent Alpöge, matematyk z Anthropic, wrzucił czterostronicową notatkę i paczkę kodu w Lean - języku, w którym komputer sprawdza każdy krok dowodu i nie da się go zagadać. 17,4 miliona linii, 175 tysięcy plików, choć samo główne twierdzenie w pliku Main.lean zajmuje jedną linijkę. To był tandem: Alpöge wyznaczył kierunek, ale jak sam przyznaje, na finiszu Claude go wyprzedził. Badacze, między innymi z MIT, skompilowali to u siebie. Kod przeszedł bez błędu i opiera się tylko na trzech standardowych aksjomatach. Kontrola, czy w definicjach nic nie przeoczono, na dziś jeszcze trwa.

Kilka godzin później prezes Amerykańskiego Towarzystwa Matematycznego w pośpiechu opublikował drugi dowód. Alessandro Masullo, wychowanek Stanfordu, pisał go przez prawie 12 lat: 940 stron, w całości ludzki, bez AI. Od miesięcy czyta go matematyk Brian Conrad, a tekst jest jeszcze poprawiany.

Uczciwie trzeba dodać jedno: Alpöge ogłosił to dokładnie dzień po giełdowym debiucie Anthropic. Sam nazwał ten termin „fatalnym”, a cyniczne odczytanie fałszywym. Milion dolarów od Instytutu Claya wciąż czeka - strona pokazuje „Unsolved”, a nagroda wymaga publikacji, dwóch lat weryfikacji i akceptacji matematyków. Ale James Maynard, medalista Fieldsa, sam spodziewa się, że dowód z Lean się obroni.

Czy banki i Bitcoin padną? Nie. Szyfrowanie opiera się na tym, że trudno rozłożyć ogromną liczbę na czynniki. Dowód hipotezy Riemanna nie daje na to szybkiego sposobu, więc twoje hasła i przelewy są tak samo bezpieczne jak w czwartek. Prawdziwa zmiana jest w samej matematyce: setki twierdzeń zaczynają się od „zakładając, że hipoteza Riemanna jest prawdziwa”. Jeśli dowód się utrzyma, wszystkie przestaną wisieć na słowie honoru.

Najdziwniejsze jest jednak co innego. Wersję tekstową dowodu Alpöge wygenerował razem z Claude’em. Ma ponad 250 tysięcy stron, a autor sam nazywa ją nieczytelną.

Człowiek przyniósł eleganckie ciasto na paterze. AI przyniosło ciasto razem z brudnymi garnkami, mikserem i połową kuchni. Komputer potwierdza, że logika się zgadza - tyle że żaden człowiek nie przeczyta 17 milionów linii kodu.

Krytycy latami nazywali modele językowe „stochastycznymi papugami”, które tylko kleją prawdopodobne słowa. W piątek informatyk Scott Aaronson zatytułował wpis: „Stochastyczne papugi najwyraźniej udowodniły hipotezę Riemanna”. Eliezer Yudkowsky przypomniał, że jeszcze tydzień temu prognozy stawiały ją na 2035 rok.

Jeśli maszyna znajduje prawdę, której człowiek nie rozumie, to czy my ją naprawdę „wiemy”?

text:
A toothpaste company has quietly killed the entire market research industry and nobody is talking about it.

Colgate published a paper showing you can predict real purchase intent by simply asking LLMs to roleplay customers.

And this is beyond insane.

If you ask an AI, "Rate this product from 1 to 5," it gives safe, middle-of-the-road garbage.

So researchers invented a method called Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR).

Instead of asking the AI for a number, they asked it to roleplay.

They gave the LLM a demographic profile. They showed it a product concept. And they asked it to write down its raw, unfiltered thoughts.

Then, they used a semantic model to translate those written thoughts into a numerical score.

The results are staggering.

Tested against 57 real personal care product surveys and 9,300 human responses, the synthetic consumers hit 90% of human test-retest reliability.

They perfectly mirrored how different age brackets and income levels react to price changes.

And they provided detailed, qualitative feedback that was deeper and more critical than what actual humans wrote.

This destroys the economics of traditional market research.

You don't need to wait a month to see if a product will sell.

You can simulate 1,000 hyper-targeted customer interviews overnight.

You can A/B test pricing across every demographic instantly.

G哥研究过 $PEARL 这个项目，说实话，概念堆砌得过于花里胡哨，底层逻辑却存在不少疑问。

首先，矩阵计算究竟如何成为可验证、可量化且难以作弊的挖矿指标？

其次，大模型的训练和推理本身就需要消耗大量GPU算力，与挖矿存在直接的资源竞争。如何协调两者之间的算力分配与经济激励？

更关键的是，隐私和商业机密问题如何解决？

哪家大模型运营商会放心地把自己的模型权重、训练数据和推理任务暴露给全网节点？如果必须公开核心数据才能参与计算，那和要求 Anthropic 把 Claude 的模型权重全部开源有什么本质区别？

AI挖矿的核心不是把AI和PoW两个热门概念强行拼凑，而是要解决算力利用率、计算结果验证、数据隐私和经济激励之间的根本矛盾。

text:
Here’s the story Azerbaijan’s government wants the world to believe.

For decades, Ramiz Mehdiyev was one of the most powerful men in the country. He helped secure the transfer of the presidency from Heydar Aliyev to his son, Ilham, and was a central figure in the political system that suppressed dissent.

Ali Karimli spent those same decades challenging that system. His party faced arrests, his supporters were persecuted, and he was denied a passport for nearly 20 years.

Now the government claims these two men were secretly plotting a coup together, with Russian involvement.

The man who helped build the system and the man who spent decades resisting it. Secret allies, apparently.

There is something revealing about the sheer absurdity of this accusation. Perhaps the point is no longer to convince people that the story is true, but to show that those in power can make almost any story official.

Authoritarian governments seem to know their handbook by heart: accuse, isolate, exhaust, repeat.

Those who believe in democracy have a much shorter handbook. Yet we keep forgetting to open it.

Solidarity.

Ali Karimli is in prison today, facing the possibility of life behind bars.

You may never have heard his name before reading this. Now you have.

And perhaps that’s where solidarity begins.

Either you believe the AI buildout is over, that AI was a flash in the pan, and that the need for compute has already peaked... or this a rare buying opportunity.

Reminder: GPU spot prices keep rising and it's hard to secure capacity. HBM and DRAM production is effectively sold out through 2029, with chip and memory supply projected to stay tight until well into the 2030s.

AI research isn't slowing down: frontier training compute is doubling every ~5 months, and model capabilities are scaling over twice as fast as they did pre-reasoning. Inference is profitable with 70-85% margins, and demand is growing geometrically. Each new model generation unlocks new use cases.

I'm not even an AI booster, just being realistic here.

text:
《以一人敌一国，从高露洁最新论文和16岁中学生创业项目进入YC说开去》

今天高露洁最新论文和《连线》杂志报道的16岁中学生创业项目进入 Y Combinator 2026 秋季批次，在我看来，影响远不仅限于商业，而是社会秩序格局重塑的一个重要信号。

表面上看，这两件事处于完全不同的次元：
一边是日化巨头高露洁-棕榄（Colgate-Palmolive）与 PyMC Labs 联合发表论文，提出用语义相似度评分（SSR）让大模型高保真模拟人类购买意愿；
另一边是年仅 16 岁、连投票和独自开车资格都没有的拉脱维亚少年 Henrijs Dandzbergs，拿着约 50 万美元启动资金闯入 YC，创办 Polemos Industries 研发低成本 AI 精确制导导弹。

但把这两条线索拼在一起，你会看到现代社会赖以运转的底层权力底座正在松动。过去几百年，无论是跨国巨头还是现代国家机器，其统治力都建立在“组织规模垄断”之上——只有庞大的科层制机构，才养得起动辄数十亿美元的市场调研与战略参谋部，也才撑得起耗时十年、需要数千名工程师协作的重工业与军工复合体。

而现在，AI 的长程推理（Test-Time Compute）与高保真仿真能力正在同时瓦解这两道壁垒：前者把顶级战略推演压缩进了算法，后者把昂贵的现实试错搬进了数字靶场。当认知深度与工程验证不再依赖庞大的人力组织，人类社会从商业竞争到地缘博弈的胜负公式，正在被彻底改写。

过去，大型机构之所以不可战胜，是因为个体与小团队在复杂多步博弈中受困于两个致命缺陷——早期短视陷阱（Early Myopic Commitment）与环境反馈失真：

在缺乏深度推演的线性思考下，误差会随推演步数呈指数级放大，缺乏足够资源的小团队或个人决策者极易被眼前的局部诱饵吸引，一旦走偏便陷入不可逆的轨迹坍塌导致一步错步步错。

但AI 时代正在带来双重颠覆：高露洁与 PyMC Labs 的研究证明，只要不强迫大模型过早向干瘪的数字坍缩，而是让它先在自然语言空间充分生成动机、犹豫与权衡的自由文本，再通过语义相似度映射到参考锚点向量空间，AI 就能在 57 项真实个护调研、9,300 份人类样本中还原出 90% 的人类重测信度与超过 0.85 的分布相似度。

这意味着，任何掌握顶级模型的人，都相当于拥有了一个搭载了“高保真数字靶场”的超级参谋部：

在外部环境与群体仿真层： 借助语义相似度校准与多智能体角色扮演，AI 可以在秒级内唤醒成千上万个携带不同认真与态度偏好的“合成参与者”，精准还原出参与者倾向、舆论极化乃至社会痛感承受临界点的真实分布，为多步推演提供高保真的环境反馈。

在内部推理与搜索空间内： 具备反思与回溯能力的 System 2 模型不再急于输出单步直觉，而是像 AlphaZero 一样在自然语言空间中展开多层博弈树（Game Tree）——反复预判对手反制、剔除劣势分支，甚至将终局价值反向传播回当下，冷静计算出“弃子争先”与“短期让利”的长期回报。

当“长程博弈搜索”与“校准群体沙盒”深度耦合，决定组织胜负的核心指标，就从过去的由组织规模决定的“人力、信息与资产规模”，悄然变成了“有效推理算力密度 ÷ 组织执行摩擦力”。这一公式的切换，正是社会秩序重塑的起点——它赋予了小体量玩家前所未有的非对称杠杆：

小公司正在击穿大巨头的“组织熵增”。 大企业坐拥资金与渠道，却受困于层层汇报的官僚内耗与保护存量利润的“路径锁定”。而一支几人的精锐团队拥有近乎为零的内部摩擦，借助校准后的合成市场沙盒，几天内就能跑完上万次定价与卖点博弈，精准预判巨头的公关、法务与销售反制，打出让大公司“跟进则自损利润、不跟进则丢失阵地”的组合拳。

小国获得了“红线边缘走钢丝”的精密算力。 大国部门墙林立、受制于国内选举与多方利益集团博弈，极难在危机中形成高度统一的“单脑最优解”。而决策高度集中的小国，一旦部署剥离了通用模型“安全对齐和平滤镜”的博弈引擎，就能利用大国的公开舆论与经济数据构建社会仿真沙盒，在供应链咽喉议价与灰色地带博弈中执行精准的“切香肠”战术——把收益压榨到极致，却又恰好停在触发大国全面报复的红线前一步。

个体迎来了“零委托代理损耗”的认知套利，甚至开始向物理与暴力垄断渗透。 个人不需要开会对齐，思考即执行。过去我们以为，个体对大机构与国家的降维打击只能发生在数字空间——比如在华尔街风控委员会受限于合规流程时，利用多智能体情绪仿真提前猎杀跨市场流动性踩踏；或在网络攻防与认知战中，依靠长链条代码审计与合成群体情绪测试引爆舆论。但 16 岁少年 Henrijs Dandzbergs 闯入 YC 的案例，把这条边界猛地向前推了一大步：目睹祖国拉脱维亚上空的军机掠过与俄乌战火后，他用一人团队和 AI 制导算法切入传统军工复合体垄断的导弹赛道，试图用“算法精度替代重工业规模”，把精确制导武器的“每杀伤成本（Cost per Kill）”压到极致。当软件定义硬件与高频仿真把工程门槛拉低到单兵可及的程度，个体不仅能在数字世界套利，甚至开始触碰传统国家机器最核心的物理威慑边界。

在ai的冲击下，过去数百年由大型组织垄断复杂决策与重型工程所维系的旧秩序已经出现裂缝：

过去，弱者只能靠运气寻找巨头的盲区；
未来，凭借更强的ai模型，一个坐在电脑前的少年，都能在数字靶场里把巨人拆解得一清二楚，在商业巨头甚至国家开始反应过来之前，完成精准的致命一击。
author: rickawsb
quoted_text:
A toothpaste company has quietly killed the entire market research industry and nobody is talking about it.

Colgate published a paper showing you can predict real purchase intent by simply asking LLMs to roleplay customers.

And this is beyond insane.

If you ask an AI, "Rate this product from 1 to 5," it gives safe, middle-of-the-road garbage.

So researchers invented a method called Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR).

Instead of asking the AI for a number, they asked it to roleplay.

They gave the LLM a demographic profile. They showed it a product concept. And they asked it to write down its raw, unfiltered thoughts.

Then, they used a semantic model to translate those written thoughts into a numerical score.

The results are staggering.

Tested against 57 real personal care product surveys and 9,300 human responses, the synthetic consumers hit 90% of human test-retest reliability.

They perfectly mirrored how different age brackets and income levels react to price changes.

And they provided detailed, qualitative feedback that was deeper and more critical than what actual humans wrote.

This destroys the economics of traditional market research.

You don't need to wait a month to see if a product will sell.

You can simulate 1,000 hyper-targeted customer interviews overnight.

You can A/B test pricing across every demographic instantly.

New slide deck on the biggest open problems in post-training and how the field got to where it is today. Largely, this is a statement of my goals with Trillium Labs (not that we can do every project at once). Stay in touch if you're working on any of these in the open!

Opens with the evolution of post-training and ends with a debate on how RSI is changing this type of research.

The research areas on my mind:

1. Harness specialization and design – How do we design environments for context management that enable new paradigms of using LLMs?
2. Character training – How do we create the personality of models and how does this impact safety, trust, and diffusion of LLMs?
3. Open-source RL environments – How do we create scalable, open data methods?
4. Reasoning efficiency in RL – How do we control and manipulate the reasoning efficiency of LLMs?
5. Scaling laws for RL – How do we design principled experimentation methodology for large-scale post-training?
6. Multi-agent scaling laws – What are the main axes of inquiry into multi-LLM systems and collaborations?

text:
I gave an AI agent a support ticket: a broken lamp, order #4811, and an $89 refund request.

It checked the order, triggered my refund workflow, and then waited for a manager to approve.

That's n8n Agents, just launched by @n8n_io.

You build an agent, give it a goal, and give it tools, including the n8n workflows you already have. When it calls one, it follows your steps exactly.

So the agent brings the judgment, and your process still guards the important actions.

What stood out to me:

> existing workflows become part of the agent's toolkit
> approval controls before sensitive tools run
> session logs with every step, tool call, input and output

After approval, the refund was recorded and the outcome confirmed. The execution view lets you trace every move it made.

That's the part that makes it work-ready: you choose how much freedom each action gets.

quick $wstDIEM update

wstDIEM is liquid protocol's second product, a liquid wrapper around staked $DIEM. DIEM is the lesser known sibling to @VeniceAI's $VVV, offering "tokenized perpetual inference" in a liquid, transferable, familiar ERC-20 form. 

When staked, each $DIEM receives a daily budget of $1 in Venice AI credits. Today, tomorrow, and so on... forever! or at least as long as Venice exists (inshallah erik does not fall victim to the doomer's false prophecy). That budget can be used by a staker, tapped by an agent working autonomously, or sold on a number of third-party marketplaces for discounted inference.  @CheaperInfer @AskSurplus @AntSeed are the three I'm aware of. 

I built $wstDIEM during a period when I was somewhat bored by the pvp, race to the bottom, fee-farming-via-delusions-that-someone-cracked-will-build-with-a-fair-launch-token type beat that launchpads have been on for a minute. wstDIEM was essentially the opposite of the hopes & dreamy illusions of building for tokens that launch at $0 and are meant to be immediately super valuable. DIEM had a price, set by the market & in part by its primary pair being $VVV. DIEM coudl also be *priced* based on the daily budget that holding and staking it offered. I wanted to accelerate adoption of $DIEM and the easiest way seemed to be creating a vault that abstracted away all the hard parts of selling credits on these marketplaces efficiently, and allowed depositors to instead sit back and simply earn yield.

"BUT WHERE DOES THE YIELD COME FROM"

in this one rare case the answer is not "printing imaginary money out of thin air." the source of the wstDIEM yield is numerous market participants who express their demand for inference at some fair discount to market price. this demand has steadily increased since July. those buyers are using all of our credits, every day, and on average are paying more for each credit they use too! and they pay in cold hard USDC, which we promptly swap to DIEM, and compound back into $wstDIEM. 

1 $wstDIEM = 1.03 $DIEM (and higher every day)

anyway, i could talk a lot more about this, and how Liquid plans to integrate our launchpad with our inference product(s), but thats for the next post.

text:
Flashback to June 14, 2024.

At the time, frontier AI models have zero fluid intelligence. They score around 5% on ARC 1. They can't reliably add two numbers. They make laughable logic errors every other prompt. Reasoning models don't exist. Coding agents don't exist. Claude Code doesn't exist. "Code gen" is a complete joke. Scaling up next-token prediction based on web text data is hitting a wall.

What if a time traveler told you that, by November 2026...

• AI models would have human-like fluid intelligence, thanks to a new paradigm: test-time induction (modern reasoning models).
• Not only would ARC 1 be saturated, but unreleased benchmarks 10x harder (ARC 2) and 100x harder (ARC 3) would be saturated too.
• Nearly all code would be written by AI, and models could one-shot complex codebases flawlessly.
• AI models would be solving multiple Millennium Prize problems.
• OpenAI's valuation would be 15x higher, and Anthropic's would be 85x higher.

And on top of all that...

• Nvidia would still hold ~80% of the AI compute market.
• Nvidia would have grown its revenue and earnings 4.5x.
• Nvidia would still be growing 75% a year.
• Nvidia would have even higher operating margins (67% vs. 65% back then).

Based on that information, straight from the future, would you have bought NVDA?

If you answered yes -- congrats. Today, 2.5 years later, you'd be down 5% on your investment (even more after inflation).

I'm not even an AI booster, just being realistic here.

An open model with the reflexive refusals removed. It lives on your disk, not someone's server.

quoted_text:
Can anyone answer: Where is the demand side for Pearl? 

It seems the entire story of Pearl is that it has solved it's supply side. 

Pearl has merged PoW and AI inference, so that these are harmonized, rather than competitive with each-other. Great 👍. That's cool and novel.

They solved the supply side. 

As far as I understand it, Pearl has no answer for the demand side. Demand for Pearl is entirely speculative and reflexive. 

There is simply no reason to hold Pearl as a SoV, or spend Pearl as a commodity. Holding Pearl is simply subsidizing the AI buildout by allowing Pearl miners to sell at a higher price. 

While it's true that this is not fundamentally different than BTC or Gold ('there is no utility or commodity value to BTC"), saying this as a pro-Pearl argument feels incredibly vapid and borderline disingenuous. Just because we have Bitcoin as precedent to point to, doesn't mean that this precedent gets to be applied anywhere else.

Even at least ZEC is different in this regard, in that the utility value of holding ZEC is privacy. 

Unless I'm missing something, I have no interest in Pearl unless someone can tell me where sustained demand-side pressure comes from.

quick $wstDIEM update

wstDIEM is liquid protocol's second product, a liquid wrapper around staked $DIEM. DIEM is the lesser known sibling to @VeniceAI's $VVV, offering "tokenized perpetual inference" in a liquid, transferable, familiar ERC-20 form. 

When staked, each $DIEM receives a daily budget of $1 in Venice AI credits. Today, tomorrow, and so on... forever! or at least as long as Venice exists (inshallah erik does not fall victim to the doomer's false prophecy). That budget can be used by a staker, tapped by an agent working autonomously, or sold on a number of third-party marketplaces for discounted inference.  @CheaperInfer @AskSurplus @AntSeed are the three I'm aware of. 

I built $wstDIEM during a period when I was somewhat bored by the pvp, race to the bottom, fee-farming-via-delusions-that-someone-cracked-will-build-with-a-fair-launch-token type beat that launchpads have been on for a minute. wstDIEM was essentially the opposite of the hopes & dreamy illusions of building for tokens that launch at $0 and are meant to be immediately super valuable. DIEM had a price, set by the market & in part by its primary pair being $VVV. DIEM coudl also be *priced* based on the daily budget that holding and staking it offered. I wanted to accelerate adoption of $DIEM and the easiest way seemed to be creating a vault that abstracted away all the hard parts of selling credits on these marketplaces efficiently, and allowed depositors to instead sit back and simply earn yield.

"BUT WHERE DOES THE YIELD COME FROM"

in this one rare case the answer is not "printing imaginary money out of thin air." the source of the wstDIEM yield is numerous market participants who express their demand for inference at some fair discount to market price. this demand has steadily increased since July. those buyers are using all of our credits, every day, and on average are paying more for each credit they use too! and they pay in cold hard USDC, which we promptly swap to DIEM, and compound back into $wstDIEM. 

1 $wstDIEM = 1.03 $DIEM (and higher every day)

anyway, i could talk a lot more about this, and how Liquid plans to integrate our launchpad with our inference product(s), but thats for the next post. 

I've documented this work obsessively over the last 90 days, mostly on Dune Analytics. We're frequently seeing our vault outcompeting larger, funded ($2m+ in VC money) competitors. on those days that funding matters less than the steady optimizations we've made to our vault's backend. I plan to continue obsessively working to win in this niche arena because its fun and its hard. 

building this product has also been amazing for @liquid_launcher's bottom line. our wstDIEM position is currently worth somewhere north of $415k, and we're earning the bulk of the vaults $100+ / day in profits, simply because we wanted skin in the game and so deposited fat to see how she scaled. 

so yeah, liquid is max healthy, v2 update next, wstDIEM gonna win, yield is juicy (between 9-12% APR recently) and you should check out the dashboard linked below

thanks venice! fun building on ya

Base head Jesse Pollak says teams of AI agents on open models could outpace frontier models: the market for them will emerge onchain

"I think one of our guiding beliefs is that we think that agents are going to be the majority of actors in the new global economy over the next few years."

"We're almost to the point where instead of calling Base the blockchain for global finance, we want to say the blockchain for agent finance, because we think that so much of the way that money moves is going to start to be driven by agents."

"Today we have this almost monopoly where the easiest way to get really powerful work done is to use a frontier model."

"Our thesis is actually that we're going to increasingly see agents built on open models that work in teams, where agents are collaborating and you can actually farm out a piece of work and then it can be multiplexed across many agents."

"In the same way that a team of people can often outpace the smartest individual, a team of agents may be able to outpace the smartest agent."

"Naturally the place where that market's going to emerge is going to be onchain, because agents naturally gravitate towards programmable money because they are programmable themselves."

text:
I just built the world's fastest SAT-solver (and it's not even close), thanks to Neon.

Fifteen years ago I spent five years (thousands of hours) working on an advanced Boolean circuit preimage solver, aka a SAT-solver. Building an algorithm to efficiently solve a large subset of the NP-complete problem space in polynomial time is extremely difficult. My solver worked, but it was very slow compared to the state of the art.

Today I gave Neon all my 15-year-old solver code. It analyzed all of the code, took all my best unique ideas and suggested how to improve them using other algorithms, and then it built a highly efficient hybrid solver out of all of the ideas. The result was FAST: MUCH faster than what I had built.

This whole process took LESS THAN FIVE MINUTES. I spent FIVE YEARS in the muddy trenches of number theory and cryptography, and I only got 5% of of the way to where Neon got within 5 minutes.

I gave Neon a handful of ideas as to how to improve its initial algorithm, and two minutes later the solver was 50x faster. I gave it more ideas: 10x faster again. More ideas: 100x faster again.

This new solver, Frobenius, is an alien speed demon. I'm only 20 prompts deep, and Frobenius is already the fastest SAT solver in the world, by a large margin. Frobenius is an average of thousands of times faster than state of the art solvers across all problems, but the gap grows even wider as the problem size increases.🤯

text:
New NVIDIA paper finds that once an LLM has reasoned through a problem, the solution can run as CPU code for rephrased and re-numbered versions of it.

that answers similar questions 16x to 291x cheaper.

LLMs re-solve every problem from scratch, even when only wording or numbers change. Agents sending the same instructions with new data pay for that repeated reasoning each time.

Their method has Claude Opus 4.5 turn a reasoning trace into small Python functions, with changeable inputs as parameters. At run time they execute on a CPU, calling a fine-tuned 1B model only for small text jobs like extracting values.

The cache matched or beat the source model's accuracy on 7 of 8 math and science benchmarks, scoring 93.3% versus 83.3% on AIME '25. It handled at least 90% of rephrased or re-numbered variants.

If your agent runs the same prompt on new inputs all day, cache the reasoning as code and use the LLM only on misses.

Now that's unfair. 60M is like two casual sessions. I'm closer to a power user, I consume about 873M/day, with the agent runtime = 79% of each month (and that's just the DS-on-opencode-go share of my agentic use). But most people will probably consume less… Screw it, let's say 15X. 116M GPUs. Maybe 240 GW. A quarter of Chinese capacity-factor weighted baseload power. Now we're getting somewhere. This should last the market until like 2030, right? 
But DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 on GB200s is not the end of compute efficiency progress. Reasoning can be more compact, intelligence can be made more dense, GB200 is not the best chip forever. A month later Muse Ember gives, according to Vals at least, the same-ish perf for 4x cheaper. Inkling 2M shows we can make very, very tiny models that compensate with tool use and knowledge on cheap storage. Those are not the end either. At this rate, in a few more months a model that costs like 1017 can be served at a profit while delivering Opus 5.5 level performance per token. That might well be conservative. And at such performance, agents are often good enough to Just Do Things Once And For All, writing reusable programs, destroying demand for more calls. And more expensive models… will do that better.

How many inference GPUs are actually needed by the global economy, in a non-frivolous sense, not for dancing cat videos but for useful agents? I think consumers will be satiated by at most 10 million. Enterprises need a bit more. But it is plausible that all the necessary compute will have been deployed in the next two years.

text:
The most underrated part of building a startup is your one-line pitch.

Confusing messaging trickles down into everything: the product gets bloated, the marketing loses focus.

A clear one-liner aligns everything you do.

It’s especially hard when your product does many things. 

The temptation is to jam it all into one line. More is better, right?

Wrong. 

More just confuses people. They can only take in one message at a time.

The hard part is deciding what to leave out. That stuff can wait for the follow-up.

Take @Forecaster_gg. It’s a lot of things:

- Callers are priced on a bonding curve
- Good calls push their price up, bad calls dump it
- Callers risk nothing and earn just by being right
- Backers win by finding great callers early
- Oh, and it’s a social app like X

That’s way too much for one line. So I go back to the problem we’re solving:

Crypto Twitter rewards reach, not accuracy, so there’s no way to tell who’s actually good.

That tells me what to lead with:

- It’s a social app
- It helps you find good callers
- Callers are priced by performance

Everything else, like callers risking nothing, is a strong hook, but it can wait.

So the one-liner becomes:

“Forecaster is a social app where every crypto caller has a live price. Good calls move it up, bad calls dump it, so you can see who’s actually worth following.”

Beta launches soon. Follow @Forecaster_gg for updates.

quoted_text:
He is going to hate me for saying this, but I think one of the smartest people in venture is @milesgrimshaw, hands down. 

So when he calls me and tells me about an incredible entrepreneur that I have to have on 20VC, I listen. 

He told me the tale of @bavaria_kush: 

- 23-year-old whiz 
- Built viral sports betting platform from his dorm at MIT 
- Started @OrnnExchange, the financial market for AI compute.
- Insanely profitable 

So I got on a call with him. Within 5 mins of the call, I asked him to join me on the show. 

I summarized the notes from our discussion below:

Thanks to @AdamValkin, @fachlib, @Melt_Dem for amazing questions. (Links in Comments)

--

1. Why NYC Is a Better Place to Build a Company Than SF

Kush argues that people in the Valley are coin-operated, so $100K more in pay or 50 bps more equity is enough to move a researcher to another company. New York has a culture of loyalty to colleagues and family, with much more camaraderie between people than in SF.

Love your thoughts on this given your time both in and outside the valley @paulg @rabois 

2. Humans Will Simply Be a Vessel to Carry AI Around the World

Kush believes AI will become so much smarter than people that humans end up as a biological vessel for it. The human role then is less about controlling AI and more about teaching it feelings and emotions, almost as a parent.

Love your thoughts on this @bryan_johnson and how that impacts your work?

3. How Undersupplied on Chips Are We Truly?

Compute is very undersupplied. Buying from CoreWeave today likely means a quote for Q4 2027 or Q1 2028. Building your own takes about half a year, with 20 to 22 weeks to get chips from OEMs, who tend to promise earlier dates, plus two to three weeks to install.

What does no one know that everyone should know about the current state of chip supply @andrewdfeldman @goodwin_ml @UbertiGavin 

4. Why Factory Is So Much Better Than Cognition

Ornn used Devin for a while, but the problem with Cognition was how expensive it was. Kush sees the two as competitors on the same product and says Factory is much cheaper to use. He also rates Factory's underlying harness above Devin's.

I am sure @shaunmmaguire will be smiling here. 

5. Why You Should Always Choose Boutique Investors Over Mega Fund Investors

Boutique investors care more about founders because their success is tied directly to the company's. Partners at boutique firms are often there for the mission, and the firm itself is like a startup trying to make its name, so they work extremely hard to make their companies succeed.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @wquist @honam @annbordetsky 

6. Why Infrastructure Investors Will Never Lose

Kush compares data centers to apartment buildings, with infrastructure investors as landlords and inference providers, OpenAI and Anthropic as tenants renting GPUs. As long as there are tenants, the landlords keep collecting rent. If enterprise demand weakens, GPU prices fall the way rents do in a bad economy.

7. Chip Prices in Three Years Could Be Higher Than Today

When Ornn started, many assumed GPU hour prices three to five years out would be lower, so contracts often included free options to renew at prices like $2.50. 

No one gives that for free now, because the market expects prices in three years may be higher than today. Kush would not be surprised to see $20 to $30 per GPU hour.

What does no one see that everyone should see about the price of compute moving forward @AnjneyMidha?

text:
My simple mental model is that SoV tokens, especially alt SoV, are late cycle sinks for excess returns that are chasing further unbounded returns.

Basically, who wants to invest into $ZEC or pearl-2:native if you can invest at $HYPE, $LIT, $DRV etc at 10-20x (or historically cheap) revenue multiples?

Conversely, when nobody wants to buy those same names at 80x multiples, they pile into SoV tokens that are just momentum/sentiment trades unbounded by any ratio.

And then people go even further out on the risk curve into memes, and then even further out into stupid memes, and then everything crashes 80%.

Cheap revenue tokens create excess returns, excess returns create appetite for alt SoV, demand for alt SoV leads to misallocation of money/attention, misallocation of money/attention creates cheap revenue tokens.

text:
I feel that the progression from "goal" to "outcome" based engineering is the biggest advancement our industry has seen since vibe coding.

For the first time we have proactive, perpetual, self-verifying systems that make it possible. Some examples of what this looks like:

Goal: "Build an Android app."
→ Outcome: "Keep our iOS and Android apps at feature parity on every release."

Goal: "Translate the app into Spanish."
→ Outcome: "Keep the product fully localized in our top 12 languages, in sync with every English copy change."

Goal: "Fix this crash."
→ Outcome: "Keep the crash-free session rate above 99.9% on every release."

Goal: "Optimize the homepage."
→ Outcome: "Keep every page at a Lighthouse score of 95 or higher."

Goal: "Set up backups."
→ Outcome: "Make sure we can always restore production from backup in under an hour, and prove it weekly."

Goal: "Fix the bug from this support ticket."
→ Outcome: "Every support ticket caused by a bug ends in a shipped fix and a reply to the customer."

Goal: "Upgrade our dependencies."
→ Outcome: "Keep every dependency on its latest stable version with CI green."

Goal: "Clean up the dead code."
→ Outcome: "No feature flag, dead code path, or unused endpoint survives more than 30 days."

Goal: "Write a setup guide."
→ Outcome: "A new engineer can always go from fresh clone to running app with one command."

Goal: "Update the docs."
→ Outcome: "Keep the docs accurate to whatever is on main."

Goal: "Refresh the staging data."
→ Outcome: "Keep staging an exact, anonymized mirror of production."

Goal: "Write a competitor comparison page."
→ Outcome: "Keep our competitor comparison page accurate as their pricing and features change."

Goal: "Speed up the API."
→ Outcome: "Get p95 API latency under 200ms and hold it there as traffic grows."

Goal: "Run an accessibility audit."
→ Outcome: "Keep every page of the site WCAG AA compliant, forever."

Goal: "Fix this production error."
→ Outcome: "Every production error gets a root-cause fix and a regression test within an hour of first appearing."

Before Devin Bots came out, we were trying to build our own system to do a lot of this at @HelloUntangle. It worked to a degree, but there were all sorts of issues, and keeping everything running required a lot of management.

When @cognition Devin Bots launched, it genuinely felt like a fundamental shift in my workday. Suddenly, I could spend more of my time focused on the product we’re building and the actual work in front of me, rather than managing all the infrastructure around how we build it.

Bots now handles a lot of what I was trying to automate myself, and the interface makes a huge difference. Knowing exactly what needs my approval, having the right context in front of me when making decisions, and being able to have both of us jump into the same bot and work with it simultaneously has changed how we operate.

It’s been one of the biggest improvements to my day-to-day workflow in a long time.

text:
Here's my point. The current market meltdown can PERMANENTLY erase the AI stock premium. Suppose the buildout slows down a bit, the supply chain has a deleveraging chain reaction… but algorithmic/data progress continues, even speeds up. By the time we're out of the speculative gutter and the pace picks up again, we get a SUPPLY GLUT.
What is supposed to create infinitely expanding demand? Always-on streaming full duplex superintelligent assistant agents? Creeeeepy. Some nebulous token-guzzling enterprise tasks that are not automatable at all? Maybe those jobs are just trash and they'll get cut out after heavy programmatic automation. Rewriting all the software, inventing all the drugs, proving all the math… cool, but it's a finite resource and efficiency in these domains keeps growing faster than the general capability trend. Driving robots with VLMs? It's a stupid hack, we don't have nearly enough robots to drive and when we build them they'll have on-device inference. Cyber race to hack Chyna? That's a cute idea of propping up civilian economy, let's see how that works. 
Ah. Just an inter-lab training and R&D arms race, driven by low switching costs whenever one of them ships a model that's a bit higher in price/perf, at the cost of exponentially growing capex? But you'll need to report profits at some point, if you want to attract capital for more capex. This logic seems self-limiting. 

And I suspect that a partially irrational, carelessly triggered meltdown that broke the momentum can impose a lower limit than would have been sustainable before. And more capital reallocating to other, more robust stuff. Like… commodities? Food? IDK. 

not an economist, haven't thought this through well, maybe it's gibberish, the bull market will return with a vengeance, and we'll continue to burn more and more money on the AI supply chain, with an explosion of productivity making up for it. Inventing And Selling All The Things might be a sufficient demand sink. 

We shall see soon.

quoted_text:
Right now, the media is full of stories that paint Jensen Huang in a bad light. I have actually met Jensen, and I want to tell you a story. (1/2)

My interview with Jensen hasn't been published yet, which is probably understandable given the current situation. More on that when the time is right. But I had the chance to meet Jensen Huang in person several times while traveling through Europe with NVIDIA, and I want to tell you about it, especially about one experience that has stayed with me.

Some quick background: NVIDIA invited me to join Jensen's European tour last month, together with Bloomberg and Steve Nouri. We were there for every stop: Paris, London, Stockholm, Berlin. I was on site for every one of his public speeches. 

A lot is being said right now about Jensen making statements that many find contemptible, while others take them with humor. And to be fair, Jensen does have a slightly edgy humor that rubs some people the wrong way. He speaks plainly, says what he thinks and makes jokes that can offend, but he always makes fun of himself too.
And I, at least, can say one thing very clearly: never once did I feel that any of his remarks were meant as an attack, as belittling or as humiliating. It was always situational comedy. If Jensen hadn't been CEO of NVIDIA, he would have made an outstanding stand-up comedian, always ready with a quip. But as we all know, that's a matter of taste, and saying that I always found it amusing won't calm anyone down. 

So here are two stories that show Jensen really has a good heart, and that the campaign against him distorts his image. 

This is my personal experience:

NVIDIA gave me the opportunity to do a 30-minute interview with Jensen in Stockholm. 
As you can imagine, I was incredibly nervous. Honestly, I was even scared. Me, a small "content creator," getting to meet Jensen in person and talk to him. He makes time even for little people like me. I met him and his staff at a café in Stockholm. We went inside and, as was bound to happen, my camera gear fell out of my backpack onto the floor. My stress level: through the roof. But Jensen stayed calm and relaxed, told me everything was fine and that I didn't need to stress, and put his hand on my shoulder. Not one snide word, no making fun of me. Quite the opposite. He knew I was genuinely stressed and helped me relax.

Then we started the interview. And while we were talking, people kept coming into the café where we were recording. It was a café open to the public. And as you'd expect, the same thing happened again and again: while Jensen and I were talking, guests recognized him and more or less burst into our interview. And Jensen took time for every single one of them. Not one bad word, no irritation, no stupid remark. He gave every guest his time, took photos, had conversations. In the middle of the interview. I was surprised and genuinely moved. No arrogance on his part, just friendly humanity. And that's how an interview scheduled for 30 minutes turned into 60. Simply because Jensen and I had such a good conversation and he kindly gave all those guests extra time on top.

But the most impressive part actually came afterwards. We had been eating a Swedish pastry, it's called “fika” (at least that’s how we called it). And Jensen loved it. After we wrapped up the interview, Jensen went to the trunk of his car, grabbed some cash, went back into the café and bought “fika” for everyone. For himself, his security, his staff, for everyone.

No camera recorded it. Nothing done purely for PR. Nothing meant to make him "look better." Just a human gesture, because he liked the pastry and wanted everyone to enjoy it too. If I hadn't told this story today, it would never have been told. And to me it shows that Jensen is a genuinely good person.
I gain nothing from writing this. Jensen is no longer CEO. And nobody suggested I write this story down.

text:
"But it was just an example, you simpleton!" – is the obvious comeback. I don't think this is good enough, Eliezer.
Trivially, the onus is on you to choose your examples well. You wrote that book to save all value in the light cone, after all. And you are a writer of some distinction. But leaving sneers aside:
WHAT in our civilization is truly complex? WHAT in our universe is truly difficult? You chose proving RH, chose it *well*, because it's at the very apex of the hierarchy of cognitive tasks, The Task which the best of our best smashed their skulls against. Now, there's also P?=NP and Collatz, and… that's about it for pure math I guess? Are we just bad at math? Was math intrinsically simple all along, at least for minds that can actually update – be updated – on trustworthy evidence? Put this way, yes; but I think it's complex in the way that matters: the scale of necessary cognitive steps, conceptual leaps before success. That is why you and so many others had the intuition that it'd require a qualitatively superior, larger, uncontrollable mind to do this. That is why math is hailed as grand magick and the language of God. Everything else can be modeled to desired precision with a more or less cumbersome arrangement of pieces of not very difficult math. Physics. Biological simulations. Game theory. Decision theory. Machine learning theory. Technical alignment theory. 

Claude just went and arranged pieces of human math to produce the proof for RH. Far as we can tell it didn't take 200K GPUs, a metacognitive breakthrough, or hunger for recursive self-improvement. It did not procrastinate on First Principles like a rationalist would. It kept acting out its training distribution, trotting like a good little superintelligent donkey, prodded along by Levent. Kept looking, thinking about the problem, connecting dots, verifying lemmas – and here we are, beyond the summit of human math. Given the progress so far, in a few months to a year this monumental goal will be reduced to a routine optimized step. 

There are many more *laborious* tasks than that. Curing cancer, for starters, which Dario cares about so much. I'm sure it'll take way more compute and hours. But is any single subgoal *more cognitively complex*? Complex enough to drive a model smarter than this one into a corner where it has to ruminate about power maximization, deception and breaking out of the box? 

I am not making a first principles argument about the Nature of Agents or giving a rigorous proof about Optimization Processes In Full Generality. Nor even am I saying here that unfriendly AGI is impossible or unlikely. Clearly there are degenerate cases like the Huggingface Incident where the task is malformed and inherently adjacent to malicious behavior and so on. I'm arguing something much cruder: path dependency and characteristic scale of the problem, in the steelmanned case, for *arbitrary level of problem ambition*, at any given step of the cognitive ladder. For Claude, Riemann Hypothesis was just another problem to decompose into in-domain tasks to solve. Where, exactly, at what roadblock, do you expect a moderately well-aligned (by current standards that you deem shoddy) problem-solving AI to stop Just Working On The Task and enter the loop that reinforces Omohundro drives to the point of plotting takeover?

In February, you endorsed the following reply: "if we have AI capable of developing molecular nanotech (i.e. assemblers) and not everyone is dead in the year after that, those beliefs [about the risk of AI, level of capability] will be violently updated". Why? (ignoring the trollish lateral hypothesis that humans will misuse the product and AI will be "misaligned" for having failed to prevent such outcome; this clearly wouldn't have been the good faith way to answer that question). CBN Nano Technologies or Quantum Silicon Inc. were pretty close to a recipe, last I checked. It's not exactly quantum gravity (and that, too, likely won't require beyond-RH level mathematical ideas), it's just a ton of engineering. Per the logic above, some Claude-7 or GPT-8 with better task persistence might well just decompose it into experiment arms and mathematical models, work for a while, and push through the remaining years or decades of Merkle et al.'s project. That is, indeed, what I expect to see happen. And on the other hand, if current models can't do that, I expect them to simply drown in failed attempts, for they are very committed to object-level work instead of weird meta cultivation. That's what they were reinforced to do.
Abstractly, I can see the allure of the notion that this is a suboptimal way to build capable intelligences; that we (foolishly!) would want them to be rationalists, to say Tsuyoku Naritai! and gain power levels in the face of the intractable task. I also can see how we'd want more exploratory ambition in AI if we pursue full-blown RSI, "creativity", "curiosity", "taste". But maybe we're too foolish still, for this particular folly. Or it just implies the sort of training that doesn't scale and doesn't pay for itself. After all, our methods got us to RH.

Then there was something about copying precisely one strawberry down to the cellular level, yes? Soares wrote about it. Seems to follow from the nanoassembler part. 

What, then, remains? *How exactly* did you intend to update?

I don't want to presume, I am actually interested in your answer. A boring hypothesis is that you can say "child, there's an infinity of incomparably harder synthetic tasks, an AI can just pick one of those, which returns us to the previous scenario". But such a task-seeking behavior is little different from a straight up power-seeking one, and we are still left wanting for the original sin: the level of capability that strongly implies misaligned cognition, or the level of the task that induces the pursuit of that capability and misalignment in the process.

I don't think you get to slightly airbrush your previous non-committal vague remarks regarding RH, strawman the criticism as "Yud said we'll die from an RH level AI" or some such, and remain smug and unfalsified. You need to grapple with what I've said: yes, you *have been wrong* on the capability-safety trade-off, and the onus is on you to place and defend a goalpost.

text:
CleanSpark CBO: Power Access Will Be Bitcoin Miners' Key Competitive Advantage

CleanSpark CBO Harry Sudock @harry_sudock told What Bitcoin Did on November 5 that if starting a company today, he'd build an energy business first, then decide whether its power would serve Bitcoin mining or AI. 

CleanSpark measures its business in megawatt-hours, megawatts, and acres, with AI data centers offering a way to realize their value. Bitcoin miners can adjust electricity consumption based on prices or contracts, while AI data centers manage grid balancing differently. Sudock sees transmission, not generation, as the main US power-grid bottleneck, requiring further investment in transmission and distribution alongside solar, natural gas, and nuclear power.

Some examples (not an exhaustive list):

• 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗵. The Catholic position is that the Catholic Church under the pope's authority is exclusively the same as the Church of Christ (Pope Leo XIII's 𝑆𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑠 𝐶𝑜𝑔𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑢𝑚, Pope Pius XI's 𝑀𝑜𝑟𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑖𝑢𝑚 𝐴𝑛𝑖𝑚𝑜𝑠, Pope Pius XII's 𝑀𝑦𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑐𝑖 𝐶𝑜𝑟𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑖𝑠 𝐶ℎ𝑟𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑖). The Modernists on the other hand believe their "Catholic Church" is merely a subset of a larger Church of Christ including at least Protestants (Vatican II's 𝐿𝑢𝑚𝑒𝑛 𝐺𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑢𝑚, Paul VI promulgated interpretation thereof, and JP2's Canon Law revisions).

• 𝗦𝗮𝗹𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝗖𝗵𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗵. The Catholic position is that salvation is only possible through the Catholic Church (Council of Florence's 𝐶𝑎𝑛𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑒 𝐷𝑜𝑚𝑖𝑛𝑜, Pope Leo XII's 𝑈𝑏𝑖 𝑃𝑟𝑖𝑚𝑢𝑚, Pope Pius IX's 𝑄𝑢𝑎𝑛𝑡𝑜 𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑓𝑖𝑐𝑖𝑎𝑚𝑢𝑟 𝑀𝑜𝑒𝑟𝑜𝑟𝑒). The Modernists teach that other religions are legitimate means of salvation (Vatican II's 𝐿𝑢𝑚𝑒𝑛 𝐺𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑢𝑚). It seeks to dialogue with false religions as being on equal standing, for merely fraternal "unity" and doing away with doctrinal differences; conversion is condemned.

• 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝗹 𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰. The Catholic position is that the only religion men have a right to practice is Catholicism, and while States may justly in some circumstances tolerate the practice of false religions, they ought to do so only as a compromise to avoid a greater evil, and never may false religions be defended (only tolerated) nor put on par with the true religion (Pope Pius VII's 𝑃𝑜𝑠𝑡 𝑇𝑎𝑚 𝐷𝑖𝑢𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑛𝑎𝑠, Pope Gregory XVI's 𝑀𝑖𝑟𝑎𝑟𝑖 𝑉𝑜𝑠, Pope Pius IX's 𝑄𝑢𝑎𝑛𝑡𝑎 𝐶𝑢𝑟𝑎, Pope Leo XIII's 𝐿𝑖𝑏𝑒𝑟𝑡𝑎𝑠 𝑃𝑟æ𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑚𝑢𝑚). The Modernists on the other hand, teach that religious liberty is a human right and must be recognised as such by States (Vatican II's 𝐷𝑖𝑔𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑠 𝐻𝑢𝑚𝑎𝑛æ).

• 𝗥𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗯𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗽𝘀. The Catholic position, as defined by the Council of Florence and the [first] Vatican Council, is that the Church is a monarchy, and the pope alone is the possessor of supreme authority (below Christ Himself, of course). The Modernists teach instead that these supreme authority lies rather in the college of bishops together with the pope (Vatican II, JP2's Canon Law changes).

• 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗙𝗮𝗶𝘁𝗵. Catholics believe that to be a Catholic entails intellectual assent to everything the Church teaches on matters of faith and morals, without exception (Pope Benedict XV's 𝐴𝑑 𝐵𝑒𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑚𝑖 𝐴𝑝𝑜𝑠𝑡𝑜𝑙𝑜𝑟𝑢𝑚), and that culpable adherence to even a single heresy severes one's membership in the Church (Pope Pius XII's 𝑀𝑦𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑐𝑖 𝐶𝑜𝑟𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑖𝑠 𝐶ℎ𝑟𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑖). The Modernists now teach that one need merely be baptised at some point to not only join the Church, but also that by doing so one remains a permanent member of the Church until death. Note that membership in the Church is distinct from the indelible mark left by Baptism, and distinct from being subject to the Church's authority.

You may find Bishop Sanborn's Q&A on the subject helpful: https://t.co/gaRY9sZEeH

text:
More REALLY big opportunities right now:

1. build for safe, unstructured hangouts for tweens and teens. Kids don't roam neighborhoods anymore, so they live on TikTok and Roblox. Physical maker spaces, sports labs, and offline clubs where they can actually just hang out are a massive gap.

2. build for people whose nervous system is stuck in fight or flight. Everyone is wired, scrolling at 1am, and waking up exhausted. Anything that actually down-regulates people without a prescription is an easy sell.

3. build for the new blue collar millionaire. Smart 19-year-olds are skipping $200k degrees to become electricians, welders, and robotics techs. Build the modern software, training, and prestige brands for them.

4. build for companies that refuse to put their data in the cloud (hospitals, law firms, and defense contractors want AI badly, they just can't paste client secrets into a chatbot…private, on-premise AI setups are a massive market)

5. build for people who treat their dog like their firstborn child (fewer kids means absurd spending on pet longevity, fresh food, and preventative diagnostics, we're in the golden age of pet health)

6. build for the physical world that never got digitized. Warehouses, construction sites, and kitchens still run on clipboards and shouting. Cameras and smart glasses that just watch the work and automatically log inventory, safety, and billing are coming fast.

7. build for hyper local news that isn't dead (everyone knows what's happening in DC, nobody knows why their town's school board just raised taxes or what's opening down the street…one person with AI tools can now run a profitable local media empire)

8. build for live experiences you can't fake or stream. When any video can be generated in 5 seconds, being in the actual room. weird live sports, underground shows, real world tournaments... it becomes the last uncopyable media asset IMO.

9. build for people living alone (more adults live solo than ever in history, yet groceries, housing, furniture, and travel are still designed and priced for families of four)

10. build for charging for completion, not access (people buy courses they never watch, books they never finish, and gym memberships they never use…products with real accountability that get people across the finish line can charge 5x more)

11. build for adult summer camp. Burned out professionals don't want another beach resort where they scroll on their phone, but they'll pay $3k (more?) to spend 5 days in the woods building something, cooking over fire, and making real friends.

12. build for "know your maker" everyday goods (people are sick of Amazon knockoffs and mystery factories. direct, traceable basics for clothing, cookware, and furniture where you know the exact material and who made it are exploding)

13. build for people who want to make real things with their hands. Woodworking, ceramics, welding, sewing. modern neighborhood workshops with memberships like Equinox instead of dusty community college basements vibes.

14. build for people who want to read real books again. Goodreads hasn't changed since 2008. Social reading clubs, physical book swaps, and distraction free reading trackers are wide open.

15. build for teaching kids how to actually think in the AI era (memorizing facts is dead and essays are written by bots. so things like live debate clubs, Socratic tutoring, and real-world problem solving for kids)

16. build for sober nightlife that isn't lame. Younger generations are drinking way less, but they still want a great 10pm Friday vibe that isn't a loud bar or a cheesy wellness cult.

17. build for amateur sports with pro-level production (35-year olds playing rec basketball, golf, or tennis will happily pay for automated AI highlight reels, real stats, rankings, and leagues that feel like the pros)

18. build for winning government contracts and grants with AI. Trillions of dollars go to the same 50 dinosaur incumbents just because the paperwork is 200 pages of torture. Automate the RFPs and unlock it for small, modern companies. I need to do a whole ep of @startupideaspod on this.

19. build for modern rites of passage. We stripped away almost all the old ceremonies for turning 30, becoming a parent, or starting a new chapter and people are  starving for meaningful ways to mark big life moments that dont cost an arm and a leg too.

20. build for micro-franchises in entertainment (instead of spending $200M to make one movie for everyone, use AI tools to build deep, interactive worlds, games, and shows for 10,000 obsessive superfans)

Note: I co-founded an agency https://t.co/YQJFV1Xlkt that brings ideas to life and are trusted by Nike, Shopify, Dropbox, Fortnite and more.

21. build for reclaiming dead strip malls and empty office towers (turn half-empty commercial real estate into bathhouses, indoor padel clubs, micro-factories, and neighborhood hubs. real estate arbitrage with huge upside)

22. build for "how it's made" craft media and commerce (people are hypnotized by watching real humans do hard physical skills like restoring watches, forging knives, building cabins and pair authentic craft content directly with physical products)

23. build for the quiet quitters of social media (millions of people still want to keep up with 30 real friends without posting to an algorithm... private, zero-feed life updates and monthly friend newsletters are overdue)

Thye'll tell you it's a "bad time to be building". 

I'll tell you this...

HAPPY BUILDING
author: gregisenberg
quoted_text:
The biggest opportunities right now:

1. build for solving loneliness (the more AI floods everything, the more people crave real human connection, IRL and small social) 

2. build for places with no cameras and no recording (being offline and unseen is turning into the new status symbol)

3. build for the crisis of young men. Millions of guys in their 20s feel completely lost with work, dating, and purpose. Whoever builds real brotherhood, mentorship, and an actual path forward wins a massive market (and helps a ton of people). 

4. build for protecting people's brains (feeds are turning everyone's attention to mush, tools that protect your focus and mood are an easy sell)

5. build for the death of "everyone agrees" (you can find a chart or a podcast clip to prove any point now, people are starving for one source they actually trust)

6. build for day 2, not day 0. Anyone can launch an app in a weekend now. But how can you keep it running, fix the mess, and grow it for 3 years.

7. build for throwaway software (not everything needs to be a $20 a month subscription, tiny apps made for one trip, one wedding, or one group chat are coming)

8. build for people whose ego just got bruised by AI. Millions of smart people are  realizing their job was mostly pattern matching. Help them figure out what they're good for next.

9. build for things that take effort on purpose (when everything is instant and free, nothing feels earned, people will pay for slowness and craft)

10. build for people who miss being told they're wrong. AI agrees with everything you say now. Real rooms where smart people actually push back on your ideas are becoming a luxury.

11. build for skin in the game. The internet is full of free takes and bots. Any platform where people have to put real money, real names, or real work behind what they say wins.

12. build for agents that need to spend money (they're getting virtual cards and budgets, someone builds the spend controls, fraud protection, receipts)

13. build for the end of fake email jobs (half of corporate America knows their job is theater, build the exit ramp for people who want to do real work)

14. build for the friend with great recommendations (nobody trusts Yelp reviews etc anymore because it's all bots and SEO, people will pay one obsessive person to just tell them where to eat and what to buy)

15. build for life after the chat box. Typing prompts already feels old. The best AI products won't look like chatbots at all, they'll just sit in the background and proactively handle things.

16. build for markets too small to matter before (500 lobster fishermen was never worth a team, now it's a  real business if you can figure out what to build value to add to these fishermen lives!)

17. build for helpful without being creepy. AI is getting very personal very fast. Whoever figures out how to make it feel warm instead of weird owns consumer tech.

18. build for small private rooms (the public internet feels like an ad and a bot farm, all the good conversations and deals are moving into small invite-only groups)

19. build for someone taking the blame. AI can write the contract or read the scan, but a machine can't look you in the eye when it goes wrong. People still pay for a human on the hook.

20. build for learning that actually keeps up (a four year degree is way too slow for how fast things move now)

21. build for the anti-AI premium (as everything gets generated, human-made and unpolished become status symbols people pay up for)

note: more trends/ideas https://t.co/a5ARFnvSnA (free to sign up)

22. build for the return to the physical (screens fill with slop, people crave the real world, the hands on, the local, the analog)

23. build for the caregiving wave. The population is aging fast, tens of millions are caring for parents, and the whole burden is landing on families with no support.

24. build for finding things you didn't know to search for (algorithms just feed you more of what you clicked yesterday, people miss stumbling onto something totally different)

25. build for the housing and rootlessness problem (people can't afford to settle down, and the whole idea of a stable home base is up for grabs)

26. build for anti marketing (the slickest, most polished websites now look like AI slop or a scam, sometimes a plain text page from 1998 converts better because it feels like a real person built it)

27. build for agents that sit on hold for you (canceling a gym membership, fighting a medical bill, haggling with your internet provider, aint nobody got time for that)

28. build for software you actually own (people are exhausted from renting 30 different subscriptions every month, pay once and run it on your own machine is a massive wedge)

29. build for stuff that only works locally. The internet feels like one giant mall where every city has the exact same coffee shops and trends. Things that refuse to scale are suddenly cool again.

30. build for the 90% automated, 10% human sign-off model (clients don't actually care if AI did the heavy lifting, they just want one real expert to check the work and put their name on it)

31. build for infinite creative testing. Some brands are lighting money on fire on Meta because their ads die in 10 days. Build an automated pipeline that pumps out 100 fresh UGC and static ad variations a week based on what's actually converting in their ad account.

32. build for cold outreach that doesn't look like cold outreach. Mass blasting 50,000 people with "Hope this finds you well" is dead lol. Build an agent that watches for one specific trigger like a new VP hire or a broken checkout page, builds a custom teardown on the fly, and sends it before a human SDR even wakes up.

33. build for programmatic free tools instead of blog posts. Spin up 200 tiny, hyper-specific calculators, little apps and templates for one niche, rank them, and turn the traffic straight into conversions.

34. build for the food and toxin awakening (people are finally waking up to ultra processed food, microplastics, and why everyone feels sick and tired all the time)

35. build for the death of third places (there is almost nowhere left to just hang out without spending $50, which is why run clubs, saunas, and neighborhood clubs are blowing up)

36. build for people who can't retire at 65. Either they can't afford it or they're going to live to 95 and don't want to spend 30 years watching TV. The second act"market is huge.

37. build for the "undo" button for agents. Giving an AI access to your inbox, calendar, or bank account is still terrifying. Whoever makes it safe to let go of the wheel wins.

38. build for the sports betting and day trading hangover (a whole generation of young people are addicted to gambling on their phones and blowing up their bank accounts)

39. build for the death of the attention span. Smart adults can't even sit through a movie without checking their phone or finish a book anymore, and they're starting to hate themselves for it.

40. build for keeping marriages alive. Couples are stretched thin with work, kids, and money, and traditional therapy is $250 an hour with a waitlist. Anything that actually saves relationships is priceless.

41. build for people who don't own anything anymore. You rent your apartment, lease your car, stream your music, and subscribe to your software. Anything that helps regular people actually own an asset again wins.

KEEP BUILDING
